title: Launch Equipment Test Facility (LETF) Vehicle Motion Simulator (VMS) Hydraulic System Failure Resulted in $500K in Electrical System Damage.
categories: Engineering Design; Safety and Mission Assurance; Systems Engineering and Analysis; Accident Investigation; Facilities; Industrial Operations; Mishap Reporting; Safety & Mission Assurance; Test Facility; Early requirements and standards definition; Maintenance; Quality; Engineering design and project processes and standards

sections.abstract:
On July 27, 2023, an incident occurred at the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) Launch Equipment Test Facility (LETF) Vehicle Motion Simulator (VMS). While pressurizing the LETF hydraulic pumps to supply hydraulic fluid to VMS-2 (to reposition it for Exploration Upper Stage Umbilical preparations), a NOSHOK pressure gauge in the LETF Pump House ruptured at 9:48 AM. The gauge failed at the normal operating pressure of 3,000 pounds per square inch gauge, resulting in approximately 75 gallons of hydraulic fluid (Mobil Dynamo, Turbine, Engine (DTE)-25) spraying throughout the Pump House.

No personnel were injured. However, the incident resulted in approximately $500,000 in replacement costs for damaged electrical equipment. The mission or launch schedule was not impacted.

The Mishap Investigation Team (MIT) determined that the damage resulted from the combination of:

- A failed hydraulic analog pressure gauge, caused by inadequate solder adhesion between the gauge bourdon tube and socket.

- High-value electronic equipment enclosures near the oil spray, which had top-entered conduit feeder assembly fittings that were not adequately sealed or protected, allowing oil to enter the electrical enclosures.
sections.driving_event: During hydraulic system pressurization for LETF operations, a NOSHOK pressure gauge ruptured while operating at normal pressures. This resulted in approximately 75 gallons of hydraulic fluid being sprayed throughout the pump house. The oil intrusion damaged various pieces of electrical equipment, costing approximately $500,000 in damages. A full mishap investigation was conducted, and the resulting report was documented in the NASA Mishap Information System (NMIS) under tracking number #23-100895.
sections.lesson_learned:
1. NASA Advisory Notice NA-KSC-2024-002 was created and released to notify other NASA Centers of the NOSHOK gauge failure. The notice was released through NANADARTS.

2. The colocation of high dollar value electrical equipment and the high-pressure hydraulic system pumps revealed that KSC did not have requirements to assess worst-case consequences from fluid leaks.

- KSC updated design requirements documentation to assess fluid systems designs for the potential to damage adjacent high value equipment (HVE) due to worst-case catastrophic fluid system ruptures or leaks.

1. Employees could not see inside pump house during operation and therfore did not easily discover the leak to shut the system down.

- Cameras were installed inside of the pump house to allow facility employees real-time visual access to the conditions inside of the pump house.

- Installation of a shunt trip was also performed to enable a quick shutdown of the system remotely if an off- nominal condition is detected.

1. Other same model gauges on the system were inspected and found to be in a degareded condition. Gauges were found with corrosion to their inside housing, complete loss of gauge glycerin, a bent pointer, and missing or embedded plugs.

- Updated pressure system preventative maintenance documented procedures and training to include looking for common signs of wear and damage on pressure gauges.
sections.recommendation:
1. Review NASA Advisory Notice NA-KSC-2024-002 and take action if needed.

2. Apply lessons learned in this mishap event to like systems and facilities that may be present at your Center/site.

# [NASA LLIS #34202] Launch Equipment Test Facility (LETF) Vehicle Motion Simulator (VMS) Hydraulic System Failure Resulted in $500K in Electrical System Damage.
- **Date:** 2025-02-24
- **Organization:** Kennedy Space Center (KSC)
- **Categories:** Engineering Design; Safety and Mission Assurance; Systems Engineering and Analysis; Accident Investigation; Facilities; Industrial Operations; Mishap Reporting; Safety & Mission Assurance; Test Facility; Early requirements and standards definition; Maintenance; Quality; Engineering design and project processes and standards
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/34202

## Abstract
On July 27, 2023, an incident occurred at the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) Launch Equipment Test Facility (LETF) Vehicle Motion Simulator (VMS). While pressurizing the LETF hydraulic pumps to supply hydraulic fluid to VMS-2 (to reposition it for Exploration Upper Stage Umbilical preparations), a NOSHOK pressure gauge in the LETF Pump House ruptured at 9:48 AM. The gauge failed at the normal operating pressure of 3,000 pounds per square inch gauge, resulting in approximately 75 gallons of hydraulic fluid (Mobil Dynamo, Turbine, Engine (DTE)-25) spraying throughout the Pump House.

No personnel were injured. However, the incident resulted in approximately $500,000 in replacement costs for damaged electrical equipment. The mission or launch schedule was not impacted.

The Mishap Investigation Team (MIT) determined that the damage resulted from the combination of:

- A failed hydraulic analog pressure gauge, caused by inadequate solder adhesion between the gauge bourdon tube and socket.

- High-value electronic equipment enclosures near the oil spray, which had top-entered conduit feeder assembly fittings that were not adequately sealed or protected, allowing oil to enter the electrical enclosures.

## Driving Event / Background
During hydraulic system pressurization for LETF operations, a NOSHOK pressure gauge ruptured while operating at normal pressures. This resulted in approximately 75 gallons of hydraulic fluid being sprayed throughout the pump house. The oil intrusion damaged various pieces of electrical equipment, costing approximately $500,000 in damages. A full mishap investigation was conducted, and the resulting report was documented in the NASA Mishap Information System (NMIS) under tracking number #23-100895.

## Lesson Learned
1. NASA Advisory Notice NA-KSC-2024-002 was created and released to notify other NASA Centers of the NOSHOK gauge failure. The notice was released through NANADARTS.

2. The colocation of high dollar value electrical equipment and the high-pressure hydraulic system pumps revealed that KSC did not have requirements to assess worst-case consequences from fluid leaks.

- KSC updated design requirements documentation to assess fluid systems designs for the potential to damage adjacent high value equipment (HVE) due to worst-case catastrophic fluid system ruptures or leaks.

1. Employees could not see inside pump house during operation and therfore did not easily discover the leak to shut the system down.

- Cameras were installed inside of the pump house to allow facility employees real-time visual access to the conditions inside of the pump house.

- Installation of a shunt trip was also performed to enable a quick shutdown of the system remotely if an off- nominal condition is detected.

1. Other same model gauges on the system were inspected and found to be in a degareded condition. Gauges were found with corrosion to their inside housing, complete loss of gauge glycerin, a bent pointer, and missing or embedded plugs.

- Updated pressure system preventative maintenance documented procedures and training to include looking for common signs of wear and damage on pressure gauges.

## Recommendation
1. Review NASA Advisory Notice NA-KSC-2024-002 and take action if needed.

2. Apply lessons learned in this mishap event to like systems and facilities that may be present at your Center/site.

title: Displacement of E-1 High Pressure Liquid Hydrogen Vent Line to Flare Stack
categories: Engineering Design; Mission Operations and Ground Support Systems; Cryogenic Systems; Energetic Materials - Explosive / Propellant / Pyrotechnic; Facilities; Ground Operations; Pressure Vessels; Test Facility; Advanced planning of safety systems; Configuration Change Control
categories_list: Mission Operations and Ground Support Systems

sections.abstract: On the morning of Monday September 25, 2023, a drive-by inspection of the E1 liquid hydrogen (LH) flare stack was performed before typical test activities revealing a detached rain shield on the vent line. Upon further inspection that morning, the vent piping was observed to be displaced north up to 36 inches, had buckling damage on the 42” Expandable Joint (EJ) assembly, damage to multiple supports, and impact damage of the 30” elbow just downstream of the 30” EJ assembly.
sections.driving_event: The damage to the vent line is believed to have occurred during Thrust Chamber Assembly ( TCA) testing on Thursday, September 21, during the first test of the day. The fuel systems being used for TCA testing are connected to the Low Pressure (LP) and High Pressure (HP) vent systems and are being used in Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) service. The Cell 3 interface bleed valve that discharges to the HP LH Vent system was inadvertently left at 100% open during the chill-in process for longer than the typical amount of time. Since this valve is usually at a lower set point or intermittently closed during the chill-in process, more than the typical amount of LNG flowed into the vent line as pre-test procedures continued as normal.
sections.lesson_learned:
The root causes of this Undesired Outcome (UO) are identified as follows: the project design processes did not identify the vent system for additional evaluation, the Process Hazard Analysis (PHA) did not identify the hazard, and there was complacency related to the vent line.

The design process looked at the adequacy of the Run Tank and connected run line piping, and the HP Flare Stack for LNG service, but it did not evaluate the vent piping between the run system and the Flare Stack. During the safety review of the design, which has multiple aspects, the hazard related to liquid and the increased loads was not identified. Finally, the complacency related to the vent line developed over time. The vent line was not maintained or inspected between tests or on a regular basis. Also, the system identity includes LH, so liquid in the system was not seen as an issue. Anecdotally, LH has been seen discharging from the flare stack, so system integrity was assumed to be adequate for current test operations.

Contributing factors for the failure are related to the inadequacy of the HP LH Vent System for LNG. Originally, the vent system was design for hydrogen service, where the worst-case loads were from venting of the HP LH Run tank at maximum pressure. LNG has a density much greater than gaseous hydrogen, so produces much higher momentum loads on the support structure when moved at similar velocities. More capable support structure would have helped but likely not prevented the UO. Lastly, had the time between the vent line being overflown with LNG and test been longer, the vent line would have warmed up enough to vaporize all the liquid in the northern section that was damaged.

Additionally, the HP vent line was overflown with LNG during chill-in because the operator left the bleed valve 100% open for longer than intended. This action was not constrained, and at the time, not seen as an issue. If liquid had been identified as an issue, the Detailed Operating Procedures ( DOP) would have likely identified constraints for chill-in procedure. Moreover, if the Cell 3 bleed had not been connected to the HP LH Vent System, this UO would have been prevented. Using the HP Vent system for disposal of ambient cryogenic propellants, even liquid hydrogen, is ill-advised.
sections.recommendation: Disciplined configuration control practices are vital to ensure that facility systems are built and maintained to the specified design. It is important to consider all the differences between the commodity used and how it will affect the entire system. Once these effects are known, they need to be clearly understood by operators and documented. Operators and technicians need to understand the limits of the system for when they need to adjust procedure for mission success. This can be difficult when encountering a failure of imagination. Additionally, when changing configuration, all individual systems must be analyzed even when a system is known to be robust.

# [NASA LLIS #33101] Displacement of E-1 High Pressure Liquid Hydrogen Vent Line to Flare Stack
- **Date:** 2023-09-21
- **Organization:** Stennis Space Center (SSC)
- **Categories:** Engineering Design; Mission Operations and Ground Support Systems; Cryogenic Systems; Energetic Materials - Explosive / Propellant / Pyrotechnic; Facilities; Ground Operations; Pressure Vessels; Test Facility; Advanced planning of safety systems; Configuration Change Control
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/33101

## Abstract
On the morning of Monday September 25, 2023, a drive-by inspection of the E1 liquid hydrogen (LH) flare stack was performed before typical test activities revealing a detached rain shield on the vent line. Upon further inspection that morning, the vent piping was observed to be displaced north up to 36 inches, had buckling damage on the 42” Expandable Joint (EJ) assembly, damage to multiple supports, and impact damage of the 30” elbow just downstream of the 30” EJ assembly.

## Driving Event / Background
The damage to the vent line is believed to have occurred during Thrust Chamber Assembly ( TCA) testing on Thursday, September 21, during the first test of the day. The fuel systems being used for TCA testing are connected to the Low Pressure (LP) and High Pressure (HP) vent systems and are being used in Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) service. The Cell 3 interface bleed valve that discharges to the HP LH Vent system was inadvertently left at 100% open during the chill-in process for longer than the typical amount of time. Since this valve is usually at a lower set point or intermittently closed during the chill-in process, more than the typical amount of LNG flowed into the vent line as pre-test procedures continued as normal.

## Lesson Learned
The root causes of this Undesired Outcome (UO) are identified as follows: the project design processes did not identify the vent system for additional evaluation, the Process Hazard Analysis (PHA) did not identify the hazard, and there was complacency related to the vent line.

The design process looked at the adequacy of the Run Tank and connected run line piping, and the HP Flare Stack for LNG service, but it did not evaluate the vent piping between the run system and the Flare Stack. During the safety review of the design, which has multiple aspects, the hazard related to liquid and the increased loads was not identified. Finally, the complacency related to the vent line developed over time. The vent line was not maintained or inspected between tests or on a regular basis. Also, the system identity includes LH, so liquid in the system was not seen as an issue. Anecdotally, LH has been seen discharging from the flare stack, so system integrity was assumed to be adequate for current test operations.

Contributing factors for the failure are related to the inadequacy of the HP LH Vent System for LNG. Originally, the vent system was design for hydrogen service, where the worst-case loads were from venting of the HP LH Run tank at maximum pressure. LNG has a density much greater than gaseous hydrogen, so produces much higher momentum loads on the support structure when moved at similar velocities. More capable support structure would have helped but likely not prevented the UO. Lastly, had the time between the vent line being overflown with LNG and test been longer, the vent line would have warmed up enough to vaporize all the liquid in the northern section that was damaged.

Additionally, the HP vent line was overflown with LNG during chill-in because the operator left the bleed valve 100% open for longer than intended. This action was not constrained, and at the time, not seen as an issue. If liquid had been identified as an issue, the Detailed Operating Procedures ( DOP) would have likely identified constraints for chill-in procedure. Moreover, if the Cell 3 bleed had not been connected to the HP LH Vent System, this UO would have been prevented. Using the HP Vent system for disposal of ambient cryogenic propellants, even liquid hydrogen, is ill-advised.

## Recommendation
Disciplined configuration control practices are vital to ensure that facility systems are built and maintained to the specified design. It is important to consider all the differences between the commodity used and how it will affect the entire system. Once these effects are known, they need to be clearly understood by operators and documented. Operators and technicians need to understand the limits of the system for when they need to adjust procedure for mission success. This can be difficult when encountering a failure of imagination. Additionally, when changing configuration, all individual systems must be analyzed even when a system is known to be robust.

title: Improved Operations and Backlog Management of NANADARTS at GRC
categories: Safety and Mission Assurance; Administration / Organization

sections.abstract: NASA Advisories, Notices and Alerts Distribution and Response Tracking System (NANADARTS) is the system that makes Government-Industry Data Exchange Program (GIDEP) Notices, NASA Advisories, and other similar documents available to the entire NASA workforce and also serves as the agency's official tool for closed loop reporting of these documents per NPR 8735.1. The incident under discussion for this “lessons learned” is the accumulation of a massive backlog of NANADARTS documents which was comprised of documents that went undistributed by center coordinators and documents that went unevaluated by required responders. This accumulation took place over a three-year period, and peaked in the year 2021, with a total backlog of several thousand documents.
sections.driving_event:
Per NPR 8735.1, NASA programs and projects must implement closed-loop reporting via NANADARTS whenever a GIDEP notice or NASA advisory may impact “critical work” as defined in NPD 8730.5. Therefore, all programs or projects that perform critical work must participate.

NASA has an agency GIDEP/NANADARTS coordinator, and each center has two center GIDEP/NANADARTS coordinators. The agency GIDEP/NANADARTS coordinator and their team are responsible for extracting any new NASA-relevant GIDEP notices from GIDEP, and along with any newly released NASA Advisories, distributing these via the NANADARTS website to each of the center GIDEP/NANADARTS coordinators. The center coordinators are responsible for distributing these, again via NANADARTS, to the participating programs and projects. These programs and projects will have a dedicated required responder who is responsible for receiving and evaluating these GIDEP notices and NASA advisories via NANADARTS. These documents are evaluated for usage by the required responders within the NANADARTS system and this information is then reported out to the agency.

Unfortunately, due to the causes described below, and not necessarily the fault of any one person, unsent and unanswered documents began accumulating both on the coordinators’ end, and the required responders’ end, which ultimately led to a dangerously large backlog.

1. Distribution of documents from the agency coordinator to the center coordinators is irregular. Sometimes a hundred new documents may be sent from the agency coordinator to the center coordinators in a day. Sometimes weeks will go by with zero new documents. This is not necessarily the fault of anyone. This is determined by external factors – mainly the rate at which new GIDEP notices have been submitted to GIDEP by other agencies and companies, and how many of those are relevant to NASA. This has the effect of making it difficult both for center coordinators and required responders to develop a regular routine.

2. The center coordinators at GRC do not have any assigned time to perform NANADARTS duties, and there exists no WBS, which leads to assigned work taking precedence over NANADARTS.

3. Center-wide there has been a history of inadequate awareness levels and somewhat low priority given to NANADARTS activities. For example, most GRC employees have never heard of NANADARTS and are unaware of how it relates to GIDEP, nor does there exist much familiarity with either the NPR or GRC work instruction that discusses it. Also, it was often not well-known across the center which projects needed to participate, how to participate, why it’s important, and what would be the potential consequences of not participating. Consequently, NANADARTS responsibilities in the past have often been given very low priority.

This significant backlog was noted as a major finding in an external audit.
sections.lesson_learned:
Several steps were taken to successfully eliminate the backlog:

1. As a result of the external audit finding, center coordinators, branch chiefs, and upper management decided on giving the NANADARTS process a higher priority and greater visibility by having center coordinators report status updates of backlog counts at the monthly Safety & Mission Assurance Management Board meetings. Management from across the center attends this meeting and was made aware of the seriousness of this issue through these out-briefs. This action continued until the backlog was eliminated.

2. To deal with the irregular pacing of incoming alerts and notices, to increase communication between everyone involved, and to promote a greater sense of importance to this task, center coordinators developed a more regular routine for the benefit of both themselves and the required responders. Center coordinators did this by utilizing NANADARTS user tools to compile backlog counts at the start of every month, and then emailing these numbers as monthly status updates to each required responder and their project manager. The required responders and Project Managers were also reminded that these backlog counts were being reported up the chain at the monthly S&MA Management Board meetings, as described above.

3. Center coordinators increased awareness of the NANADARTS process:

a. Center coordinators gave presentations to individual codes on the NANADARTS process so that the Program/Project Managers could better understand the process, the importance of it, and to determine whether their program or project should be participating.

b. Center coordinators were able to add a link to the NANADARTS website on GRC’s one-stop-shop front page, “Inside Glenn,” under the “Employee Tools” dropdown. (https://nasa.sharepoint.com/sites/grc)

c. Center coordinators hosted a booth for GIDEP/NANADARTS activities at GRC’s annual Safety Day and will continue to do so at future safety days.

4. GRC center coordinators reached out to other center’s coordinators for guidance:

a. Other center’s coordinators provided guidance on how they conducted NANADARTS training to required responders and project managers. The GRC center coordinators incorporated some of the other centers’ training documentation into their own to improve their training process. Once GRC’s training materials were updated, training sessions were held with all required responders and their project managers.

b. Other center’s coordinators also provided their centers’ work instructions on NANADARTS. The GRC center coordinators took guidance from these documents and published a new revision of the center’s work instruction offering finer details and more direction.

5. Center coordinators invited all other NASA center coordinators to attend a face-to-face event at GRC to discuss other ways to improve how NANADARTS is implemented both center-wide and agency-wide.
sections.recommendation:
1. There should be center-wide awareness of NANADARTS. Programs and projects should be aware of whether they should be participating, how they participate, why it’s important, and what the potential consequences are of not participating.

2. NANADARTS documents should be distributed by the center coordinators on a regular basis to the appropriate required responders. Then, these documents should be responded to in a timely manner by those required responders

Additional steps that could be taken:

- The center coordinators at GRC do not have any assigned time to perform NANADARTS duties, and there exists no WBS, which leads to assigned work taking precedence over NANADARTS.

- Additionally, coordinators are having to charge time spent on NANADARTS activities to their projects. Most other NASA centers have funding for their center coordinators, while GRC does not.

title: Hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) and Hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFC) Fire Suppressants Exacerbate Fires in Space Vehicles and Require Extended Dwell Time to Achieve Extinguishment
categories: Fire Protection; Flight Equipment; Crew Survival Systems

sections.abstract:
The effectiveness of HFC-227ea (FM200), a common fire suppressant, was evaluated for extinguishing fires involving materials relevant to spacecraft, such as P213 tape and cotton. Tests were conducted in simulated spacecraft environments with oxygen concentrations of 20.9% and 21.4% (balance nitrogen) and suppressant concentrations from 3 vol% to 30 vol% (terrestrial fires are reportedly effectively suppressed at 6.8 vol%). The burn rate of the materials and dwell time (the time required for the suppressant to fully extinguish the fire) were measured. Results showed:

1. The amount of HFC-227ea needed to extinguish spacecraft materials was significantly higher than the concentration (6.8%) considered effective for terrestrial fires.

2. Suppression required a dwell time of nearly 30 seconds.

3. Materials exposed to insufficient concentrations of the suppressant burned faster than the same materials burning with no suppressant at all.

Literature reviews indicate all HFC suppressants exhibit this phenomenon due to their chemical properties. These findings demonstrate a significant hazard associated with HFC suppressants in spacecraft.
sections.driving_event: After flammable materials were identified in human-rated spacecraft, an effort was undertaken to evaluate the effectiveness of the fire suppression system on the materials of concern. The vehicle design used a commercial-off-the-shelf PFE containing HFC-227ea. Testing of the suppressant with the materials of concern revealed the described issues.
sections.lesson_learned: Hydrofluorocarbon fire suppressants increase the burn rate of solid materials, relative to the burn rate with no suppressant present, until extinguishment is achieved and require extended dwell time due to their inherent chemistry and extinguishment mechanism.
sections.recommendation: HFC and HCFC suppressants should not be used in spacecraft.

# [NASA LLIS #34301] Hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) and Hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFC) Fire Suppressants Exacerbate Fires in Space Vehicles and Require Extended Dwell Time to Achieve Extinguishment
- **Date:** 2023-03-31
- **Organization:** NASA (NESC)
- **Categories:** Fire Protection; Flight Equipment; Crew Survival Systems
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/34301

## Abstract
The effectiveness of HFC-227ea (FM200), a common fire suppressant, was evaluated for extinguishing fires involving materials relevant to spacecraft, such as P213 tape and cotton. Tests were conducted in simulated spacecraft environments with oxygen concentrations of 20.9% and 21.4% (balance nitrogen) and suppressant concentrations from 3 vol% to 30 vol% (terrestrial fires are reportedly effectively suppressed at 6.8 vol%). The burn rate of the materials and dwell time (the time required for the suppressant to fully extinguish the fire) were measured. Results showed:

1. The amount of HFC-227ea needed to extinguish spacecraft materials was significantly higher than the concentration (6.8%) considered effective for terrestrial fires.

2. Suppression required a dwell time of nearly 30 seconds.

3. Materials exposed to insufficient concentrations of the suppressant burned faster than the same materials burning with no suppressant at all.

Literature reviews indicate all HFC suppressants exhibit this phenomenon due to their chemical properties. These findings demonstrate a significant hazard associated with HFC suppressants in spacecraft.

## Driving Event / Background
After flammable materials were identified in human-rated spacecraft, an effort was undertaken to evaluate the effectiveness of the fire suppression system on the materials of concern. The vehicle design used a commercial-off-the-shelf PFE containing HFC-227ea. Testing of the suppressant with the materials of concern revealed the described issues.

## Lesson Learned
Hydrofluorocarbon fire suppressants increase the burn rate of solid materials, relative to the burn rate with no suppressant present, until extinguishment is achieved and require extended dwell time due to their inherent chemistry and extinguishment mechanism.

## Recommendation
HFC and HCFC suppressants should not be used in spacecraft.

# [NASA LLIS #33301] Chilled Water Line Failure Under Facility Concrete Slab Resulted In Over $1.5M In Facility Damages
- **Date:** 2022-12-22
- **Organization:** Kennedy Space Center (KSC)
- **Categories:** Engineering Design; Safety and Mission Assurance; Accident Investigation; Facilities; Acquisition / procurement strategy and planning; Early requirements and standards definition; Maintenance; Engineering design and project processes and standards
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/33301

## Abstract
At the Kennedy Space Center, the Operations Support Building 1 (OSB 1) had an 8-inch PVC chilled water return pipe catastrophically fail under the facility while operating within the manufacturers allowable pressure rating. A failure analysis of the pipe concluded the pipe elbow was improperly glued together when it was originally installed 40 years ago. In order to prevent a reoccurrence, it is recommended PVC pipe not be used either outside or under facilities for chilled water systems. Allowable other materials are either steel, polypropylene or copper pipe.

## Driving Event / Background
The Kennedy Space Center Operations Support Building (OSB) 1 experienced a catastrophic failure of the PVC chilled water return line which ruptured the concrete floors in the southwest corner of the building and flooded a portion of the first floor. The chilled water campus loop had been leaking for years and multiple attempts to find the source of the leak were not successful, because the source of the leak was an elbow under the facility. Personnel in the damaged area of the facility evacuated. The catastrophic failure resulted in a chilled water plant shutdown due to water loss in the system. This resulted in a loss of cooling to all the facilities that are supplied by the chilled water plant including the Launch Control Center and other essential buildings. A Mishap Investigation Team documented the findings in NMIS Case Number: 22-101302.

## Lesson Learned
Chilled water pipe should not be routed under facilities because it can't be inspected, and long term, is subject to stresses induced from settling foundations and shifting soils.

## Recommendation
PVC should not be used for chilled water piping either outside, inside or under facilities.

1. Do not allow the use of PVC piping for chilled water lines inside or outside facilities.

2. Do not allow chilled water piping to be routed under floors/concrete inside facilities.

SpecsIntact Master specification 33 61 14 section 2.2.3 and 2.2.4 currently allows for Plastic Reinforced Thermosetting Resin (RTR) and PVC piping in chilled water systems outside facilities. SpecsIntact Master specification 23 64 26 section 1.7.3 Accessibility requires pipes be accessible inside facilities. A clarifying statement is chilled water pipe should not be routed under facilities because it can't be inspected, and long term, is subject to stresses induced from settling foundations and shifting soils.

title: Controlling Triboelectrification Effects on Spacecraft Ethernet Cabling

sections.abstract: Triboelectric charging of a spacecraft and launch vehicles on ascent may occur due to the process of contact and separation between the vehicle skin and aerosols, dust, ice, water droplets, smoke, and other particulates encountered in the flight path. Depending on characteristics at the atomic and molecular levels of the vehicle skin’s surface and the substances and particulates encountered, electrical charge will transfer between the vehicle and the encountered substances, resulting in an accumulation of electrical charge on the vehicle skin. If the vehicle skin is conductive and electrically bonded such that in its entirety it presents an equipotential surface, then the accumulated electrical charge will spread in a nearly uniform manner leaving all regions with a nearly equal potential with respect to each other and the surrounding environment. Regions that are not electrically bonded as described, or surfaces that have resistivity values, can reach different potentials than the surrounding surfaces. When this happens, the differing potentials may grow to very large magnitudes, leading to electrostatic discharge events between the regions. As the vehicle rises in altitude, the breakdown potential between these regions of differing potential decreases commensurate with decreases in atmospheric density and pressure. If the potential differences between surfaces of the vehicle become equal to or exceed the breakdown potential, one or more discharge events may occur, each of them generating voltage and current transients that can easily damage or interfere with the designed operation of on-board electrical, avionic, and communications and navigation systems. This lesson learned discusses an in-flight anomaly caused by triboelectric discharge events and exacerbated by the lack of adequate cable shielding that affected flight computer communication links. Also discussed are mitigations to prevent this occurrence.
sections.driving_event: On multiple flights, disruption of multiple launch vehicle Ethernet communication links occurred during ascent at an altitude of between 10 km and 15 km. Three redundant Ethernet links used to communicate from the spacecraft to the launch vehicle all detected multiple false carriers. An Ethernet false carrier indicates a corrupted idle symbol. Ethernet transmits idle symbols when data are not otherwise being transmitted to maintain synchronization between transmitters and receivers. False carriers tend to be extremely rare events since an Ethernet link typically exhibits a bit error rate on the order of 1 in 10 billion. Although false carriers do not necessarily result in a loss of Ethernet communication, they are an indicator of a degraded connection. Of particular concern was the common cause nature of the anomaly occurring nearly simultaneously on all three redundant Ethernet links.
sections.lesson_learned:
After modeling of atmospheric charging effects and laboratory electrostatic discharge (ESD) testing on flight-like harness and cable/connector assemblies, the most probable root cause was determined to be electrostatic discharges associated with the spacecraft’s triboelectric charging. Primary contributing factors were the colocation of the three Ethernet cable runs through two connectors near each other and inadequate cable shielding. It was observed the spacecraft did not use static dissipative paint on two missions, but one mission with the paint, which should have minimized potentials, also had false carriers.

During harness qualification, IEC 61000-4-2 ESD testing was conducted at Level 4 (8kv), but false carriers were not observed. In hindsight, it was noted that the following likely contributed to not detecting the vulnerability during testing:

1. The harness tested was not the same length as the flight harness. This is significant because the longer harness would be capable of coupling more energy from the radiated electric and magnetic fields associated with the impulse.

2. The connectors in the test harness used a different, more electrically conductive, alloy than the flight harness. This is significant because the more conductive alloy would present a lower impedance to the local equipotential reference and would thus act to reduce the magnitude of the threat waveform.

3. The ESD gun discharge was not injected at the connectors where the susceptibility was later observed and verified.
sections.recommendation:
1. For redundant systems, physical separation should be utilized to prevent a discharge event from affecting multiple harnesses or avionics systems.

2. Harness and connector shield integrity should be verified by ESD testing on a fully configured flight harness. Multiple test discharge locations should be tested including shield termination points and all connectors. Such testing should be performed on cables exposed to ESD sources, including triboelectrification effects and spacecraft plasma charging effects.

3. Transfer impedance measurements on assembled harnesses should be performed as a diagnostic assessment to ascertain the shield performance as a function of frequency. This testing is nondestructive and could therefore be considered for performance on a flight harness, rather than on a flight representative harness differing in length or construction from the actual flight articles. If the transfer impedance is known prior to assembly, or the level of shielding effectiveness required to demonstrate immunity is known, a test of the assembled harnesses could demonstrate a weakness in the assembled cabling.

4. Additionally, common mode conducted emissions and conducted and/or radiated susceptibility (CS and/or RS) testing should be performed during component certification to gain information pertaining to shield performance as a function of frequency not readily obtained via the ESD or transfer impedance testing. Results from these measurements, coupled with those from ESD testing and from transfer impedance testing, provide a relatively complete “picture” of shield performance, and provide the assurance that the shielding will perform as required during all phases of operation. Thus, the goal is to ensure the as-built harness shield performance is comparable with the shield performance of harnesses used during unit level conducted and radiated susceptibility testing. This could be done using shield transfer impedance measurements or other shield performance measurements.

5. Design approaches and techniques should be considered to improve harness and connector shielding effectiveness, including: [refs. 1 – 9] Double shielding the cable. “Double shielding” is an ambiguous term and may carry a different connotation to different organizations. Multiple factors can impact the “double shield” approach, including but not limited to: 1) the configuration of the shield (i.e., only braided shielding, only solid shielding, a combination of braid and solid shielding, one layer of shielding of either type, multiple shield layers of one or both types that are ohmically isolated from each other, multiple shield layers of one or both types that are ohmically connected at both ends, multiple shield layers of one or both types that are ohmically connected only at one end, etc.); 2) the percentage optical coverage of the shield (higher is better; typically > 85% is considered an acceptable minimum percentage coverage for braided cabling used in aerospace applications, whereas foil may be near 100% with the exception of possible leakage along the seam). Note that a braid shield normally provides good attenuation at “lower” frequencies (< 400 kHz to 500 kHz), while a foil shield is able to provide superior attenuation at “higher” frequencies (> 500 kHz); and 3) use of peripheral termination (no pigtails) of shields into cable and harness backshells with low resistance electrical bond magnitude, typically ≤ 2.5 mΩ per interface/joint in the shield to backshell stack-up. The use of pigtails for shield termination introduces impedance discontinuities into the shield circuit that can completely negate any capability of the cable shield to mitigate electromagnetic interference. The use of pigtail terminations is extremely poor practice, is ill-advised, and is strongly discouraged. Cable manufacturers of Cat 5e, Cat 6/6A, and Cat 8/8.1 Ethernet cables typically employ a foil layer over unshielded twisted pairs (single layer approach), while for shielded Cat 7/7A and Cat 8.2 Ethernet cables, a configuration using a braid shield layer over one or more foil-covered twisted shielded pairs is employed (double layer approach, by definition). Controlled impedance connectors and ethernet cables qualified to applicable current military and/or industry Ethernet cabling standards should be used. The use of Quadrax contacts in standard connectors or specialty connectors with controlled impedance contacts with a shielded interconnect is encouraged. Multiple vendors offer both connectors and cables for Ethernet applications, and some may also offer turnkey fabrication. Not all vendor products are the same, and the final choice of a cable/connector configuration should be carefully specified and assessed for performance in the intended application. Exercise care in maintenance of the twist of each twisted pair in the cable at the entry point into the connector. Almost without exception, Ethernet cable vendors employ twisted pairs in their products, and will specify a different number of twists per inch for each pair such that no two pairs in a cable have the same twist rate, or pitch rate. Pitch rates vary from as little as ½ twist per inch (TPI) to 7 TPI or greater, with the larger number of twists associated with lower crosstalk and higher data rates. Regardless of TPI for a given cable, according to TIA-568 and cabling best practices, wire pairs should not be untwisted more than 13 mm (~ ½ inch) for Cat 5e, Cat 6, and higher. Do not exceed the minimum bend radius of 8 times the outside diameter of the cable. Anything less affects the twist rate, reducing noise rejection. When installing long runs, be careful not to stretch the cable. This could alter the twist rate, again reducing noise rejections. Due to the high frequency of digital transmissions, the phenomenon of skin effect could occur. Be careful not to nick the copper wire. If the run is in a space that is used for air circulation, be sure to use plenum-rated Ethernet cabling. If Ethernet cabling is run in parallel with high-potential lines, it should be separated by at least 15 cm distance away, 30 cm is better. If Ethernet cabling must cross a high-voltage line, do so as close to a 90-degree angle as possible.

1. In general, assume triboelectric charging on vehicle surfaces will occur during ascent and possibly descent. Develop a mitigation strategy to manage this, which can be a multifaceted approach that may include but not be limited to: Design and placement of harnesses and avionics systems Charging models to characterize the expected environment Testing of flight systems to expected ESD environments Application of dissipative paints to the exterior of vehicle surfaces to minimize charging Use of and adherence to launch commit criteria to minimize charging

REFERENCES

[1] R. T. Milton, “Design Handbook Electromagnetic Compatibility,” Section 3.4, General Electric Company, 1963, National Technical Information Service Accession # N70-72903.

[2] “Electromagnetic Compatibility Principles and Practices,” Section 11.4.5, NASA Issuance Number NHB 5320.3, Apollo Documentation Number RA-016-001-1, Oct 1965.

[3] E. F. Vance, “Coupling to Shielded Cables,” John Wiley & Sons, Hoboken, New Jersey, 1978.

[4] J. Goedbloed, “Electromagnetic Compatibility,” Chapter 5, Prentice Hall International (UK) Ltd., Campus 400, Maylands Avenue, Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, UK, 1992.

[5] J. P. Mills, “Electromagnetic Interference,” Chapter 4, PTR Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, 1993.

[6] A. Tsaliovich, ”Shielding for Electromagnetic Compatibility,” Section 3.6, Van Nostrand Reinhold New York, NY 1995.

[7] K. L. Kaiser, “Electromagnetic Compatibility Handbook,” Chapter 18, CRC Press, Boca Raton, FL, 2004.

[8] C. R. Paul, “Introduction to Electromagnetic Compatibility,” 2ed, Section 9.7.5, John Wiley & Sons, Hoboken, New Jersey, 2006.

[9] H. W. Ott, “Electromagnetic Compatibility Engineering,” 2ed, Section 2.15.2.4, John Wiley & Sons, Hoboken, New Jersey, 2009.

# [NASA LLIS #32728] Joint Polar Satellite System-2 Verification Planning
- **Date:** 2022-07-28
- **Organization:** Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC)
- **Categories:** Program Management; Systems Engineering and Analysis; Communications between different offices and contractor personnel; Planning of requirements verification processes
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/32728

## Abstract
During the Joint Polar Satellite System-2 (JPSS-2) Environmental test program, engaging the engineering team's focus on the requirements sell-off was challenging. For effective progress, it was essential for the teams to maintain regular communication with both the vendors and the government team. Consistent dialogue enabled an organized and swift sell-off before shipping to the launch base and established a framework for the JPSS-3 and JPSS-4 missions to be proactive in their upcoming Pre-Ship reviews.

## Driving Event / Background
Pre-Ship review

## Lesson Learned
For verifications, the primary lesson learned is that continuous communication between the verification stakeholders needs to occur.

## Recommendation
Establish a process for regular meetings to address verifications, which should be maintained throughout the program's development.

title: E-1 Triethyl Aluminum-Triethyl Borane (TEA-TEB) System Contamination
categories: Integration and Testing; Configuration Management; Energetic Materials - Explosive / Propellant / Pyrotechnic; Test Facility; Ground support systems; Configuration Change Control

sections.abstract:
On June 28th, 2022, during post test inspections, test operations personnel noted that the E-1 Cell 2 Triethyl Aluminum-Triethyl Borane (TEA-TEB) injection supply tubing was warm to the touch. This indicated that there could have been a TEA-TEB reaction occurring inside the tubing. Personnel identified the source of air was coming from FireX Master Facility Panel (MFP) Station 6. No personal injury or facility damage was sustained.

Background

The FireX MFP Station 6 was originally designed and installed to service valve actuation of all stand FireX systems, and as such the system is branched and routed throughout the stand and all three E-1 test cell locations.

TEA-TEB is a pyrophoric liquid which ignites when exposed to air and water, and is often used as an ignition method for rocket testing. It is stable when stored and operated with dry and inert purges until ready to be injected into the rocket components for ignition.

The TEA-TEB storage system and run system had been installed for a previous test project in Cell 1 in 2016. The design tapped into a nearby GN system downstream from MFP Station 6 for the required GN purge and pressurization. At this time, MFP drawing and panel labeling was not changed to reflect the additional purpose of Station 6 for TEA-TEB purging.

Configuration Control of Inactive Systems

In preparation for inclement weather in September 2021, the FireX MFP supply was swapped from gaseous nitrogen to high pressure air (HPA) to conserve nitrogen usage at E-1 and had remained in this configuration ever since.

# [NASA LLIS #31401] E-1 Triethyl Aluminum-Triethyl Borane (TEA-TEB) System Contamination
- **Date:** 2022-06-28
- **Organization:** Stennis Space Center (SSC)
- **Categories:** Integration and Testing; Configuration Management; Energetic Materials - Explosive / Propellant / Pyrotechnic; Test Facility; Ground support systems; Configuration Change Control
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/31401

## Abstract
On June 28th, 2022, during post test inspections, test operations personnel noted that the E-1 Cell 2 Triethyl Aluminum-Triethyl Borane (TEA-TEB) injection supply tubing was warm to the touch. This indicated that there could have been a TEA-TEB reaction occurring inside the tubing. Personnel identified the source of air was coming from FireX Master Facility Panel (MFP) Station 6. No personal injury or facility damage was sustained.

Background

The FireX MFP Station 6 was originally designed and installed to service valve actuation of all stand FireX systems, and as such the system is branched and routed throughout the stand and all three E-1 test cell locations.

TEA-TEB is a pyrophoric liquid which ignites when exposed to air and water, and is often used as an ignition method for rocket testing. It is stable when stored and operated with dry and inert purges until ready to be injected into the rocket components for ignition.

The TEA-TEB storage system and run system had been installed for a previous test project in Cell 1 in 2016. The design tapped into a nearby GN system downstream from MFP Station 6 for the required GN purge and pressurization. At this time, MFP drawing and panel labeling was not changed to reflect the additional purpose of Station 6 for TEA-TEB purging.

Configuration Control of Inactive Systems

In preparation for inclement weather in September 2021, the FireX MFP supply was swapped from gaseous nitrogen to high pressure air (HPA) to conserve nitrogen usage at E-1 and had remained in this configuration ever since.

The TEA-TEB system was inactive at the time of the configuration change as the Cell 1 project had concluded and the upcoming Cell 2 project was still in the design/build phase.

For this new project, a new TEA-TEB run system was added to Cell 2 in 2022 and was designed to utilize the same TEA-TEB storage system and GN source as the Cell 1 system.

## Driving Event / Background
Root Cause In preparation for inclement weather in September 2021, the FireX MFP supply was swapped from gaseous nitrogen to high pressure air to conserve nitrogen usage at E1. The FireX MFP remained in HPA service post hurricane season to continue to conserve nitrogen usage. E-1 FireX Master Facility Panel Station 6 is used to purge the TEA-TEB. By using this purge/press system with the HPA supply, air was introduced into the TEA-TEB system.

Contributing Factors:

The Station 6 description did not state that Station 6 was serving as a purge to the TEA-TEB System. Test Operations made a time-critical decision to respond to a stressful situation due to limited deliveries of Liquid Nitrogen to the High-Pressure Gas Facility post Hurricane Ida. The implementation proceeded as a permanent change instead of a temporary change. This did not allow the Test Operations Team a chance to fully review the system configuration without the stress of limited GN and post major hurricane.

## Lesson Learned
Corrective Actions and Recommendations The air source was removed, and the MFP drawing was labeled for “GN service only” and to indicate that Station 6 supplies the TEA-TEB Cart Pressurization and Purge. These labels were also physically added to the MFP Station 6 panel for operators in the field. In addition, a label was added to the TEA-TEB cart door indicating that GN source pressure was routed from MFP Station 6. Ideally, the team would like to fabricate and install a separate and dedicated GN-only station exclusively for the TEA-TEB system.

Some other long term actions are being considered for further action. Infrared cameras could be utilized to detect thermal heating in TEA-TEB system tubing, enabling the test conductor to monitor system conditions prior to releasing personnel back to the test stand facility. This capability is already used in other areas, particularly on hydrogen systems.

The team is also exploring ways to mistake proof the design and configuration control processes, to use automated systems to identify and flag systems which have commodity restrictions. SEE ATTACHED DOCUMENT

## Recommendation
1. Ensure proper labeling of system source panels, and especially pay attention to restrictions of commodity sources to avoid unintentional contamination.

2. Always use processes which establish constraints or required verifications prior to reactivating systems which have been inactive for a period of time.

title: SharePoint Nintex Licensing
categories: Integration and Testing; Program Management; Systems Engineering and Analysis; Administration / Organization; Communication Systems; Information Technology / Systems; Configuration Change Control

sections.abstract:
KSC SharePoint 2019:

The Nintex Workflow/Forms license expired, causing no workflows to run during the downtime to get new licenses.
sections.driving_event: KSC recently upgraded from SharePoint 2016 (a web-based collaboration platform) to SharePoint 2019. A third party tool, Nintex Workflow used to automate business processes in SharePoint, only allowed for a 30 day migration license. All SharePoint sites were migrated in time. However, the migration license was not updated to the production license . When the migration license ran out, users were not able to use Nintex workflow or forms.
sections.lesson_learned: We learned that we need to improve our communication for license upgrades and plan the steps involved. It took almost 6 hours for the new licenses to be acquired.
sections.recommendation:
Corrective Action Plan:

- Improve our communication with vendors to ensure we have a thorough understanding of the license upgrade steps.

- Add a lessons learned to the SharePoint 2019 Upgrade Project and to the Knowledge Management Articles webpage for future reference.

- Scheduled a quarterly review of SharePoint licensing so the team and the NASA point of contact are aware of upcoming expirations.

KSC recently upgraded from SharePoint 2016 (a web-based collaboration platform) to SharePoint 2019. A third party tool, Nintex Workflow used to automate business processes in SharePoint, only allowed for a 30 day migration license. All SharePoint sites were migrated in time. title: AIAA/ANSI Standard S-120A-2015_R2019, Mass Properties Control for Space Systems, should be applied in context.
categories: Extra-Vehicular Activity; Transportation; Extra-Vehicular Activity/Mobility/Space Suits; Lander Systems; Robotics; Planetary Operations; Vehicle concepts; Engineering design and project processes and standards; Mission definition and planning
categories_list: Engineering design and project processes and standards

sections.abstract: Mass properties control is a critical aspect of space system development. American National Standards Institute/American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics (ANSI/AIAA) Standard S-120A and the International Society of Allied Weight Engineers (SAWE) RP A-3, Recommended Practice for Mass Properties Control for Space Systems [ref. 1], define the terminology and document common processes and approaches for managing mass of space systems. The lesson learned through the efforts of the Pressurized Rover (PR) Red Team Assessment, performed by the NASA Engineering and Safety Center in 2022, is that the standard has been developed and applies to space vehicles, upper stages, payloads, reentry vehicles, launch vehicles and ballistic vehicles. It does not specifically address space systems (e.g., rovers) that are operational on other surfaces, and it does not address associated hardware categories (e.g., suspension and drive train assemblies).
sections.driving_event: The overarching purpose of the NESC PR Red Team was to evaluate and assess the mass management activities of the potential PR providers, assess the mass growth allowances (MGA) provided by the concept developers, and apply system and subsystem expertise to the proposed approaches, with an eye toward expected mass impacts of those design approaches. The team set out to use the S-120A MGA table and soon found gaps in the hardware categories. For instance, although the standard’s table cites “mechanisms” as a hardware category, and there are mechanisms on the rover, there is no reference information for the suspension and drive train required for a roving vehicle.
sections.lesson_learned: In the early stages of the NESC PR Red Team’s assessing PR mass management approaches, it became apparent that, although the S-120A MGA standard table provided a variety of ranges in a variety of typical space system hardware categories, it was important to use them only as a framework. The team developed additional hardware categories to address the suspension and drivetrain of a rover space system and used the “mechanisms” hardware category as a starting point. The application of system-specific experience required 1) the development of different categories and adjusted approaches for this specific space system application, and 2) the development of a tailored MGA table that took into account different hardware categories or systems from the typical designs for which S-120A is applied.
sections.recommendation:
Space system developers should utilize the framework, concepts, and approaches outlined in S-120A and the recommended practices of SAWE RP A-3 as a guide , but tailor the MGA table for each system’s specific Concept of Operations and design.

Reference

1. International Society of Allied Weight Engineers (SAWE) RP A-3, Recommended Practice for Mass Properties Control for Space Systems. January 26, 2016.

full_text:
# [NASA LLIS #31801] AIAA/ANSI Standard S-120A-2015_R2019, Mass Properties Control for Space Systems, should be applied in context.
- **Date:** 2021-12-12
- **Organization:** NASA (NESC)
- **Categories:** Extra-Vehicular Activity; Transportation; Extra-Vehicular Activity/Mobility/Space Suits; Lander Systems; Robotics; Planetary Operations; Vehicle concepts; Engineering design and project processes and standards; Mission definition and planning
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/31801

## Abstract
Mass properties control is a critical aspect of space system development. American National Standards Institute/American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics (ANSI/AIAA) Standard S-120A and the International Society of Allied Weight Engineers (SAWE) RP A-3, Recommended Practice for Mass Properties Control for Space Systems [ref. 1], define the terminology and document common processes and approaches for managing mass of space systems. The lesson learned through the efforts of the Pressurized Rover (PR) Red Team Assessment, performed by the NASA Engineering and Safety Center in 2022, is that the standard has been developed and applies to space vehicles, upper stages, payloads, reentry vehicles, launch vehicles and ballistic vehicles. It does not specifically address space systems (e.g., rovers) that are operational on other surfaces, and it does not address associated hardware categories (e.g., suspension and drive train assemblies).

## Driving Event / Background
The overarching purpose of the NESC PR Red Team was to evaluate and assess the mass management activities of the potential PR providers, assess the mass growth allowances (MGA) provided by the concept developers, and apply system and subsystem expertise to the proposed approaches, with an eye toward expected mass impacts of those design approaches. The team set out to use the S-120A MGA table and soon found gaps in the hardware categories. For instance, although the standard’s table cites “mechanisms” as a hardware category, and there are mechanisms on the rover, there is no reference information for the suspension and drive train required for a roving vehicle.

## Lesson Learned
In the early stages of the NESC PR Red Team’s assessing PR mass management approaches, it became apparent that, although the S-120A MGA standard table provided a variety of ranges in a variety of typical space system hardware categories, it was important to use them only as a framework. The team developed additional hardware categories to address the suspension and drivetrain of a rover space system and used the “mechanisms” hardware category as a starting point. The application of system-specific experience required 1) the development of different categories and adjusted approaches for this specific space system application, and 2) the development of a tailored MGA table that took into account different hardware categories or systems from the typical designs for which S-120A is applied.

## Recommendation
Space system developers should utilize the framework, concepts, and approaches outlined in S-120A and the recommended practices of SAWE RP A-3 as a guide , but tailor the MGA table for each system’s specific Concept of Operations and design.

Reference

1. International Society of Allied Weight Engineers (SAWE) RP A-3, Recommended Practice for Mass Properties Control for Space Systems. January 26, 2016.

title: Failure Of Design Review Process To Adequately Validate Late-Stage Changes
categories: EEE Parts; Spacecraft and Spacecraft Instruments; Configuration control and data management; Contractor relationships; Configuration Change Control

sections.abstract: Late-stage design changes and insufficient engineering review, compounded by schedule pressure, led to a flight printed circuit board being damaged during component assembly. Heatsinks were added to two components after the initial drawing release but the changes were reviewed through a fast-track process and not the accepted Engineering Order process. The added heatsinks interfered with thermistors already installed on the electronic components, which were damaged when the heatsinks were torqued down. The assembly contractor tasked with installing the heatsinks suspected there were interference issues while developing work instructions but assumed a thorough design review had been conducted by NASA.
sections.driving_event:
Wildcat Processor Card (WPC) #3 was damaged during work at a NASA/GSFC contractor facility tasked with conformal coating, component staking, and installation of two heat sinks on the fully populated printed circuit board. The damage occurred when the heatsinks were installed and torqued on top of a Processor and Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA). The heatsinks and associated thermal material interfered with thermistors already installed on top of the two components. Both components were destroyed in the event, and WPC #3 was eventually downgraded to non-flight status after part replacement yielded additional concerns.

The requirement to add the heatsinks was determined after the initial drawing release for the WPC and was based on thermal analysis of the FPGA and Processor when operating at nominal power dissipations under hot operational conditions. Thermal-vacuum testing of engineering test unit cards showed positive thermal margin on the parts without the heatsinks, but they were added to the flight design as a precaution.

The addition of the heatsinks was communicated verbally and through emails, not through an official engineering change order process. The revisions were reviewed and approved in the project configuration management system using 2-dimensional drawings, but the interference between the heatsinks and thermistors on the two parts was not identified.

Members of the contractor engineering staff questioned the rationale of mounting the heatsinks in the manner they were being asked to implement and even held conversations with some members of management. But, due to the maturity of the flight board, everyone involved assumed that the WPC product development team had already calculated and approved the necessary clearances needed to attach the heat sinks without damaging the processors.
sections.lesson_learned:
- Tight schedules can adversely impact review processes and important decision making.

- All project personnel (civil servant & contractor) must be empowered to raise questions, express concerns, and point out anomalies.
sections.recommendation:
1. Schedule pressure should not be a reason to avoid formal engineering review processes, even for what are considered a minor change.

2. Project leadership should explicitly and continually express the need for everyone to bring concerns forward.

# [NASA LLIS #33502] Failure Of Design Review Process To Adequately Validate Late-Stage Changes
- **Date:** 2021-12-12
- **Organization:** Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC)
- **Categories:** EEE Parts; Spacecraft and Spacecraft Instruments; Configuration control and data management; Contractor relationships; Configuration Change Control
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/33502

## Abstract
Late-stage design changes and insufficient engineering review, compounded by schedule pressure, led to a flight printed circuit board being damaged during component assembly. Heatsinks were added to two components after the initial drawing release but the changes were reviewed through a fast-track process and not the accepted Engineering Order process. The added heatsinks interfered with thermistors already installed on the electronic components, which were damaged when the heatsinks were torqued down. The assembly contractor tasked with installing the heatsinks suspected there were interference issues while developing work instructions but assumed a thorough design review had been conducted by NASA.

## Driving Event / Background
Wildcat Processor Card (WPC) #3 was damaged during work at a NASA/GSFC contractor facility tasked with conformal coating, component staking, and installation of two heat sinks on the fully populated printed circuit board. The damage occurred when the heatsinks were installed and torqued on top of a Processor and Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA). The heatsinks and associated thermal material interfered with thermistors already installed on top of the two components. Both components were destroyed in the event, and WPC #3 was eventually downgraded to non-flight status after part replacement yielded additional concerns.

The requirement to add the heatsinks was determined after the initial drawing release for the WPC and was based on thermal analysis of the FPGA and Processor when operating at nominal power dissipations under hot operational conditions. Thermal-vacuum testing of engineering test unit cards showed positive thermal margin on the parts without the heatsinks, but they were added to the flight design as a precaution.

The addition of the heatsinks was communicated verbally and through emails, not through an official engineering change order process. The revisions were reviewed and approved in the project configuration management system using 2-dimensional drawings, but the interference between the heatsinks and thermistors on the two parts was not identified.

Members of the contractor engineering staff questioned the rationale of mounting the heatsinks in the manner they were being asked to implement and even held conversations with some members of management. But, due to the maturity of the flight board, everyone involved assumed that the WPC product development team had already calculated and approved the necessary clearances needed to attach the heat sinks without damaging the processors.

## Lesson Learned
- Tight schedules can adversely impact review processes and important decision making.

- All project personnel (civil servant & contractor) must be empowered to raise questions, express concerns, and point out anomalies.

## Recommendation
1. Schedule pressure should not be a reason to avoid formal engineering review processes, even for what are considered a minor change.

2. Project leadership should explicitly and continually express the need for everyone to bring concerns forward.

title: Button Battery Power Supply to Real Time Clock for the ISS Urine Processing Assembly (UPA) Technology Upgrades Purge Pump Separator Assembly (PPSA)
categories: Engineering Design; Integration and Testing; Manufacturing and Assembly; Computers; EEE Parts; Hardware; Payloads; Power; DDT/E

sections.abstract: Inspection of data obtained during the thermal cycle test showed that the serial Real-Time Clock (RTC) had reset itself during the hot restart. Investigation of the hardware design determined the most probable cause of the reset was due to an issue with the button battery holder or how the battery was staked into the holder. A corrective action was successfully implemented by removing the existing battery holder and replacing it with a surface mount battery that was staked directly to the board.
sections.driving_event:
A serial Real-Time Clock (DS1306) is used within an electronics box to provide an accurate time reading. The clock utilizes a button battery (CR1025) to keep track of time when the external power supply is off. The clock will reset if there is an interruption of this secondary power source while the main power is off.

Per the Environmental Acceptance Test plan, thermal cycle testing of the electronics box was done from 20°F to 140°F (-7°C to 60°C). While at the hot plateau, a hot restart of the box was performed by turning off the external power supply then turning it back on. In a nominal condition, during recycle of external power the RTC will utilize the power from the button battery to keep track of time.

After completion of the thermal cycle test, it was noted that the clock had reset during the hot restart. Investigation of the design determined that the battery holder design and/or how the button battery was staked with epoxy into the holder was the most probable cause. As shown in Figure 1, a BH401 coin cell battery holder was used to hold the battery. This holder has an open design for a battery to slide in and uses a spring-loaded positive lead to press the battery into the negative lead. The battery was additionally staked into the holder to prevent it from slipping out during vibration testing. It was determined during the investigation that staking the battery into the holder effectively over constrains the battery and may prevent the spring-loaded positive lead from pressing the battery into the negative terminal from thermal expansion effects over a large temperature range. A similar setup was recreated on an engineering unit; however, the fault did not occur at the hot plateau. This indicates that there may be variability in the battery holder, installation process, and tolerances (e.g. the epoxy staking) causing some builds work well while others do not, which is unacceptable in a flight application. Additionally, testing of the flight battery holder/battery once it was removed confirmed that a slight movement of the battery negative lead caused loss of power.

A fix was implemented by installing and staking a surface mount battery directly to the board. This is shown in Figure 2. The surface mount battery comes with a positive and negative lead spot welded to the battery. The updated design successfully passed thermal cycle testing.
sections.lesson_learned:
- A slip-in button cell battery holder was implemented in the design to easily replace the battery if needed. However, staking the battery down for the flight design effectively eliminates the ability to easily replace the battery and may result in loss of power over a large temperature range. Staking down a surface mount battery allows for a more robust permanent design. If replacement of the flight battery is needed for future applications, a glider battery holder where the battery snaps into place has been successfully used on other projects, see Figure 3.

- Due to difference in tolerances and processes between engineering and flight units, issues may occur in some units but not others.
sections.recommendation:
- If a COTS item is being modified to eliminate a design weakness, investigate if there are other COTS items that may not have that design weakness.

- Monitor for over constraints in spring-loaded designs.

- Review all data obtained from test, and not just what is listed in a test procedure to check. This includes reviewing data obtained late in the life cycle, for example during environmental acceptance testing, because there may be differences between hardware builds.

title: Considerations for Helium Environments
categories: Integration and Testing; Flight Equipment; Hardware; Launch Process; Parts; Materials; & Processes; Payloads; Research & Development; Test & Verification; Spacecraft and Spacecraft Instruments

sections.abstract: A helium purge detrimentally impacted the Navigation Doppler Lidar (NDL) on the Blue Origin New Shepherd NS-17 flight . Investigation revealed that helium permeation of an optical filter and the high thermal conductivity of helium was responsible for this failure. The specific properties of helium motivate the need to thoroughly test systems in any intended helium environments.
sections.driving_event:
The Navigation Doppler Lidar (NDL) is a laser-based sensor capable of providing precision velocity and altitude relative to three laser-illuminated spots. The NDL transmits three laser beams in fixed directions relative to each other. Signals from each beam provide platform velocity and range to the ground along the laser line of sight. Figure 1 shows a schematic of the NDL system.

Figure 1. Diagram of the Navigation Doppler Lidar (NDL)

The NDL failure on the Blue Origin New Shepherd NS-17 flight can be traced to a helium purge that occurred prior to launch. The purge reduced the optical filter temperature, resulting in a filter center frequency shift. The shift in the filter center frequency degraded the fiber amplifier input power, leading to a laser energization failure. Without laser energization, the system could not collect the desired velocity and range data.

After the flight failure, controlled tests were performed to confirm the impacts of helium on the functioning of NDL.

When the optical filter was purged with helium, nitrogen, and air in separate test environments, different effects were seen on the optical filter. Figure 2 shows the fiber amplifier input power in these different tests. The top left plot shows what happened during the NS 17 flight. The power decayed after the helium purge was initiated. The lower left plot shows the fiber amplifier input power maintaining its nominal power during a nominal power-on and a power-on with a nitrogen purge introduced into a chamber containing the optical filter. The top right plot shows different behavior after a helium purge is introduced into the chamber containing the optical filter. Here, there is significant power decay. Finally, the lower right plot contrasts the fiber amplifier input power with the filter located inside the chamber subjected to the helium purge (as in the top right plot) and with the optical filter located outside the chamber. The only instance of a fiber amplifier power drop occurred when the optical filter was exposed to helium. The tests demonstrate that it is the optical filter exposure to the helium purge that is responsible for the decay in the fiber amplifier power.
