# [NASA LLIS #32201] Considerations for Helium Environments
- **Date:** 2021-08-26
- **Organization:** Langley Research Center (LARC)
- **Categories:** Integration and Testing; Flight Equipment; Hardware; Launch Process; Parts; Materials; & Processes; Payloads; Research & Development; Test & Verification; Spacecraft and Spacecraft Instruments
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/32201

## Abstract
A helium purge detrimentally impacted the Navigation Doppler Lidar (NDL) on the Blue Origin New Shepherd NS-17 flight . Investigation revealed that helium permeation of an optical filter and the high thermal conductivity of helium was responsible for this failure. The specific properties of helium motivate the need to thoroughly test systems in any intended helium environments.

## Driving Event / Background
The Navigation Doppler Lidar (NDL) is a laser-based sensor capable of providing precision velocity and altitude relative to three laser-illuminated spots. The NDL transmits three laser beams in fixed directions relative to each other. Signals from each beam provide platform velocity and range to the ground along the laser line of sight. Figure 1 shows a schematic of the NDL system.

Figure 1. Diagram of the Navigation Doppler Lidar (NDL)

The NDL failure on the Blue Origin New Shepherd NS-17 flight can be traced to a helium purge that occurred prior to launch. The purge reduced the optical filter temperature, resulting in a filter center frequency shift. The shift in the filter center frequency degraded the fiber amplifier input power, leading to a laser energization failure. Without laser energization, the system could not collect the desired velocity and range data.

After the flight failure, controlled tests were performed to confirm the impacts of helium on the functioning of NDL.

When the optical filter was purged with helium, nitrogen, and air in separate test environments, different effects were seen on the optical filter. Figure 2 shows the fiber amplifier input power in these different tests. The top left plot shows what happened during the NS 17 flight. The power decayed after the helium purge was initiated. The lower left plot shows the fiber amplifier input power maintaining its nominal power during a nominal power-on and a power-on with a nitrogen purge introduced into a chamber containing the optical filter. The top right plot shows different behavior after a helium purge is introduced into the chamber containing the optical filter. Here, there is significant power decay. Finally, the lower right plot contrasts the fiber amplifier input power with the filter located inside the chamber subjected to the helium purge (as in the top right plot) and with the optical filter located outside the chamber. The only instance of a fiber amplifier power drop occurred when the optical filter was exposed to helium. The tests demonstrate that it is the optical filter exposure to the helium purge that is responsible for the decay in the fiber amplifier power.

Figure 2. Fiber Amplifier input power under numerous conditions.

These issues were caused by helium’s ability to permeate into the cavity of the optical filter combined with the high thermal conductivity of helium relative to air. When the helium purge occurred, helium was able to enter the optical filter cavity, greatly increasing the thermal conductivity of the resultant gas mixture in the cavity. The increased thermal conductivity of the gas mixture enhanced the rate at which heat could be transferred from the optical filter, and exceeded the ability of the heaters to maintain the set temperature. This result led to cooling in the optical filter and a subsequent shift in the filter center frequency, resulting in failed laser energization.

The NDL project was treated as a highly risk tolerant mission. The higher risk tolerance led to certain concessions in terms of testing and analysis during the development and assembly, integration and test. Exposure to helium was considered benign from a material compatibility perspective. Thus, during instrument development, the optical filter was tested in both air and vacuum, but not in a helium environment. Post-failure, elevated thermal conductivity representing the presence of helium was incorporated into the thermal analysis, and that analysis showed a possible reduction in average filter temperature sufficient to impact the bandpass frequency and produce a failure to energize. However, testing was required to fully support the analysis.

Helium’s relatively small molecular diameter coupled with its chemical inertness enhances its ability to penetrate many seals. In another helium-related failure, during the development of Hemispherical Resonator Gyroscopes (HRGs), a secondary vacuum cavity surrounding the primary cavity containing the HRG was added to bring the leak rate down to an acceptable level (David Rozelle, The Hemispherical Resonator Gyro: From Wineglass to the Planets , January 2009, Advances in the Astronautical Sciences 134:1157-1178). Helium permeation appears to have also been the culprit in the immobilization of hospital employee iPhones in 2018 after a helium leak occurred in an Illinois Hospital ( iPhones are Allergic to Helium , Kyle Wiens, October 30, 2018, IFIXIT; Helium temporarily bricks iPhones and Apple Watches in Chicago hospital, Android devices immune , Michael Potuck, October 31, 2018, 9TO5Mac).

## Lesson Learned
1. Helium has a higher thermal conductivity than air and therefore can affect the thermal stability of systems. Testing in air and in vacuum does not envelope the thermal environment in which helium may be present.

2. Helium’s small molecular size and chemical inertness enables it to permeate into instruments and devices exposed to helium. Seals that are not specifically designed to prevent helium intrusion are susceptible.

## Recommendation
- Helium has a higher thermal conductivity than air, this difference in thermal conductivity must be considered in system thermal analysis when applicable.

- Special seals may be required to prevent helium permeation into susceptible devices.

- If a mission exposes devices and/or instruments to helium, they should be screened and/or tested for helium susceptibilities. Generally speaking, systems should be tested in environments they will see through all mission phases. This recommendation goes hand in hand with NASA’s “Test as you fly, fly as you test” philosophy.

| Communication | Ensure Facility Managers are aware of scope and timeline Keep stakeholders updated and aware of progress Establish prime stakeholder meeting frequency Utilize Gantt chart where possible to project path and communicate with stakeholders |
| --- | --- |

| Project Requirements | Determine speed needed as a larger scope tends to take much longer to accomplish |
| Cost/ Finance | Determine need for Basis of Estimate from contractor and acquire Determine support costs for planning Ensure finance terms and review Points of Contact (POC)s are defined and followed |

sections.recommendation:
Organization

| Title | Driving Event | Lesson(s) Learned | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Determine full POC list as soon as possible | Saves time alarming folks ahead of time to prevent restarting process of sharing with each group later | Have people involved earlier in the process (need specifics) | Perform a stakeholder awareness meeting as soon as possible and reconvene at each phase (Preliminary Assessment, Feasibility Study, etc.) |
| Determine stakeholders and responsibilities early | Decide on which parties to manage the UESC and which phases, such as Preliminary Assessment, Feasibility Study, and Design and Implementation | Procurement Officer may need to be delegated more responsibility | May need to consider benefits and ramifications |

Cost/ Finance

| Title | Driving Event | Lesson(s) Learned | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Determine support costs for planning | Essential for budgeting, planning, and the PPBE cycle(s) | Know contingency and BOSS / NEMCON support activities and approximate cost | KSC estimates plan ~6% for SEIS/Shop support, ~2% Environmental, ~10% Contingency |
| Ensure Finance terms and review POCs are defined and followed | Prevents committal to non-ideal terms or higher expense to NASA over life of loan | Finance elements: have full list of requirements from lenders reviewed by finance and procurement prior to ESCO (FPL) engaging with lenders. | Establish a proper POC list of stakeholders for making a decision (KSC: finance, procurement, legal) and communicate timeline for decision need (5 business days) |
| Determine need for Basis of Estimate from contractor and acquire | For Sole Sourcing - "Certificate for Current Cost and Pricing," employees will work on job. If labor rates are less, CO can sign a "Certificate of Defective Pricing" asking for money back. | Need to get Basis of Estimate from contractor to save time in the long run | Determine need for Basis of Estimate from contractor and acquire |

| Title | Driving Event | Lesson(s) Learned | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Keep stakeholders updated and aware of progress | Ensure scope is tracked to prevent duplication of work by other groups and keep customers/stakeholders aware of status | Customer engagement: continue to engage at every stage of UESC with each review cycle to maintain awareness | Beneficial to have all programs in same meeting vs separate meetings for each program |
| Ensure Facility Managers are aware of scope and timeline | Program managers may not be aware of information that Facility Managers have that could contribute to project success | Ensure every facility in scope has Facility Manager (FM) identified throughout process | Alt could be Program Manager if no FM is available; however, engage at beginning of Feasibility Study and at 100% at minimum |
| Utilize Gantt chart where possible to project path and communicate with stakeholders | Non-essential delays are incurred in determining next steps | Determine if potential parallel activities can be done | Scope compiled, Construction of Facilities (CoF) to complete actions, programs to review and approve |

| Title | Driving Event | Lesson(s) Learned | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Determine speed needed as larger scope tends to take much longer to accomplish | KSC's UESC Phase 1 Feasibility Study took ~2 years to accomplish due to significant size of scope and POC's involved | Benefit of having UESC limited to single program vs a multi-program effort | Split UESC based on scope type (i.e., Lighting) or by Program (i.e., ISS) |
| Compile Special Conditions document draft early | Special Conditions document discussions and decisions can take a decent time to complete; desire is to not have this as a long-lead event extending timeline | Special Conditions document to be started earlier -- at possibly 90% stage rather than Tech Eval | Seek template from EEP or prior center project template to copy and paste |

Technical Reviews

| Title | Driving Event | Lesson(s) Learned | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Determine need for Tech Eval | Tech evaluations take time and can become challenging if long periods of time exist between review cycles | Potentially limit Tech Eval to once every ‘x’ months | Recommend having at 90%, 100%, and Final only |
| Ensure review cycles are established | Prevents extra, unnecessary reviews and potential additional incurred costs for Utility and/or government | Include in contract how many review cycles to include to avoid incurring an additional cycle | A 45%, 90%, 100%, Final, with no additional updates to Final submittal |

Documentation

| Title | Driving Event | Lesson(s) Learned | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Compile 1509 draft early | 1509 reviews can take up to 3 weeks, delaying project from moving forward if not planned properly | 1509 actions – ensure payback verbiage is well documented and available for response | Meet with local center and NASA HQ POCs to ensure process and data are drafted correctly and reviewed, which would expedite final 1509/1510 submittal |
| Ensure proper UESC project title | From discussing the KSC named "UESC Phase 1" effort became confusing with discussion with NREL, NASA HQ, and CoF as "phase" can mean many different things | Project naming convention needs consistency and clarity as “Phases” tend to be confusing since the term can imply Feasibility Study vs Preliminary Assessment or others | Name effort based on project category or program (example: Lighting, ISS) |

| Properly document legal requirements and NASA process | Without prepared response to common questions, time is wasted in researching responses, or worse, not following protocol | Figure out how to eliminate past impressions of UESC (example: 10-year ‘legal’ limit vs preferences on payback) | Utilize working groups to raise awareness of future intent that is not based on past projects |

title: Cable Harness Wiring and Connector Anomalies Caused by Induced Damage in Human Spaceflight Vehicles
categories: Flight Equipment; Ground Operations; Hardware; Parts; Materials; & Processes; Spacecraft; Test & Verification; Ground processing and manifesting; Reliability

sections.abstract: Early indications show that the commercial spacecraft developers and operators are experiencing a reduced incidence of wiring anomalies compared to the Space Shuttle Program (SSP). There are differences in implementation of wiring designs between the new vehicles and the Space Shuttle. Recognition of these differences and an appreciation of where SSP failure mechanisms can pose a risk to new crewed launch vehicles and spacecraft can help to manage the incidence of wiring anomalies. Decisions that reduce wire inspection and testing post installation may need to be revisited if the factors resulting in reduced wire incidents change.
sections.driving_event:
NASA has found that the commercial spacecraft developers and operators have a reduced incidence of wiring anomalies compared to the Space Shuttle and has identified causes for this reduced incidence. This reduction can potentially be attributed to:

1. Limited re-use compared to the SSP

2. Reduced exposed wiring in modern spacecraft routing designs

3. New vehicles being integrated in a single orientation, allowing better access control, and enable ground crew to avoid sensitive areas and causing collateral damage

4. The reduced size of ground crew and scope of processing

5. Less wire, smaller length of wire

6. New insulations that replaced Kapton

7. Use of Scoop Proof MIL-DTL-38999 connectors to prevent damaging pins during connector mating

8. System Separation

9. System Architecture (avionics box consolidation and greater incorporation of printed circuit boards (PCB) to eliminate wiring

10. Lower Level of Inspections and Reporting/Inspection Criteria

11. Reduced testing scope for the detection of post-installation failures

Additionally, as NASA moves away from legacy quality standards to industry consensus standards and commercial providers transition to a re-use production environment with larger systems and ground crews, there is a greater risk of increase incidence of wire and harness anomalies pre-launch. A consequence of the move to industry standards is the loss of user post-installation testing with reliance on manufacturing testing alone. NASA can offer relevant wire anomaly experience to help manage the incidence of wiring anomalies.
sections.lesson_learned:
As a result of many years of expensive lessons learned, NASA imposed electrical tests after installation in locations where it was determined that the majority of cable / wiring harness damage occurs during installation and maintenance actions. The probability of incurring immediate or latent damage depends on the robustness of the cable / harness assembly and the installation itself. Installation of a cable / harness assembly into an avionics box would not be expected to carry as much risk as installation / routing of the cable / harness assembly through the bulkheads and wiring trays of a large vehicle. NASA has discovered wiring damage issues in every crewed vehicle system (Apollo, Shuttle, ISS, and now Orion) as well as some issues in commercial spacecraft developers and operators’ vehicles.

While it is agreed that post-installation electrical testing takes time (and by extension

increased cost), it is often less difficult (and less costly) to find and repair damage BEFORE vehicle integration proceeds to the point that access is no longer possible without disassembly of the vehicle. Functional testing may not identify a degraded signal path or latent defect condition. Applying a high voltage does have a high probability of locating a degraded dielectric path or latent defect. Of the three (3) tests listed in NASA-STD-8739.4, Rev A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring, [18.2.8], the two (2) most commonly used are (in sequence):

(1) Continuity and Shorts, and

(2) Insulation Resistance (IR).

These electrical tests will not identify a potential short circuit that may occur during the dynamic loading phase of a flight if there is no detectable amount of current leakage during test – or if the test wasn’t required because the wiring had been previously tested. The most notorious example is the loss of two main engine control units during launch of STS-93 due to a wire in the payload bay rubbing against the sharp edge of a screw head and shorting as it moved under launch load. This was a close call.

Specific lessons learned on post installation testing are:

1. All boxes, mounted or not, should be isolated from the potential harmful effects of the test voltages. Ensure avionics boxes will not be affected by high voltage testing by not connecting harnesses to mounted boxes.

2. Verify the system complies with NASA Standard 8739.4 for assembly and integration: NASA-STD-8739.4, unless tailored, requires the integrators to perform dielectric withstanding voltage (DWV) tests on all harnesses after installation. This requirement is imposed to identify potential damage caused during the installation of the harnesses and provides guidance on applying IR and DWV to wire harnesses.

3. Application of post installation testing Is especially important in difficult-to-access areas where physical access to perform visual inspection is hampered, high traffic areas, and where harnesses are manipulated to install them.

4. Access to the harness connectors and to the harnesses themselves drives the integration approach to provide field joints to simplify testing, eliminate very long test harnesses, and excessive manipulation of the harnesses to access them safely. If excessive manipulations of the harnesses are required, then the benefit of the post installation testing is negated due to the additional handling and potential to damage the harnesses during testing.

NASA’s has not yet seen the same incidence of discrepancies in the new generation of vehicles as was seen in the historical data of discrepancies experience on Apollo and Space Shuttle. The Space Shuttle has a complex wiring system with approximately 600 harnesses, 7,000 connectors, 120,000 wire segm ents and 228 miles of wire. NASA’s experience shows handling-induced damage or damage resulting from work in close proximity is a primary source of wiring anomalies. Figure 1 shows a breakdown of the types of wire related problems encountered in the Orbiter fleet. The types of wire related problems shown include chafe protection, Kapton damage, jacket damage, shield damage, exposed conductor, and conductor damage.

Figure 1. Orbiter Wiring Problem Breakdown.

Adapted from: Evaluation of Cable Harness Post-Installation Testing: Part B, NASA/TP-2011-216300R, p.10, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20110014609 .

A detailed examination of the number of problem reports on Orbiter wiring per year from 1979 to 2007 shows a relationship between the number of Wire Problem Reports (PRs) per year (bars) and flights per year. From the data, shown in Figure 2, one key point is that there is no indication that wiring PRs decrease with vehicle maturity in the case of the Orbiter. Also, per Orbiter Electrical PK-F Electrical Division, Kennedy Space Center), there are two major reasons that Orbiter wiring PRs increase during low flight rate years. First, inspections of wiring go up during those years. Second, as the flight rate decreases there is more traffic in the ship resulting in an increase in collateral damage.

Figure 2. Shuttle (Orbiter) Wiring Problem Reports and Flight Rate from 1979-2000

(Note that the flight rate data is erroneously shifted to the right one year.)

Adapted from: Evaluation of Cable Harness Post-Installation Testing: Part B, NASA/TP-2011-216300R, p.9, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20110014609 .

NASA did conduct a lessons-learned review after the Space Shuttle was retired and the following observation were made with respect to the electrical wiring system:

- It is important to perform detailed closeout inspection after work on cables or connectors.

- Wiring is easily damaged by nearby work activity.

- Training of personnel is critical both to prevent damage and to detect damage.

- Wire chafe protection should be used to protect critical* wiring.

- Separate critical* redundant wire runs and/or install barrier materials to protect against the effects of arc tracking.

- The effects of aging, operation, environmental exposure, re-use should be factored into the expected operational life of the wiring system

* Critical wires are wires that, should they fail, pose a catastrophic hazard (loss of crew risk or loss of mission) risk

# [NASA LLIS #30101] Cable Harness Wiring and Connector Anomalies Caused by Induced Damage in Human Spaceflight Vehicles
- **Date:** 2021-02-28
- **Organization:** NASA (NESC)
- **Categories:** Flight Equipment; Ground Operations; Hardware; Parts; Materials; & Processes; Spacecraft; Test & Verification; Ground processing and manifesting; Reliability
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/30101

## Abstract
Early indications show that the commercial spacecraft developers and operators are experiencing a reduced incidence of wiring anomalies compared to the Space Shuttle Program (SSP). There are differences in implementation of wiring designs between the new vehicles and the Space Shuttle. Recognition of these differences and an appreciation of where SSP failure mechanisms can pose a risk to new crewed launch vehicles and spacecraft can help to manage the incidence of wiring anomalies. Decisions that reduce wire inspection and testing post installation may need to be revisited if the factors resulting in reduced wire incidents change.

## Driving Event / Background
NASA has found that the commercial spacecraft developers and operators have a reduced incidence of wiring anomalies compared to the Space Shuttle and has identified causes for this reduced incidence. This reduction can potentially be attributed to:

1. Limited re-use compared to the SSP

2. Reduced exposed wiring in modern spacecraft routing designs

3. New vehicles being integrated in a single orientation, allowing better access control, and enable ground crew to avoid sensitive areas and causing collateral damage

4. The reduced size of ground crew and scope of processing

5. Less wire, smaller length of wire

6. New insulations that replaced Kapton

7. Use of Scoop Proof MIL-DTL-38999 connectors to prevent damaging pins during connector mating

8. System Separation

9. System Architecture (avionics box consolidation and greater incorporation of printed circuit boards (PCB) to eliminate wiring

10. Lower Level of Inspections and Reporting/Inspection Criteria

11. Reduced testing scope for the detection of post-installation failures

Additionally, as NASA moves away from legacy quality standards to industry consensus standards and commercial providers transition to a re-use production environment with larger systems and ground crews, there is a greater risk of increase incidence of wire and harness anomalies pre-launch. A consequence of the move to industry standards is the loss of user post-installation testing with reliance on manufacturing testing alone. NASA can offer relevant wire anomaly experience to help manage the incidence of wiring anomalies.

## Lesson Learned
As a result of many years of expensive lessons learned, NASA imposed electrical tests after installation in locations where it was determined that the majority of cable / wiring harness damage occurs during installation and maintenance actions. The probability of incurring immediate or latent damage depends on the robustness of the cable / harness assembly and the installation itself. Installation of a cable / harness assembly into an avionics box would not be expected to carry as much risk as installation / routing of the cable / harness assembly through the bulkheads and wiring trays of a large vehicle. NASA has discovered wiring damage issues in every crewed vehicle system (Apollo, Shuttle, ISS, and now Orion) as well as some issues in commercial spacecraft developers and operators’ vehicles.

While it is agreed that post-installation electrical testing takes time (and by extension

increased cost), it is often less difficult (and less costly) to find and repair damage BEFORE vehicle integration proceeds to the point that access is no longer possible without disassembly of the vehicle. Functional testing may not identify a degraded signal path or latent defect condition. Applying a high voltage does have a high probability of locating a degraded dielectric path or latent defect. Of the three (3) tests listed in NASA-STD-8739.4, Rev A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring, [18.2.8], the two (2) most commonly used are (in sequence):

(1) Continuity and Shorts, and

(2) Insulation Resistance (IR).

These electrical tests will not identify a potential short circuit that may occur during the dynamic loading phase of a flight if there is no detectable amount of current leakage during test – or if the test wasn’t required because the wiring had been previously tested. The most notorious example is the loss of two main engine control units during launch of STS-93 due to a wire in the payload bay rubbing against the sharp edge of a screw head and shorting as it moved under launch load. This was a close call.

Specific lessons learned on post installation testing are:

1. All boxes, mounted or not, should be isolated from the potential harmful effects of the test voltages. Ensure avionics boxes will not be affected by high voltage testing by not connecting harnesses to mounted boxes.

2. Verify the system complies with NASA Standard 8739.4 for assembly and integration: NASA-STD-8739.4, unless tailored, requires the integrators to perform dielectric withstanding voltage (DWV) tests on all harnesses after installation. This requirement is imposed to identify potential damage caused during the installation of the harnesses and provides guidance on applying IR and DWV to wire harnesses.

3. Application of post installation testing Is especially important in difficult-to-access areas where physical access to perform visual inspection is hampered, high traffic areas, and where harnesses are manipulated to install them.

4. Access to the harness connectors and to the harnesses themselves drives the integration approach to provide field joints to simplify testing, eliminate very long test harnesses, and excessive manipulation of the harnesses to access them safely. If excessive manipulations of the harnesses are required, then the benefit of the post installation testing is negated due to the additional handling and potential to damage the harnesses during testing.

NASA’s has not yet seen the same incidence of discrepancies in the new generation of vehicles as was seen in the historical data of discrepancies experience on Apollo and Space Shuttle. The Space Shuttle has a complex wiring system with approximately 600 harnesses, 7,000 connectors, 120,000 wire segm ents and 228 miles of wire. NASA’s experience shows handling-induced damage or damage resulting from work in close proximity is a primary source of wiring anomalies. Figure 1 shows a breakdown of the types of wire related problems encountered in the Orbiter fleet. The types of wire related problems shown include chafe protection, Kapton damage, jacket damage, shield damage, exposed conductor, and conductor damage.

Figure 1. Orbiter Wiring Problem Breakdown.

Adapted from: Evaluation of Cable Harness Post-Installation Testing: Part B, NASA/TP-2011-216300R, p.10, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20110014609 .

A detailed examination of the number of problem reports on Orbiter wiring per year from 1979 to 2007 shows a relationship between the number of Wire Problem Reports (PRs) per year (bars) and flights per year. From the data, shown in Figure 2, one key point is that there is no indication that wiring PRs decrease with vehicle maturity in the case of the Orbiter. Also, per Orbiter Electrical PK-F Electrical Division, Kennedy Space Center), there are two major reasons that Orbiter wiring PRs increase during low flight rate years. First, inspections of wiring go up during those years. Second, as the flight rate decreases there is more traffic in the ship resulting in an increase in collateral damage.

Figure 2. Shuttle (Orbiter) Wiring Problem Reports and Flight Rate from 1979-2000

(Note that the flight rate data is erroneously shifted to the right one year.)

Adapted from: Evaluation of Cable Harness Post-Installation Testing: Part B, NASA/TP-2011-216300R, p.9, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20110014609 .

- Wiring is easily damaged by nearby work activity.

- Training of personnel is critical both to prevent damage and to detect damage.

- Wire chafe protection should be used to protect critical* wiring.

- Separate critical* redundant wire runs and/or install barrier materials to protect against the effects of arc tracking.

sections.abstract: Space flight instruments containing rotational elements often employ copper/Kapton flexible wiring harnesses (a.k.a. flex harnesses) to transfer electrical signals and power to fixed elements of the payload throughout the rotational range of motion. Achieving reliable design and fabrication of dynamically flexed flex harnesses, particularly harnesses exposed to high cycle fatigue (defined as cycle count ≥ 500 per IPC-TR-484), can be extremely challenging. Historically, multiple space flight projects have experienced developmental challenges with dynamically flexed harnesses. When a flex harness problem occurs, diagnosis and correction can be very difficult and time consuming. It is therefore important to develop prototypes and conduct life testing early in the project life cycle (Phase B).
sections.driving_event:
The initial design of the HyperSpectral Instrument for Climate Science (HySICS) Pointing System (HPS) within the Climate Absolute Radiance and Refractivity Observatory (CLARREO) Pathfinder payload utilized dynamically flexed, multi-layer flex harnesses in an “Omega” configuration for transmission of electrical signals and power between elements of the payload throughout the pointing system range of motion. The HPS provides rotation of the HySICS instrument boresight about an azimuthal axis and elevation axis; thus two separate dynamically flexed harnesses – one azimuth and one elevation - both with “Omega” configurations, were incorporated into the pointing system design. Figure 1 shows a representation of the multi-layer flex harness in its intended operational configuration. Figure 2 shows a representation of one ribbon within the flex harness laid flat; the semi-circular region forms the “Omega” portion of the ribbon. Figure 3 shows the installed flex harness in the azimuth gimbal. The semi-circular portion experiences dynamic flexing via “rolling” as the harness rotates about the center of the semi-circle. Figure 4 shows the installation orientation of the elevation flex harness. The azimuth flex harness contained six individual multilayer copper/Kapton tapes; the elevation flex harness contained four individual multi-layer copper/Kapton tapes. Individual tapes within each harness were not physically bonded together. Small mechanical retaining clamps were installed near the ends of the “omega” flexing region to clamp the harness, through slight mechanical pressure, to the fixed and rotating elements of the harness structural channel. Rotation of the rotating element of the structural channel (e.g., Figure 3, semi-transparent top surface) would thus result in a “rolling” flexural motion of the “omega” portion of the harness within the channel.

Within the flexing/rolling region, the individual flex tapes were layered but not bonded, which allowed for some small amount of sliding of the tapes relative to each other as the flexing region “rolled” throughout the rotational range of motion. Because the individual tapes were not bonded together, each individual tape retained its own neutral bending axis. Each tape was comprised of outer Kapton layers, a copper trace layer, a middle Kapton layer, and a copper crosshatch-pattern shield layer. Figure 5 shows the single tape layer stackup for the original design. Note the copper layers are not at the neutral bending axis (middle) of the tape, which causes increased strain and fatigue on the copper during bending. The same basic flex harness design had previously been successfully life tested to approximately 2000 flex cycles for the Total and Solar Irradiance Sensor-1 (TSIS-1) project and flown in the TSIS-1 payload. On orbit, the TSIS-1 flex harnesses experienced dynamic flexing only once during the mechanism deployment phase during payload commissioning.

| Material | Tape Stackup | Thickness (mils) | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kapton® | | 1 | Outer Layer |
| Acrylic | | 1 | Adhesive |
| Copper | | 1.4 | Crosshatch Shield Pattern |
| Kapton® | | 4 | Insulating Dielectric Layer |
| Copper | | 1.4 | Signal and Power Traces |
| Acrylic | | 1 | Adhesive |
| Kapton® | | 1 | Outer Layer |
| | Total Tape Thickness (mils) | 10.8 | |

Figure 5: Tape layer stackup for original tape design. Middle three layers (bolded in red) was a commercially available double-sided copper substrate product; copper layers were subsequently etched to create copper crosshatch shield layer and copper signal/power trace layer. Note the copper layers are not at the neutral bending axis (middle) of the tape which causes increased strain and fatigue on the copper during bending.

The initial CLARREO Pathfinder HPS flex harness design was derived from the TSIS-1 flex harness design in consideration of the prior life test for TSIS-1. The minimum flexural life needed for the CLARREO Pathfinder harnesses was 15,000 cycles, equivalent to 1x mission life. A life test to 2x mission life (30,000 cycles) was planned in the project schedule but was delayed in execution due to multiple factors, including necessary maturation of the flex harness design, limited number of vendors with the capability to fabricate the harnesses, lengthy production schedules, and COVID-19. A life test of the HPS azimuth flex harness life test unit was initiated in summer 2020 after the project’s Critical Design Review and an extended facility shutdown due to COVID-19. Figure 6 shows a photograph of the life test fixture with test harness installed. Copper traces within the life test harness began exhibiting inconsistent and high resistance values starting at approximately 2000 cycles, indicating signs of early failure. Under continued flexing additional copper traces exhibited high resistance/open circuit. The life test was deemed a test failure and stopped at 20,000 cycles, at which time nearly all coppr traces exhibited signs of failure.

The CLARREO Pathfinder project initiated an investigation into the HPS flex harness life test failure mechanism(s) and harness design. Technical assistance was sought from the NASA Engineering and Safety Center (NESC) who contributed personnel with expertise that greatly assisted in the investigation. The investigation lasted approximately five months concluding in January 2021. Multiple non-destructive evaluation (NDE), destructive physical analysis (DPA), and analytical techniques were used to identify and characterize mechanisms contributing to the failure of copper traces within the flex harness. The root cause of the copper trace failures was fatigue cracking of the copper signal traces predominantly in locations that were overlapped by the crosshatch copper traces within the shield layer. A factor contributing to the copper trace failures was that each flex tape within the harness was a “double-sided” layup configuration where the copper signal trace layer was located away from the neutral bending axis of the tape, causing increased mechanical strain and fatigue on the traces during flexing.

The investigation produced multiple recommendations for a redesigned flex harness and life testing methodology. Key recommendations for redesign were:

1. Use single-sided copper ribbons with the copper as close as possible to the neutral plane

2. Use wider copper traces than the original design. Consider 30 mils. Use modeling to validate if ½ oz copper is the best option for meeting the life test requirement for the flex ribbon harness.

3. Add IPC 2223 dynamic flex requirements to design requirements (minimum flex cycles per IPC test method

4. Add a second vendor source

5. Assess CLARREO on-orbit operational requirements to determine the life test parameters

6. Include temperature extremes in the life test and if possible vacuum conditions.

Many of the NESC’s recommendations were adopted and incorporated into the redesigned HPS azimuth and elevation flex harnesses and life testing plan. A redesigned azimuth flex harness successfully passed a 4X life test (60,000 cycles) in December 2021. Test cycles were completed at ambient, hot operational, and cold operational temperatures at atmospheric pressure (not vacuum). Key design aspects for the redesigned flex tapes comprising the harnesses were:

- Single-sided flex tape layup construction with copper trace layer located in the center of the tape, at the neutral bending axis, as shown in Figure 7.

- Elimination of crosshatch copper shield layer within the tapes. A separate tape consisting of only the copper crosshatch pattern was added to the harness for shielding purposes.

- Single-sided copper clad polyimide substrate. Consists of 2-mil Kapton coverlay and 0.7 mil (e.g. ½ oz.) copper layer

- ½-oz. Rolled Highly Annealed Copper, minimum 30 mil trace width

- Kapton® coverlay 1 mil thick, 1 mil acrylic coverlay adhesive

- No part identification markings (i.e., silk-screened lettering) in the flexing portion of the tape (no such markings existed in the flexing portion of the tape in the original design, but restated here due to importance)

| Material | Tape Stackup | Thickness (mils) | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kapton® | | 1 | Outer Layer |
| Acrylic | | 1 | Adhesive |
| Copper | | 0.7 | Signal and Power Traces |
| Kapton® | | 2 | Outer Layer |
| | Total Tape Thickness (mils) | 4.7 | |

Figure 7: Tape layer stackup for revised tape design. The two layers bolded in red are a commercially available single-sided copper substrate product; the copper layer was subsequently etched to create the copper signal/power trace layer. Note the copper signal/power trace layer is at the neutral bending axis (middle) of the tape which minimizes strain and fatigue during bending.

- IPC-D-330, IPC Design Guide, Section 7

- IPC-4572A-WAM1, Metal Foil for Printed Board Applications

- IPC-TM-650, Test Methods Manual, Section 2.4.3.1

- Sandia Report SAND2011-0564, Assessing the Operational Life of Flexible Printed Boards

Intended for Continuous Flexing Applications - a Case Study https://www.o sti.gov/servlets/purl/1011218

- NASA Engineering and Safety Center Technical Assessment Report NASA/TM20210018831 Climate Absolute Radiance and Refractivity Observatory (CLARREO) Pathfinder (CPF) Flex Harness Cable Technical Assessment, May 18, 2021 https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20210018831

- Sood, B., Wusk, M.E., Burke, E., Dawicke, D., Lebair, S., and Slenski, G., “Analysis of a Dynamic Flexed Flat Cable Harness”, IPC APEX EXPO, January 25-27, 2022, San Diego,

CA

https://www.ipcapexexpo.org/

NOTE: IPC Technical Standards Documentation is available at the following links:

- NASA Internal: https://standards.nasa.gov/ NASA External: https://ipc.org/
sections.lesson_learned: Dynamically flexed flex tapes and/or harnesses should be considered an engineering development activity in project formulation, particularly for tapes/harnesses that will experience high cycle fatigue with cycle counts ≥ 500. Therefore, projects should plan to develop test coupons and prototypes and conduct testing at representative strain levels and life cycle counts early in the project, ideally Phase B. These early tests can help to evaluate the design principles, the selected material system, and vendor fabrication capabilities. Identifying and using more than one vendor provides additional options.
sections.recommendation:
Some specific flex-tape recommendations for dynamically flexed tapes include:

- Keep the copper traces as close to the neutral bending axis as possible. Whenever possible, use single-sided flex layup construction (i.e., Kapton – Copper – Kapton) with the copper trace layer located at the neutral bending axis of the tape. Ensure there is no part identification markings (e.g., silk-screened lettering) in the flexing region of the tape/harness. The presence of silk-screened lettering can locally skew the location of the neutral bending axis, and the edges of the silk-screen lettering can act as stress concentrators that could lead to localized copper trace failures. If multi-layer “double-sided” flex tape layups must be used, avoid having copper traces overlap each other. This results in an “I-beam” effect that increases mechanical strain on the traces which may cause copper trace fracture (see Figure 7-11 in Fjelstad, J., Flexible Circuit Technology, 4th Edition).

- High-purity, rolled, annealed copper is generally preferred for high-cycle flexural applications. If rolled annealed copper is selected, be aware that rolled annealed copper typically exhibits anisotropy in the copper grain structure due to the rolling process. This anisotropy is often identified using the convention of “Machine” vs. “Cross-Machine” directions, referring to the direction in which the copper was rolled in the rolling machine. For high cycle dynamic flexing applications rolled annealed copper should be oriented such that the “Machine” direction runs parallel to the copper traces.

- Flex tapes/harness designs configured in a “clock spring” configuration may be preferable to tapes/harnesses in an “Omega” configuration as the clock spring design may offer lower mechanical strain on the copper traces.

- When life testing, ensure the test is representative of the in-service conditions expected including range and rate of motion as well as environmental conditions. NASA-STD-5001B specifies a service life factor of 4.0 be applied for fatigue life assessments. For very-high-cycle applications that would make life testing prohibitively long in duration, fatigue cycle tests of coupons in a flexural testing machine (see IPC-TM-650 Section 2.4.3.1) can be used to construct a Manson-Coffin plot to evaluate predicted fatigue life.

- When a copper trace failure occurs as indicated by an increase in resistance or open circuit, thermographic imaging of the traces with current flowing through them has been demonstrated to be an effective method for quickly diagnosing the approximate location of the break. Additional diagnostic methods that have been used successfully are XRay/Computed Tomography (CT) imaging and Time Domain Reflectometry.

The investigation lasted approximately five months concluding in January 2021. Multiple non-destructive evaluation (NDE), destructive physical analysis (DPA), and analytical techniques were used to identify and characterize mechanisms contributing to the failure of copper traces within the flex harness. The root cause of the copper trace failures was fatigue cracking of the copper signal traces predominantly in locations that were overlapped by the crosshatch copper traces within the shield layer. A factor contributing to the copper trace failures was that each flex tape within the harness was a “double-sided” layup configuration where the copper signal trace layer was located away from the neutral bending axis of the tape, causing increased mechanical strain and fatigue on the traces during flexing.

The investigation produced multiple recommendations for a redesigned flex harness and life testing methodology. Key recommendations for redesign were:

1. Use single-sided copper ribbons with the copper as close as possible to the neutral plane

2. Use wider copper traces than the original design. Consider 30 mils. Use modeling to validate if ½ oz copper is the best option for meeting the life test requirement for the flex ribbon harness.

3. Add IPC 2223 dynamic flex requirements to design requirements (minimum flex cycles per IPC test method

4. Add a second vendor source

5. Assess CLARREO on-orbit operational requirements to determine the life test parameters

6. Include temperature extremes in the life test and if possible vacuum conditions.

Many of the NESC’s recommendations were adopted and incorporated into the redesigned HPS azimuth and elevation flex harnesses and life testing plan. A redesigned azimuth flex harness successfully passed a 4X life test (60,000 cycles) in December 2021. Test cycles were completed at ambient, hot operational, and cold operational temperatures at atmospheric pressure (not vacuum). Key design aspects for the redesigned flex tapes comprising the harnesses were:

- Single-sided flex tape layup construction with copper trace layer located in the center of the tape, at the neutral bending axis, as shown in Figure 7.

- Elimination of crosshatch copper shield layer within the tapes. A separate tape consisting of only the copper crosshatch pattern was added to the harness for shielding purposes.

- Single-sided copper clad polyimide substrate. Consists of 2-mil Kapton coverlay and 0.7 mil (e.g. ½ oz.) copper layer

- ½-oz. Rolled Highly Annealed Copper, minimum 30 mil trace width

- Kapton® coverlay 1 mil thick, 1 mil acrylic coverlay adhesive

- No part identification markings (i.e., silk-screened lettering) in the flexing portion of the tape (no such markings existed in the flexing portion of the tape in the original design, but restated here due to importance)

| Material | Tape Stackup | Thickness (mils) | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kapton® | | 1 | Outer Layer |
| Acrylic | | 1 | Adhesive |
| Copper | | 0.7 | Signal and Power Traces |
| Kapton® | | 2 | Outer Layer |
| | Total Tape Thickness (mils) | 4.7 | |

Figure 7: Tape layer stackup for revised tape design. The two layers bolded in red are a commercially available single-sided copper substrate product; the copper layer was subsequently etched to create the copper signal/power trace layer. Note the copper signal/power trace layer is at the neutral bending axis (middle) of the tape which minimizes strain and fatigue during bending.

- IPC-TR-484, Results of IPC Copper Foil Ductility Round Robin Study

- IPC-D-330, IPC Design Guide, Section 7

- Fjelstad, J., Flexible Circuit Technology, 4^th Edition http://iconnect007.com/index.php?cID=788

- NASA Engineering and Safety Center Technical Assessment Report NASA/TM20210018831 Climate Absolute Radiance and Refractivity Observatory (CLARREO) Pathfinder (CPF) Flex Harness Cable Technical Assessment, May 18, 2021 https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20210018831

- Sood, B., Wusk, M.E., Burke, E., Dawicke, D., Lebair, S., and Slenski, G., “Analysis of a Dynamic Flexed Flat Cable Harness”, IPC APEX EXPO, January 25-27, 2022, San Diego,

CA

https://www.ipcapexexpo.org/

NOTE: IPC Technical Standards Documentation is available at the following links:

- NASA Internal: https://standards.nasa.gov/ NASA External: https://ipc.org/

## Lesson Learned
Dynamically flexed flex tapes and/or harnesses should be considered an engineering development activity in project formulation, particularly for tapes/harnesses that will experience high cycle fatigue with cycle counts ≥ 500. Therefore, projects should plan to develop test coupons and prototypes and conduct testing at representative strain levels and life cycle counts early in the project, ideally Phase B. These early tests can help to evaluate the design principles, the selected material system, and vendor fabrication capabilities. Identifying and using more than one vendor provides additional options.

## Recommendation
Some specific flex-tape recommendations for dynamically flexed tapes include:

- Keep the copper traces as close to the neutral bending axis as possible. Whenever possible, use single-sided flex layup construction (i.e., Kapton – Copper – Kapton) with the copper trace layer located at the neutral bending axis of the tape. Ensure there is no part identification markings (e.g., silk-screened lettering) in the flexing region of the tape/harness. The presence of silk-screened lettering can locally skew the location of the neutral bending axis, and the edges of the silk-screen lettering can act as stress concentrators that could lead to localized copper trace failures. If multi-layer “double-sided” flex tape layups must be used, avoid having copper traces overlap each other. This results in an “I-beam” effect that increases mechanical strain on the traces which may cause copper trace fracture (see Figure 7-11 in Fjelstad, J., Flexible Circuit Technology, 4th Edition).

- High-purity, rolled, annealed copper is generally preferred for high-cycle flexural applications. If rolled annealed copper is selected, be aware that rolled annealed copper typically exhibits anisotropy in the copper grain structure due to the rolling process. This anisotropy is often identified using the convention of “Machine” vs. “Cross-Machine” directions, referring to the direction in which the copper was rolled in the rolling machine. For high cycle dynamic flexing applications rolled annealed copper should be oriented such that the “Machine” direction runs parallel to the copper traces.

- Flex tapes/harness designs configured in a “clock spring” configuration may be preferable to tapes/harnesses in an “Omega” configuration as the clock spring design may offer lower mechanical strain on the copper traces.

- When life testing, ensure the test is representative of the in-service conditions expected including range and rate of motion as well as environmental conditions. NASA-STD-5001B specifies a service life factor of 4.0 be applied for fatigue life assessments. For very-high-cycle applications that would make life testing prohibitively long in duration, fatigue cycle tests of coupons in a flexural testing machine (see IPC-TM-650 Section 2.4.3.1) can be used to construct a Manson-Coffin plot to evaluate predicted fatigue life.

- When a copper trace failure occurs as indicated by an increase in resistance or open circuit, thermographic imaging of the traces with current flowing through them has been demonstrated to be an effective method for quickly diagnosing the approximate location of the break. Additional diagnostic methods that have been used successfully are XRay/Computed Tomography (CT) imaging and Time Domain Reflectometry.

sections.abstract: Trace contaminants in high-purity hydrazine (HPH) propellant impact a wide variety of commercial, Department of Defense (DoD), and NASA missions. Several impactful contaminants are not currently controlled in the current MIL-PRF-26356 specification which governs procurement. A number of these elemental contaminants have recently undergone an assessment to shed light on potential contaminants present following changes in the HPH supply chain. A round robin analysis utilizing four separate laboratories resulted in unacceptably high variability in the quantification of these contaminants. Efforts were made to ascertain the causes of this lab-to-lab variability. These efforts highlighted several sample preparation and analytical method considerations that can impact laboratory results. The principal objective of this lesson learned, and these recommendations, is to establish an analysis methodology which yields accurate and repeatable quantification by providing best practices for both quantitation methodology and strategies for avoiding sample contamination during analysis.
sections.driving_event:
Hypergolic propellants (e.g., hydrazine (N2H4)) and monomethylhydrazine (MMH) are used to power monopropellant and bipropellant propulsion systems across a wide variety of commercial, DoD, and NASA programs. Detailed understanding of the hypergolic fluid properties and characteristics is critical to their successful use in short and long duration missions. Investigations to better understand HPH manufacturing processes and the associated introduction of contaminants have been a priority for the HPH user community after the chemical reaction scheme employed to produce a precursor to HPH, which is used as the feedstock by the Defense Logistics Agency’s sole source HPH provider, changed in mid-2018.

Particular concern arose regarding the possible introduction of organic species (e.g., carbonaceous compounds) and elemental content (e.g., cadmium (Cd)) to the final HPH product, as this carries an increased risk of performance degradation and/or flow-path blockage to thruster system valves, softgoods and catalyst beds.

Analysis was completed to identify extraneous unknown carbonaceous materials present in current HPH in addition to comprehensive elemental profiling by four laboratories, based on NESC-developed analytical methodology, to develop a full elemental profile of the commodity in relation to heritage HPH stocks.

The elemental laboratory data from each of the four laboratories unexpectedly found varying and/or high levels of multiple elements outside of nominal laboratory-to-laboratory variation, which was confirmed by the Kennedy Space Center-Component Refurbishment & Chemical Analysis Laboratory. The NESC concluded that, while there was variation in the elemental content of the samples, there was also an apparent inconsistent handling of samples within each of the four laboratories that, in some cases, led to widely varying elemental assay results.
sections.lesson_learned: There was an unexpectedly wide variation in elemental assay results from the analysis of single batch-sourced samples from four laboratories. Further analysis revealed that the provided samples themselves exhibited variation, possibly as a result of pre-laboratory handling. However, in some cases, large discrepancies were determined to have been caused by differences in analytical procedures and methods at the laboratories themselves. Refinement of analytical methodology for HPH, or other hydrazine derivative, sample handling and processing, as well as the instrumental analysis methodology for extended elemental content, are essential to gaining accurate and equivalent results from multiple laboratories performing this type of analysis.
sections.recommendation:
The recommendations to prevent this lesson from being relearned in the future take the form of best practices for conducting the elemental analysis process and are tabulated below:

A. Glassware usage should be minimized in all steps of the analytical process to minimize sample contamination. This includes the evaporation vessel used in the non-volatile residue (NVR) step (platinum recommended); storing of water, acids, standards, reagents, etc., used for the NVR step, acid digestion, and inductively coupled plasma analysis. Polypropylene and polymethyl pentene are regarded as good storage materials for this application but other plastics are also suitable.

B. Blanks for water and acid stock solutions used in sample preparation should be prepared alongside, and analyzed with, each batch of samples analyzed to ensure any contamination, particularly silicon, is accounted for from the process.

C. When using platinum evaporation dishes, adequate cleaning between samples should be ensured; two method options are suggested: i. Option 1: Gently scrub the pan with a synthetic fiber scouring pad in deionized water to remove any visibly discolored areas. When no more deposits are noted, rinse with 25% by volume concentrated nitric acid in deionized water, allowing the acid to sit in the pans for several minutes and swirling to ensure it has contacted the entire interior. Complete a final rinse with deionized water, then heat in a muffle furnace at 800°C for 1 hour minimum. ii. Option 2: Thoroughly rinse the pan with 5% nitric acid in deionized water and gently scrub to remove any visibly discolored areas. When no more deposits are noted, rinse the pan with deionized water and dry with lint-free wipes. Place the pans in a chemical fume hood and rinse with hydrofluoroether HFE-7100 precision cleaning solvent. (Note: other non-polar volatile organic solvents may be used for cleaning if directed by the chemist in charge). Give each pan a final rinse with the last solvent. Gently blow any remaining liquid off the dishes with filtered gaseous nitrogen, then place the dishes in a 110°C oven for 30 minutes. Prior to use for analysis, place the pans on a hot plate, then fill with 5% nitric acid and bring to a boil and hold at a boil for 5 minutes. Cool the pans, and rinse with deionized water.

D. Method detection limits and reporting limits should be established for all elements in analysis for proper reporting of trace elemental levels.

E. For ICP-OES (Inductively Coupled Plasma - Optical Emission Spectrometry) or ICP-MS (Inductively Coupled Plasma - Mass Spectrometry) analysis, it is important to survey the elements that are to be analyzed and determine what possible interferences may exist for those elements, which should be addressed prior to analysis. - When using ICP-OES, inter-element correction factors should be established and routinely checked for accuracy with spiked standards for accurate quantification of all elements in the analysis. An internal standard should always be used to ensure accurate quantification from any variation in instrument performance during operation. Yttrium is one such suitable internal standard option. - For ICP-MS, a suggested set up includes the ability to use helium mode, when needed, to remove polyatomic interferences. If sample load is very low, calibration achieved by bracketing the sample(s) between check standards in lieu of using an internal standard is acceptable. If sample load is high and regular, robust calibration and internal standard use is typical.

F. Samples should be analyzed in duplicate or triplicate, when possible. Preferable replicate relative percent difference levels are less than or equal to 20%.

# [NASA LLIS #29801] Best Practices for the Elemental Profiling of High-Purity Hydrazine
- **Date:** 2020-12-14

## Abstract
Trace contaminants in high-purity hydrazine (HPH) propellant impact a wide variety of commercial, Department of Defense (DoD), and NASA missions. Depending on thruster design, contaminants must be kept at extremely low levels and are verified as such by routine analysis. Several impactful contaminants are not currently controlled in the current MIL-PRF-26356 specification which governs procurement. A number of these elemental contaminants have recently undergone an assessment to shed light on potential contaminants present following changes in the HPH supply chain. A round robin analysis utilizing four separate laboratories resulted in unacceptably high variability in the quantification of these contaminants. Efforts were made to ascertain the causes of this lab-to-lab variability. These efforts highlighted several sample preparation and analytical method considerations that can impact laboratory results. The principal objective of this lesson learned, and these recommendations, is to establish an analysis methodology which yields accurate and repeatable quantification by providing best practices for both quantitation methodology and strategies for avoiding sample contamination during analysis.

## Driving Event / Background
Hypergolic propellants (e.g., hydrazine (N2H4)) and monomethylhydrazine (MMH) are used to power monopropellant and bipropellant propulsion systems across a wide variety of commercial, DoD, and NASA programs. Analysis was completed to identify extraneous unknown carbonaceous materials present in current HPH in addition to comprehensive elemental profiling by four laboratories, based on NESC-developed analytical methodology, to develop a full elemental profile of the commodity in relation to heritage HPH stocks.

There was an unexpectedly wide variation in elemental assay results from the analysis of single batch-sourced samples from four laboratories. Further analysis revealed that the provided samples themselves exhibited variation, possibly as a result of pre-laboratory handling. However, in some cases, large discrepancies were determined to have been caused by differences in analytical procedures and methods at the laboratories themselves. Refinement of analytical methodology for HPH, or other hydrazine derivative, sample handling and processing, as well as the instrumental analysis methodology for extended elemental content, are essential to gaining accurate and equivalent results from multiple laboratories performing this type of analysis.

B. Blanks for water and acid stock solutions used in sample preparation should be prepared alongside, and analyzed with, each batch of samples analyzed to ensure any contamination, particularly silicon, is accounted for from the process.

C. When using platinum evaporation dishes, adequate cleaning between samples should be ensured; two method options are suggested: i. When no more deposits are noted, rinse with 25% by volume concentrated nitric acid in deionized water, allowing the acid to sit in the pans for several minutes and swirling to ensure it has contacted the entire interior. Yttrium is one such suitable internal standard option. - For ICP-MS, a suggested set up includes the ability to use helium mode, when needed, to remove polyatomic interferences. If sample load is very low, calibration achieved by bracketing the sample(s) between check standards in lieu of using an internal standard is acceptable. sections.abstract: Aerodynamically unstable spacecraft limit contingency and backup options in the event of software or computer errors. Design decisions regarding stability can require computer control and place a greater need for computer fault tolerance and software assurance. full_text:
# [NASA LLIS #33205] Mitigating Possible Software Errors During Reentry of Crewed Spacecraft
- **Date:** 2020-12-11
- **Organization:** NASA (NESC)
- **Categories:** Software; Spacecraft; Entry Systems; DDT/E; Level 0/1 Requirements; Early requirements and standards definition; Reliability
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/33205

## Abstract
Aerodynamically unstable spacecraft limit contingency and backup options in the event of software or computer errors. Design decisions regarding stability can require computer control and place a greater need for computer fault tolerance and software assurance. NASA should explicitly express a preference for stable designs that enable greater robustness and to not require computer control to safely return crew to Earth.

## Driving Event / Background
The NESC assessed contingency and backup operations for historical crewed spacecraft during reentry. Several American and Russian crewed spacecraft had backup methods to ensure safe reentries that did not rely on common software computer control. These methods were possible because of the inherent stability and controllability of the spacecraft. However, if a vehicle is unstable transonically and cannot initiate or continue a safe reentry without active computer control, or there are skewed RCS thrusters requiring algorithmic logic to perform uncoupled rotations about individual axes, or there is no provision for manual control, reentry can be difficult, if not impossible, to recover from common mode software or hardware flight computer failures during this critical time.

## Lesson Learned
Spacecraft aerodynamic instability and reaction thruster off-axis skewing greatly reduce contingency or backup options for safe return of crew in the event of a single common flight control computer failure. Inherently unstable spacecraft configurations, skewed thruster configurations, and lack of manual controls and displays require reliance on-board flight control computers which bring the inherent risk of common software failure that makes a successful, uncontrolled reentry unlikely.

## Recommendation
NASA should explicitly express a preference for stable designs that enable greater robustness and to not require computer control to safely return crew to Earth. A stable spacecraft can allow manual or non-controlled reentry options that can save the lives of the crew. NASA should avoid unstable designs that require working compute elements and software with no errors. If such a design is necessary, this additional computer risk should be considered.

title: Copper Tube Pinch Failure
categories: Engineering Design; Integration and Testing; Manufacturing and Assembly; Computer-Aided Design / Manufacturing / Engineering; Flight Equipment; Flight Operations; Ground Equipment; Ground Operations; Hardware; Parts; Materials; & Processes; Payloads; Pressure Vessels; Research & Development; Risk Management / Assessment; Safety & Mission Assurance; Test & Verification; Ground processing and manifesting; Ground support systems; Quality; Reliability

sections.abstract: While pinching copper tubes is a standard practice for many applications on Earth, it is not ideal for critical spaceflight applications due to uncertainty in the verification process and the potential for a seemingly “good” pinch to separate at a later time if a cold weld isn't achieved. However, if a copper tube must be pinched, it is useful to perform a Computerized Tomography (CT) scan and inverted metallography on the pinch if possible. The likelihood of damaging the pinch point also significantly decreases when a physical protective barrier (often an epoxy) is used to protect the pinch point.
sections.driving_event: A copper tube was pinched as a test for the Mass Spectrometer observing lunar operations (MSolo) Calibration Gas System (CGS). A CT scan revealed that a pinch that was seemingly acceptable later separated to form a leak path.
sections.lesson_learned:
The pinch was initially visually inspected and helium leak checked and no visual anomalies or leaks were detected. After a CT scan revealed that the seemingly acceptable pinch separated after the helium leak check to form a leak path, an investigation was started to try to form an empirical method for verifying that a pinch has cold welded correctly. The team first turned to industry experts on copper tube pinching. While they offered a plethora of tips and tricks to try to get the best pinch possible, they were not able to provide an empirical method to ensure that a flight pinch is sealed correctly. The MSolo team then performed CT scans and inverted metallography on several copper tube pinches in an attempt to find measurements on the pinch cross-section that could be taken to distinguish a “good” pinch from a “bad” one. The results were documented, but they varied and were not useful for definitively deeming a pinch to be acceptable or not. The CT scans and inverted metallography did, however, provide insight into the shape of the pinch. A pinch with a nominal shape is more likely to have cold welded correctly. This was useful in conjunction with how the operator “felt” the pinch went. The pinch tool operator pinched several dozen practice samples and could tell from experience when a pinch didn't feel right. When some of those samples were CT scanned, the scan showed an off-nominal shape. An off-nominal shape does not guarantee that the pinch did not cold weld but when conducting our final flight pinch, we re-pinched to increase the chances of flying a successful pinch with a nominal shape.

The team also took into account some lessons learned from copper tube pinch failures for spaceflight applications in the past. The pinch point is delicate and can potentially leak if impacted. These lessons learned urged those using pinched copper tubes in spaceflight applications to protect the pinch point of the copper tube during transit and in-flight, if possible.
sections.recommendation:
- Have pinch tool operator perform several practice pinches until he/she has an intuitive feel for the pinch tool kickback that occurs for a quotgoodquot pinch versus a quotbadquot pinch.

- Perform CT scans and/or inverted metallography to observe the shape of the pinch.

- Use some means of protection for the pinch point during transit and in-flight, if possible.

# [NASA LLIS #29103] Copper Tube Pinch Failure
- **Date:** 2020-10-17
- **Organization:** Kennedy Space Center (KSC)
- **Categories:** Engineering Design; Integration and Testing; Manufacturing and Assembly; Computer-Aided Design / Manufacturing / Engineering; Flight Equipment; Flight Operations; Ground Equipment; Ground Operations; Hardware; Parts; Materials; & Processes; Payloads; Pressure Vessels; Research & Development; Risk Management / Assessment; Safety & Mission Assurance; Test & Verification; Ground processing and manifesting; Ground support systems; Quality; Reliability
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/29103

## Abstract
While pinching copper tubes is a standard practice for many applications on Earth, it is not ideal for critical spaceflight applications due to uncertainty in the verification process and the potential for a seemingly “good” pinch to separate at a later time if a cold weld isn't achieved. However, if a copper tube must be pinched, it is useful to perform a Computerized Tomography (CT) scan and inverted metallography on the pinch if possible. The likelihood of damaging the pinch point also significantly decreases when a physical protective barrier (often an epoxy) is used to protect the pinch point.

## Driving Event / Background
A copper tube was pinched as a test for the Mass Spectrometer observing lunar operations (MSolo) Calibration Gas System (CGS). A CT scan revealed that a pinch that was seemingly acceptable later separated to form a leak path.

## Lesson Learned
The pinch was initially visually inspected and helium leak checked and no visual anomalies or leaks were detected. After a CT scan revealed that the seemingly acceptable pinch separated after the helium leak check to form a leak path, an investigation was started to try to form an empirical method for verifying that a pinch has cold welded correctly. The team first turned to industry experts on copper tube pinching. While they offered a plethora of tips and tricks to try to get the best pinch possible, they were not able to provide an empirical method to ensure that a flight pinch is sealed correctly. The MSolo team then performed CT scans and inverted metallography on several copper tube pinches in an attempt to find measurements on the pinch cross-section that could be taken to distinguish a “good” pinch from a “bad” one. The results were documented, but they varied and were not useful for definitively deeming a pinch to be acceptable or not. The CT scans and inverted metallography did, however, provide insight into the shape of the pinch. A pinch with a nominal shape is more likely to have cold welded correctly. This was useful in conjunction with how the operator “felt” the pinch went. The pinch tool operator pinched several dozen practice samples and could tell from experience when a pinch didn't feel right. When some of those samples were CT scanned, the scan showed an off-nominal shape. An off-nominal shape does not guarantee that the pinch did not cold weld but when conducting our final flight pinch, we re-pinched to increase the chances of flying a successful pinch with a nominal shape.

The team also took into account some lessons learned from copper tube pinch failures for spaceflight applications in the past. The pinch point is delicate and can potentially leak if impacted. These lessons learned urged those using pinched copper tubes in spaceflight applications to protect the pinch point of the copper tube during transit and in-flight, if possible.

## Recommendation
- Have pinch tool operator perform several practice pinches until he/she has an intuitive feel for the pinch tool kickback that occurs for a quotgoodquot pinch versus a quotbadquot pinch.

- Perform CT scans and/or inverted metallography to observe the shape of the pinch.

- Use some means of protection for the pinch point during transit and in-flight, if possible.

full_text:
# [NASA LLIS #31901] For NASA programs using risk-based independent verification and validation (IV&V), detailed NASA-developed/supported simulation of key flight phases provides deeper government insight and certification ability.
- **Date:** 2020-08-02
- **Organization:** NASA (NESC)
- **Categories:** Mission Operations and Ground Support Systems; Flight Operations; Independent Verification and Validation; Safety & Mission Assurance; Test & Verification; Orbiting Vehicles; Spacecraft and Spacecraft Instruments
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/31901

## Abstract
For NASA programs engaging in risk-based IV&V of contractor-provided flight systems, a detailed, independently developed simulation of deorbit, entry, descent, and landing (DEDL) phases proved invaluable to the Commercial Crew Program (CCP) in providing government insight into and certification of the flight systems. The independent DEDL simulation also informed the CCP by allowing government investigation into areas of concern with the flight system design and/or operation during DEDL. Rapid post-flight support of a CCP spacecraft in-flight anomaly (IFA) was possible with this independent DEDL simulation, demonstrating its potential application for future flights.

## Driving Event / Background
Recent application of risk-based IV&V on NASA flight programs (e.g., CCP, Artemis Human Landing System (HLS)) relies heavily on government insight and certification of contractor-developed flight systems. One element to insight involves government review of contractor-provided detailed verification objectives demonstrating flight system acceptability relative to Program-defined constraints. Review of contractor-provided flight system descriptions and results alone provides a limited understanding of key flight system elements and operation.

## Lesson Learned
Review of contractor-provided system documentation and detailed verification objective results alone did not provide sufficient insight into the flight system for certification for the CCP. The process of developing an independent 6 degree-of-freedom DEDL simulation, using contractor-provided detailed descriptions of the flight system and its operation and using the simulation to independently generate critical detailed verification objective results, provided the depth of understanding needed for government insight and vehicle certification. As part of the development process, interaction with contractor personnel to confirm that the government simulation models correctly reflected the flight system and provided results consistent with the contractor simulations led to confidence in both government and contractor simulation-generated results. Another byproduct of this process was the good communication and interactions between NASA and contractor engineering teams (e.g., Guidance, Navigation, and Control (GNC)) that persisted throughout development, certification, and operational flights. Once developed, the independent DEDL simulation allowed NASA to investigate challenging cases in the flight system operational space without distracting the contractor during final flight system development and operations unless an issue was uncovered. A more NESC-focused capability afforded by this independent DEDL simulation was the ability of the team to rapidly participate in an IFA investigation by looking into several possible causes using the previously developed and checked out simulation.

## Recommendation
NASA programs using risk-based IV&V to certify a contractor-provided flight system (e.g., CCP and Artemis HLS) should independently develop detailed simulations in key flight phases (e.g., DEDL, ascent, and rendezvous/proximity operations) to model, investigate, and confirm detailed verification objective results to provide the insight necessary to understand the system for certification. Interaction between government and contractor engineers should be encouraged during the development process to confirm that simulation models and results are consistent between the government and contractor simulations. This simulation capability should be maintained after certification (during operational flights) to permit government assistance to contractor flight systems during an IFA or post-flight investigation of an IFA.

sections.abstract:
The Launch Release Subsystem (LRS) is a critical electrical subsystem located on the Mobile Launcher (ML). LRS generates the signals used to release and retract the umbilicals from the Space Launch System (SLS) vehicle at T-0/launch. It is also used to command and monitor the Launch Abort System (LAS) and Booster Ignition Safe and Arm (S&A) devices as well as Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage (ICPS) functions.

Due to the critical nature of most LRS functions, redundancy was heavily considered during the design and development phase; however, an issue with the redundancy architecture was identified after the subsystem already completed certification. The root cause of the problem was that the redundancy and failure analysis for LRS was incomplete. The analysis only reviewed how LRS interfaced with the end items (umbilical release mechanisms, S&A devices, etc) and did not consider potential failure scenarios of other subsystems that interface with LRS.

During the design and development phase, a complete end-to-end evaluation/analysis of redundancy and potential failure scenarios should be performed. The analysis should not be limited to only the subsystem under review but should also account for all interfacing subsystems.
