# [NASA LLIS #18802] Software Traceability
- **Date:** 2016-11-04
- **Organization:** Langley Research Center (LARC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Aeronautics Research; Human Exploration and Operations; Science; Space Technology
- **Categories:** Software; Software Engineering
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/18802

## Abstract
Handling software requirements differently than other project requirements creates unnecessary work. The Stratospheric Aerosol and Gas Experiment III on the International Space Station (SAGE III on ISS) Project met the intent of the NASA Procedural Requirement (NPR) for Software Engineering (NPR 7150.2) requirements by tracking them within the existing Requirements Management processes established by the project’s Systems Engineers.

## Driving Event / Background
NPR 7150.2 requires four process requirements related to bidirectional traceability. These requirements consist of tracking software requirements at six multiple levels from the top-down and bottom-up. This includes between the software requirements and higher-level requirements, software requirements and software architecture, software architecture and software design, software requirements and software design, software design and software code, and software requirements and software test procedures. SAGE III on ISS met the intent of these requirements by tracking them within the existing Requirements Management processes established by the project’s Systems Engineers. This process established a structured method of handling requirements definition, management, and verification using CORETM as their primary tool. This process provided for systematic identification of the flight software requirements and automated the traceability of the software requirements to the higher and lower level requirements along with the verification artifacts. The verification process included the normal software test processes that ensured the requirements and software works in the intended operational environment. This confidence is gained by running the software at various levels against test scenarios designed to detect failures or defects while accomplishing the intended functions (requirements). The software product’s technical excellence was assured through the normal project and Branch-level Peer Reviews and project technical reviews which involved the project management, engineering, assurance, and Branch-level Technical Authorities.

## Lesson Learned
Software requirements can be successfully managed within a project’s existing project-level requirements management and verification processes.

## Recommendation
Manage flight software requirements within existing project-level requirements management and verification processes as successfully demonstrated by the SAGE III on ISS Project.

sections.abstract:
The spectrum of the quartz lamps originally used for the Stratospheric Aerosol and Gas Experiment (SAGE) III on the International Space Station (ISS) Instrument Assembly (IA) Thermal VACuum (TVAC) testing did not match the assumed spectrum used in the thermal model.

To achieve correlation with the thermal model, a test was performed to characterize the solar flux level within the chamber as well as the chamber thermal gradients. This allowed for an improved correlation of the IA model; however, the additional time and resources required to perform the characterization test and complex model correlation were not ideal.

For the Instrument Payload (IP) TVAC test, a heater plate system was designed, built and installed in the facility. This system, coupled with the chamber’s cold shroud, provided the necessary environments for the IP to reach its temperature targets without using the quartz lamps.

To achieve correlation with the thermal model, a test was performed to characterize the solar flux level within the chamber as well as the chamber thermal gradients. This allowed for an improved correlation of the IA model; however, the additional time and resources required to perform the characterization test and complex model correlation were not ideal.

For the Instrument Payload (IP) TVAC test, a heater plate system was designed, built and installed in the facility. This system, coupled with the chamber’s cold shroud, provided the necessary environments for the IP to reach its temperature targets without using the quartz lamps.

## Driving Event / Background
The spectrum of the quartz lamps originally used for the Stratospheric Aerosol and Gas Experiment (SAGE) III on the International Space Station (ISS) Instrument Assembly (IA) Thermal VACuum (TVAC) testing did not match the assumed spectrum used in the thermal model.

To achieve correlation with the thermal model, a test was performed to characterize the solar flux level within the chamber as well as the chamber thermal gradients. This allowed for an improved correlation of the IA model; however, the additional time and resources required to perform the characterization test and complex model correlation were not ideal.

For the Instrument Payload (IP) TVAC test, a heater plate system was designed, built and installed in the facility. This system, coupled with the chamber’s cold shroud, provided the necessary environments for the IP to reach its temperature targets without using the quartz lamps.

## Lesson Learned
Quartz lamps supply radiant heat largely in the solar spectrum, but the distribution depends upon lamp setting which creates significant complications for model correlation. Correlating results with a thermal model may be easier and more successful by using heater plates rather than developing a thermal model to account for the necessary details of the lamp spectrum.

## Recommendation
If it is desired to correlate thermal models to TVAC test data, it is best to avoid the use of quartz lamps.

title: Software Triple Redundancy

categories: Software; Software Engineering

sections.abstract: Where storage is not an issue, using triple redundancy for all stored data is simpler and more robust than double redundancy or a mix of double and triple redundancy for error checking.
sections.driving_event: The Interface Adapter Module (IAM) of the Stratospheric Aerosol and Gas Experiment III on the International Space Station (SAGE III on ISS) provides electronics interfaces between the various elements of the instrument and the ISS. The IAM flight software is responsible for ensuring that its stored data is not lost or unusable by a single corruption or failure of flash memory.
sections.lesson_learned: Triple redundancy for items in flash memory is a simple and uniform way of identifying memory corruption in space. The advantage to triple redundancy is the ability to detect which copy of a file is corrupt, and correct it either autonomously or by command. Combining triple redundancy with a Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) allows the software to determine which files have been corrupt, and to ensure that files are correctly read, even when they are read by voting the contents of the three copies. The IAM flight software images are triple redundant. Triple redundancy is simpler and more uniform than the implementation of double redundancy in the IAM flight software. In the case of double redundancy there was a main and redundant copy, while for triple redundancy all copies were equal. Having code to treat each copy differently added some complexity because with double redundancy there is no ability to vote, so there is a need for some other strategy like nominating one as the main. In this case all data had CRCs, so it was not a problem of determining which copy to use, only that having non-equal treatment of each copy meant that the code needed special cases to distinguish between the two copies. For us, the trade was in available space – the only advantage of double redundancy would have been less space used. This was not an issue in this specific case, so we would have been better off using triple redundancy for all items stored in flash memory.
sections.recommendation: The recommendation is to consider triple redundancy the default option for storing persistent data on flight systems. It provides a simple and well known way to solve the problem of data corruption and provides the opportunity to correct corrupt data by command or autonomously. It is also recommended to store a Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) along the three copies of each file to ensure that the correct image can be identified.

# [NASA LLIS #18803] Software Triple Redundancy
- **Date:** 2016-11-04
- **Organization:** Langley Research Center (LARC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Aeronautics Research; Human Exploration and Operations; Science; Space Technology
- **Categories:** Software; Software Engineering
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/18803

## Abstract
Where storage is not an issue, using triple redundancy for all stored data is simpler and more robust than double redundancy or a mix of double and triple redundancy for error checking.

## Driving Event / Background
The Interface Adapter Module (IAM) of the Stratospheric Aerosol and Gas Experiment III on the International Space Station (SAGE III on ISS) provides electronics interfaces between the various elements of the instrument and the ISS. The IAM flight software is responsible for ensuring that its stored data is not lost or unusable by a single corruption or failure of flash memory.

## Lesson Learned
Triple redundancy for items in flash memory is a simple and uniform way of identifying memory corruption in space. The advantage to triple redundancy is the ability to detect which copy of a file is corrupt, and correct it either autonomously or by command. Combining triple redundancy with a Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) allows the software to determine which files have been corrupt, and to ensure that files are correctly read, even when they are read by voting the contents of the three copies. The IAM flight software images are triple redundant. Triple redundancy is simpler and more uniform than the implementation of double redundancy in the IAM flight software. In the case of double redundancy there was a main and redundant copy, while for triple redundancy all copies were equal. Having code to treat each copy differently added some complexity because with double redundancy there is no ability to vote, so there is a need for some other strategy like nominating one as the main. In this case all data had CRCs, so it was not a problem of determining which copy to use, only that having non-equal treatment of each copy meant that the code needed special cases to distinguish between the two copies. For us, the trade was in available space – the only advantage of double redundancy would have been less space used. This was not an issue in this specific case, so we would have been better off using triple redundancy for all items stored in flash memory.

## Recommendation
The recommendation is to consider triple redundancy the default option for storing persistent data on flight systems. It provides a simple and well known way to solve the problem of data corruption and provides the opportunity to correct corrupt data by command or autonomously. It is also recommended to store a Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) along the three copies of each file to ensure that the correct image can be identified.

sections.abstract: Typical software developments require interfacing with commercial hardware through software applications called drivers. These drivers are often identified early during the design and implementation, installed onto the development machines, and then overlooked without being configuration managed. However without these support drivers, the developed solution cannot be transitioned to other similar hardware. In addition if the hardware being used experiences failure, it can become a research effort to re-identify the required drivers, locate their sources, and re-establish the supporting environment (hardware and software).
sections.driving_event: Typical software developments require interfacing with commercial hardware through software applications called drivers. These drivers are often identified early during the design and implementation, installed onto the development machines, and then overlooked without being configuration managed. However without these support drivers, the developed solution cannot be transitioned to other similar hardware. In addition if the hardware being used experiences failure, it can become a research effort to re-identify the required drivers, locate their sources, and re-establish the supporting environment (hardware and software).
sections.lesson_learned: As software solutions are designed, any supporting software application driver or third party supporting software needs to be clearly documented in the software design documentation. These supporting applications (and associated documentation) must be then configuration controlled just like the software being developed. The configuration control needs to account for any changes to the installed or uninstalled versions. In order to verify the required information exists, the first formal test of the developed software should start from a generic hardware platform and then load the required supporting drivers to verify the installation/build process. Otherwise, the final software solution may be dependent on a particular set and version of drivers that was not properly documented or tested.set and version of drivers that was not properly documented or tested.
sections.recommendation: Configuration manage and test all software required for the final solution. This includes the developed software and supporting drivers. Although not done for in the context of the current project, it has been suggested that the lesson be expanded to suggest submitting any drivers written from scratch as a New Technology Report (NTR – see https://invention.nasa.gov/ ). This will get the drivers recorded in NASA’s software catalog (https://software.nasa.gov/) and will help prevent the wheel from being reinvented by other projects who may need similar drivers.

## Abstract
Typical software developments require interfacing with commercial hardware through software applications called drivers. These drivers are often identified early during the design and implementation, installed onto the development machines, and then overlooked without being configuration managed. However without these support drivers, the developed solution cannot be transitioned to other similar hardware. In addition if the hardware being used experiences failure, it can become a research effort to re-identify the required drivers, locate their sources, and re-establish the supporting environment (hardware and software).

## Driving Event / Background
Typical software developments require interfacing with commercial hardware through software applications called drivers. These drivers are often identified early during the design and implementation, installed onto the development machines, and then overlooked without being configuration managed. However without these support drivers, the developed solution cannot be transitioned to other similar hardware. In addition if the hardware being used experiences failure, it can become a research effort to re-identify the required drivers, locate their sources, and re-establish the supporting environment (hardware and software).

## Lesson Learned
As software solutions are designed, any supporting software application driver or third party supporting software needs to be clearly documented in the software design documentation. These supporting applications (and associated documentation) must be then configuration controlled just like the software being developed. The configuration control needs to account for any changes to the installed or uninstalled versions. In order to verify the required information exists, the first formal test of the developed software should start from a generic hardware platform and then load the required supporting drivers to verify the installation/build process. Otherwise, the final software solution may be dependent on a particular set and version of drivers that was not properly documented or tested.set and version of drivers that was not properly documented or tested.

## Recommendation
Configuration manage and test all software required for the final solution. This includes the developed software and supporting drivers. Although not done for in the context of the current project, it has been suggested that the lesson be expanded to suggest submitting any drivers written from scratch as a New Technology Report (NTR – see https://invention.nasa.gov/ ). This will get the drivers recorded in NASA’s software catalog (https://software.nasa.gov/) and will help prevent the wheel from being reinvented by other projects who may need similar drivers.

title: Reliance on Part Hermeticity and Residual Gas Analysis on GOES-R Bipolar Junction Transistors
categories: Integration and Testing; Parts; Materials; & Processes; Quality; Reliability; Engineering design and project processes and standards
categories_list: Engineering design and project processes and standards

sections.abstract: As with most large projects, GOES-R relied on hermetic, Joint Army Navy military grade (JANS) parts to assure reliability, and the limited effectiveness in the inherent processes to prevent corrosion in ambient, but controlled conditions. Two JANS bipolar junction transistors (BJTs) experienced failures in testing resulting in excessive use of resources and a significant slip in launch date to replace parts without any assurance that replacement parts were better than those installed.
sections.driving_event: Late in development of the first in the GOES-R satellite series, an in-circuit failure of a JANS2N3637 bipolar junction transistor (BJT) in a TO-39 package was encountered that was traced to corrosion in one of the bondwires. Failure analysis and residual gas analysis (RGA) of the failed part revealed the presence of moisture and atmospheric ingress. Within a few weeks of this event a similar failure was encountered involving a JANS2N2222a BJT in a TO-18 package on the Insight project, experienced by the same prime contractor. This part showed elevated moisture in the internal cavity. It appears that some parts in the lot had elevated hydrogen that may have then been involved in a chemical reaction prompted by handling of the part and weakness in the seal. Both of these parts problems prompted the project to replace dozens of parts without any proof or indication that the replacement parts were from better lots than the original lots, at the cost of multiple millions of dollars and a significant launch delay. In both cases on the same project, the reliance on part hermeticity and RGA combined with fine and gross leak testing cost the project enormous amount of money, months of schedule usage, and elevated the risks to the project substantially due to the excessive amounts of rework, without any certainty in the improvement of the lots. The “partial hermeticity” in each case likely trapped moisture and contaminants to cause ideal conditions for corrosion. The project had no choice but to replace the parts because there was no way to provide assurance that the remaining parts would be able to survive 15 years on-orbit, while new parts that have not experienced any anomalies provide maximum confidence. Unfortunately, there are no statistically significant means to assure the integrity of hermeticity across the parts being used with high confidence without destroying most of the parts.
sections.lesson_learned:
- The reliance on hermetic parts can drive up both technical and programmatic risk by (1) trapping contaminants in the parts during the manufacturing process, (2) allowing contaminants to enter the parts for those that are on the fine edge of being hermetic, and (3) providing false confidence that the use of such parts provides substantial protection against part failure due to corrosion.

- The sample size for RGA testing under MIL-PRF-19500 only provides a top-level indicator that parts in the lot are free from significant elevated moisture or contaminants. Furthermore, there is no practice increased sample size that would provide enough statistical basis.

- Before replacing parts always verify with certainty that the replacement parts are better than the existing parts.

- The use of JANS parts is neither necessary or sufficient for assuring integrity or reliability of parts through integration and testing (I&T).

- Sound system level testing is an essential means to flesh out many problematic parts issues. There should never be a consideration that the use of JANS parts can supersede good design or robust environmental testing.
sections.recommendation:
1. Recognize that parts intended to be hermetic are subject to screening and destructive physical analysis ( DPA) processes that are not statistically significant. This leaves an opportunity for escapes in hermetic parts subject MIL-PRF-19500 (to include JANS cavity parts such as BJTs in TO cans).

2. Do not replace parts based on a part failure or alert without considering fully the risk of replacement and confirmation that the replacement lot is statistically better than the installed lot.

## Abstract
As with most large projects, GOES-R relied on hermetic, Joint Army Navy military grade (JANS) parts to assure reliability, and the limited effectiveness in the inherent processes to prevent corrosion in ambient, but controlled conditions. Two JANS bipolar junction transistors (BJTs) experienced failures in testing resulting in excessive use of resources and a significant slip in launch date to replace parts without any assurance that replacement parts were better than those installed.

## Driving Event / Background
Late in development of the first in the GOES-R satellite series, an in-circuit failure of a JANS2N3637 bipolar junction transistor (BJT) in a TO-39 package was encountered that was traced to corrosion in one of the bondwires. Failure analysis and residual gas analysis (RGA) of the failed part revealed the presence of moisture and atmospheric ingress. Within a few weeks of this event a similar failure was encountered involving a JANS2N2222a BJT in a TO-18 package on the Insight project, experienced by the same prime contractor. This part showed elevated moisture in the internal cavity. It appears that some parts in the lot had elevated hydrogen that may have then been involved in a chemical reaction prompted by handling of the part and weakness in the seal. Both of these parts problems prompted the project to replace dozens of parts without any proof or indication that the replacement parts were from better lots than the original lots, at the cost of multiple millions of dollars and a significant launch delay. In both cases on the same project, the reliance on part hermeticity and RGA combined with fine and gross leak testing cost the project enormous amount of money, months of schedule usage, and elevated the risks to the project substantially due to the excessive amounts of rework, without any certainty in the improvement of the lots. The “partial hermeticity” in each case likely trapped moisture and contaminants to cause ideal conditions for corrosion. The project had no choice but to replace the parts because there was no way to provide assurance that the remaining parts would be able to survive 15 years on-orbit, while new parts that have not experienced any anomalies provide maximum confidence. Unfortunately, there are no statistically significant means to assure the integrity of hermeticity across the parts being used with high confidence without destroying most of the parts.

## Lesson Learned
- The reliance on hermetic parts can drive up both technical and programmatic risk by (1) trapping contaminants in the parts during the manufacturing process, (2) allowing contaminants to enter the parts for those that are on the fine edge of being hermetic, and (3) providing false confidence that the use of such parts provides substantial protection against part failure due to corrosion.

- The sample size for RGA testing under MIL-PRF-19500 only provides a top-level indicator that parts in the lot are free from significant elevated moisture or contaminants. Furthermore, there is no practice increased sample size that would provide enough statistical basis.

- Before replacing parts always verify with certainty that the replacement parts are better than the existing parts.

- The use of JANS parts is neither necessary or sufficient for assuring integrity or reliability of parts through integration and testing (I&T).

- Sound system level testing is an essential means to flesh out many problematic parts issues. There should never be a consideration that the use of JANS parts can supersede good design or robust environmental testing.

## Recommendation
1. Recognize that parts intended to be hermetic are subject to screening and destructive physical analysis ( DPA) processes that are not statistically significant. This leaves an opportunity for escapes in hermetic parts subject MIL-PRF-19500 (to include JANS cavity parts such as BJTs in TO cans).

2. Do not replace parts based on a part failure or alert without considering fully the risk of replacement and confirmation that the replacement lot is statistically better than the installed lot.

title: A NASA Project Manager Shouldn't Overreact to In-Flight ‘Emergencies’ or ‘The Value of Doing Nothing’
mission_directorate: Human Exploration and Operations; Science; Space Technology
categories: Flight Operations; Mishap Reporting; Payloads; Risk Management / Assessment; Spacecraft; Mission control Planning; Mission operations systems; Affect of Cultural factors on long-term human and robotic missions; Communications between different offices and contractor personnel; Cross Agency coordination; Education and public engagement; International partner coordination; Program planning / development and management; Risk management
categories_list: Affect of Cultural factors on long-term human and robotic missions

sections.abstract: In a July 2016 Pause & Learn session attended by JPL project managers, Jim Erickson explained the value of a planned and consistent response to a putative in-flight emergency. The project manager should closely monitor developments and provide early and frequent reports to the project team and to upper management. Because spacecraft in-flight safing events that require an immediate ground response are rare, it is important for the project manager to avoid precipitous action.
sections.driving_event:
James K. Erickson of the NASA/Caltech Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) is the project manager post-launch for the Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) project. During Phase E, he also served as project manager for the Galileo mission to Jupiter, project manager for the Mars Exploration Rovers (MER), and project manager for the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) project, as well as worked on a number of other JPL spaceflight projects. On July 19, 2016, he gave a Pause & Learn presentation (Reference (1)) to a meeting of JPL project managers on “The Value of Doing Nothing.”

During his service as the project manager on the four successful NASA “flagship” missions, Jim recalled experiencing 50 flight system entries into safe mode on 5 spacecraft/probes—Mars Science Laboratory (MSL), Spirit, Opportunity, MRO, and Galileo. Of these 50 anomalies, only the MSL Sol 200 Anomaly (Reference (2)) and perhaps a couple others were truly emergencies that had to be dealt with promptly. For example, doing nothing was not an option for the Sol 200 Anomaly; but when the Opportunity rover became stuck in the Martian sand in May 2005 (Reference (3)), JPL had months to resolve the issue.

Some vehicles experienced recurrent anomalies including some that, in retrospect, could have been predicted:

- Galileo experienced 29 safe mode entries, to the point where the project even developed a software patch that “ignored” one particular type of reset. It was related to the radiation environment and occurred during near approaches to Jupiter.

- MRO experienced several categories of resets that would occur periodically.

Jim explained that for each of the safe mode anomalies, “at least initially I had the sick feeling in the pit of my stomach that this might be ‘the one’.”

Jim suggests that the foremost job of a project manager during a putative operational emergency is to inform and manage up the chain of authority-- both at JPL and NASA HQ. “Managing” in this context refers to insulating the project team that is working the technical problem from the distractions caused by outside parties’ interest in the anomaly. All interactions with JPL management, NASA, and the media should pass through the project manager.

References:

1. Jim Erickson, “Reflections on Spacecraft Emergencies, or ‘The Value of Doing Nothing’,” July 19, 2016.

2. “MSL Sol 200 Anomaly,” NEN #11201, NASA Lesson Learned Information System, April 29, 2014. https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/11201

3. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FNPDlSgUo5A

4. “FSW ASSERT During AM MRO Window,” JPL Incident Surprise Anomaly (ISA) No. 59834, July 3, 2016.
sections.lesson_learned:
Much value can be derived from a planned and consistent response to a putative in-flight emergency. A project manager should exhibit a steady, calm demeanor in all interactions with upper management, and most importantly, with the project team. This is because the project team members take their cues from the project leadership. If the project manager exhibits confidence in the team, both the team members and JPL upper management feel confident.

In contrast, allowing panic to spread within the project and to upper management is unlikely to elicit the optimal response, and may be counter-productive.
sections.recommendation:
1. What to do first: - Make sure your team is properly notified that there is an issue! - Make sure your pre-identified anomaly contacts are beginning to work the problem: If not, get them engaged. - Review (at least mentally) your anomaly response procedure(s). - Make sure your response team is organized, with an anomaly lead to serve as the PM’s point of contact. - Take your first pulse on the anomaly: Is this a limited impact, slowly unfolding, issue? Is the vehicle taking care of itself? Did the flight system’s autonomous fault protection respond to the anomaly properly? Does downlinked health data indicate that the vehicle status is degrading? Degrading rapidly?

2. What to do next: - Identify the basics about your vehicle state, even if it is tentative, or you have limited knowledge. Be aware that you must cope with limited information flow from the spacecraft. For example, at the 10 bps emergency mode, Galileo telemetry took a long time to generate all the information necessary for complete state knowledge. Mars surface assets may have only orbital relay capability, or extremely limited direct-to-Earth downlink. - Communicate what you know upwards, even if all you can do is phone your JPL boss and the NASA HQ contact and give them a 2-minute rundown. Keeping communications flowing to your superiors is vital, particularly in the rapid-pace social media climate. You don’t want your boss to be blindsided by media that have been tipped to an issue by bloggers. An e-mail to the JPL Director is not sufficient, as he may be asleep or in a press conference where he is about to be blindsided by a blogger. Also, let the Director know specifically when you plan to provide more information. Write a crisp concise summary to follow a phone chat. Figure 1 (Reference (4)) is a sample that was sent to the Mars Program Manager, the NASA Principal Investigator, and senior MSL project staff. Make sure your team (including all science members) knows what is going on. On one flagship mission, the mission scientists weren't aware the spacecraft was in safe mode until they realized they hadn't been receiving their science return. When distributing anomaly information, be sensitive to ITAR/EAR restrictions.

| Fuk/Dave- Curiosity is healthy, stable, and currently operating nominally in safe mode. On July 2 [2016] at about 3:00 pm PDT, Curiosity did not communicate with MRO as expected. Afterwards, an Odyssey pass did not occur, and the team began listening with the DSN [NASA Deep Space Network] for safe mode carrier, and detected it. Subsequently, at about 2:00 am July 3, the MSL team received telemetry via MRO that indicated we are in surface standby, with nothing marked unhealthy by Curiosity’s prime computer, the Rover Compute Element B (RCE-B), in safe mode. Flight software seems to indicate it asserted a Fatal interrupt, but subsequent expected re–boots occurred normally. Fault protect seems to indicate at least one reset, and possibly more. On the first look with limited data, Power looks nominal, bus balance indicates the RTG [Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator] short is still in place as expected. With limited data, it appears that flight software detected a error in a transaction between the Malin Science Camera (MastCAM - MCAM) [Mast Camera] and the RCE. The indication was that the data write from the MCAM was attempted in a different location than the RCE gave permission to MCAM to write in. At this time, there is no indication that any hardware was involved in the error, but more analysis is required. Monitor the incident continuously so that you understand the time remaining to analyze the situation and to make a decision on a course of action. - There is much value in “doing nothing” when an improper action may be irreversible. No decision may be superior to a decision that was timely but bad. # [NASA LLIS #18201] A NASA Project Manager Shouldn't Overreact to In-Flight ‘Emergencies’ or ‘The Value of Doing Nothing’
- **Date:** 2016-10-18
- **Organization:** Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations; Science; Space Technology
- **Categories:** Flight Operations; Mishap Reporting; Payloads; Risk Management / Assessment; Spacecraft; Mission control Planning; Mission operations systems; Affect of Cultural factors on long-term human and robotic missions; Communications between different offices and contractor personnel; Cross Agency coordination; Education and public engagement; International partner coordination; Program planning / development and management; Risk management
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/18201

## Abstract
In a July 2016 Pause & Learn session attended by JPL project managers, Jim Erickson explained the value of a planned and consistent response to a putative in-flight emergency. The project manager should closely monitor developments and provide early and frequent reports to the project team and to upper management. Because spacecraft in-flight safing events that require an immediate ground response are rare, it is important for the project manager to avoid precipitous action.

## Driving Event / Background
James K. Erickson of the NASA/Caltech Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) is the project manager post-launch for the Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) project. During Phase E, he also served as project manager for the Galileo mission to Jupiter, project manager for the Mars Exploration Rovers (MER), and project manager for the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) project, as well as worked on a number of other JPL spaceflight projects. On July 19, 2016, he gave a Pause & Learn presentation (Reference (1)) to a meeting of JPL project managers on “The Value of Doing Nothing.”

During his service as the project manager on the four successful NASA “flagship” missions, Jim recalled experiencing 50 flight system entries into safe mode on 5 spacecraft/probes—Mars Science Laboratory (MSL), Spirit, Opportunity, MRO, and Galileo. Of these 50 anomalies, only the MSL Sol 200 Anomaly (Reference (2)) and perhaps a couple others were truly emergencies that had to be dealt with promptly. For example, doing nothing was not an option for the Sol 200 Anomaly; but when the Opportunity rover became stuck in the Martian sand in May 2005 (Reference (3)), JPL had months to resolve the issue.

Some vehicles experienced recurrent anomalies including some that, in retrospect, could have been predicted:

- Galileo experienced 29 safe mode entries, to the point where the project even developed a software patch that “ignored” one particular type of reset. It was related to the radiation environment and occurred during near approaches to Jupiter.

- MRO experienced several categories of resets that would occur periodically.

Jim explained that for each of the safe mode anomalies, “at least initially I had the sick feeling in the pit of my stomach that this might be ‘the one’.”

Jim suggests that the foremost job of a project manager during a putative operational emergency is to inform and manage up the chain of authority-- both at JPL and NASA HQ. “Managing” in this context refers to insulating the project team that is working the technical problem from the distractions caused by outside parties’ interest in the anomaly. All interactions with JPL management, NASA, and the media should pass through the project manager.

References:

1. Jim Erickson, “Reflections on Spacecraft Emergencies, or ‘The Value of Doing Nothing’,” July 19, 2016.

2. “MSL Sol 200 Anomaly,” NEN #11201, NASA Lesson Learned Information System, April 29, 2014. https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/11201

3. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FNPDlSgUo5A

4. “FSW ASSERT During AM MRO Window,” JPL Incident Surprise Anomaly (ISA) No. 59834, July 3, 2016.

## Lesson Learned
Much value can be derived from a planned and consistent response to a putative in-flight emergency. A project manager should exhibit a steady, calm demeanor in all interactions with upper management, and most importantly, with the project team. This is because the project team members take their cues from the project leadership. If the project manager exhibits confidence in the team, both the team members and JPL upper management feel confident.

In contrast, allowing panic to spread within the project and to upper management is unlikely to elicit the optimal response, and may be counter-productive.

## Recommendation
1. What to do first: - Make sure your team is properly notified that there is an issue! - Make sure your pre-identified anomaly contacts are beginning to work the problem: If not, get them engaged. - Review (at least mentally) your anomaly response procedure(s). - Make sure your response team is organized, with an anomaly lead to serve as the PM’s point of contact. - Take your first pulse on the anomaly: Is this a limited impact, slowly unfolding, issue? Is the vehicle taking care of itself? Did the flight system’s autonomous fault protection respond to the anomaly properly? Does downlinked health data indicate that the vehicle status is degrading? Degrading rapidly?

2. What to do next: - Identify the basics about your vehicle state, even if it is tentative, or you have limited knowledge. Be aware that you must cope with limited information flow from the spacecraft. For example, at the 10 bps emergency mode, Galileo telemetry took a long time to generate all the information necessary for complete state knowledge. Mars surface assets may have only orbital relay capability, or extremely limited direct-to-Earth downlink. - Communicate what you know upwards, even if all you can do is phone your JPL boss and the NASA HQ contact and give them a 2-minute rundown. Keeping communications flowing to your superiors is vital, particularly in the rapid-pace social media climate. You don’t want your boss to be blindsided by media that have been tipped to an issue by bloggers. An e-mail to the JPL Director is not sufficient, as he may be asleep or in a press conference where he is about to be blindsided by a blogger. Also, let the Director know specifically when you plan to provide more information. Write a crisp concise summary to follow a phone chat. Figure 1 (Reference (4)) is a sample that was sent to the Mars Program Manager, the NASA Principal Investigator, and senior MSL project staff. Make sure your team (including all science members) knows what is going on. On one flagship mission, the mission scientists weren't aware the spacecraft was in safe mode until they realized they hadn't been receiving their science return. When distributing anomaly information, be sensitive to ITAR/EAR restrictions.

| Fuk/Dave- Curiosity is healthy, stable, and currently operating nominally in safe mode. On July 2 [2016] at about 3:00 pm PDT, Curiosity did not communicate with MRO as expected. Afterwards, an Odyssey pass did not occur, and the team began listening with the DSN [NASA Deep Space Network] for safe mode carrier, and detected it. Subsequently, at about 2:00 am July 3, the MSL team received telemetry via MRO that indicated we are in surface standby, with nothing marked unhealthy by Curiosity’s prime computer, the Rover Compute Element B (RCE-B), in safe mode. sections.abstract: Flooding of the Mars 2020 project testbed was only averted because an alert engineer observed an indicator light warning that an evaporator overflow pan was about to overflow. Subsequent review revealed a trend of incidents in which JPL building utility anomalies posed a threat to high-value JPL products. Buildings housing critical facilities or hardware should be assessed for their vulnerability to building structural and utility anomalies. New construction should seek to avert such vulnerabilities.
sections.driving_event:
The NASA/Caltech Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) makes extensive use of high fidelity testbeds, incorporating flight or flight-like hardware and software, for system development and for system-level test with the equipment powered. During mission operations following launch, the testbed also performs an essential role in reproducing and correcting the problems and failures that occur to spacecraft during spaceflight and surface operations. Assuring that a JPL project has adequate components to support extensive testing in the testbed has proven to be a success factor for projects that typically launch only a single spacecraft. Consequently, a system testbed may contain hardware that the project cannot replace.

The system testbed for the Mars 2020 rover project is located in a JPL test facility that also houses the testbeds for Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) and Mars Exploration Rover (MER). They share a common humidifier system for treating ambient airflow in the vicinity of the testbeds. At 7:00 am on July 2, 2014, a project engineer observed that a warning indicator light on the humidifier’s secondary containment drip evaporator overflow pan was illuminated, and he immediately covered the hardware on the Mars 2020 testbed with an anti-static plastic sheet. A few minutes later, water streamed onto the covered equipment (Reference (1)).

It was quickly determined that the humidifier system strainer was plugged, causing water (instead of steam for humidity control) to spray into the air plenum located in the ceiling and to stream onto the covered equipment (Figure 1). No damage to any testbed equipment occurred. The humidifier alarm is connected to an emergency notification system that alerted the JPL (on duty 24/7) facility maintenance contractor; they responded to the alarm, turned off the water and cleaned the plugged strainers. Subsequent investigation, however, established that the preventative maintenance instructions for the building did not show the location of the strainers; nor did they require periodic cleaning of the strainers, which had never been cleaned (Reference (2)).

JPL System Safety (Reference (3)) views this incident as a "close call": if it had occurred late at night or if alert staff had not been present, significant damage to irreplaceable Mars 2020 flight development and flight support hardware would have resulted. In addition, the incident presented a personnel safety slip hazard because the secondary drain routed overflow onto the smooth tile floor directly in front of the access doors to the facility. This incident also added to the impression that the testbed facility has had a trend of anomalies since 2003, including a negative pressure event (Reference (4)) where the air conditioning vents pulled air out instead of blowing it in. (This made it “nearly impossible” to open the outward-hinged doors.) It was discovered after this air conditioning event that (like the building reported in Reference (5) that experienced a flood) the building was not on the JPL critical facility list.

References:

1. JPL Mishap Report No. 3087 (Bldg. 317), July 2, 2014.

2. “Water leak on ceiling in RCE lab on 7/2/2014,” JPL Problem/Failure Report No. 56641, July 8, 2014.

3. “July 2014 Testbed Mishap,” e-mail from Matthew Riley, May 11, 2016.

4. “Water leak in CETB lab,” JPL Problem/Failure Report No. 56630, July 7, 2014.

5. “Poor Coordination of Routine Maintenance Spoiled an Important Test,” NEN No. 10401, NASA Lesson Learned Information System (LLIS), August 11, 2014.

6. “Provide Adequate Maintenance and Hazard Response for UPS Units,” NEN No. 12101, NASA Lesson Learned Information System (LLIS), July 14, 2014.

7. JPL Mishap Report No. 0100 (Bldg. 318), November 11, 2002.

8. JPL Mishap Report No. 1995 (Bldg. 306), November 13, 2009.

9. JPL Mishap Report No. 2001 (Bldg. 306), November 24, 2009.

10. JPL Mishap Report No. 2365 (Bldg. 317), February 17, 2011.

11. JPL Mishap Report No. 1822 (Bldg. 179), February 14, 2009.

12. “Ensure Test Monitoring Software Imposes Limits to Prevent Overtest,” NEN No. 1529, NASA Lesson Learned Information System (LLIS), October 11, 2004.

13. “Contamination of the Mars Observer Spacecraft by Environmental Conditioning,” NEN No. 441, NASA Lesson Learned Information System (LLIS), August 23, 1996.
sections.lesson_learned:
There exists a trend of incidents (see References (5) and (6)) with JPL building utility anomalies posing a threat to JPL products, and the JPL critical facility list does not appear to have been effective in forestalling them. Indeed, ceiling leaks from clogged humidifier or air conditioning drains are fairly commonplace at JPL (References (7) through (10)). For example, in March 2006 (Reference (7)), a wet ceiling tile fell, narrowly missing the Power Processing Unit (PPU) test area for the Dawn project (Figures 1 and 2). Without proactive steps as JPL buildings age, problems like corroded pipes (Reference (11)) and leaky roofs could become more prevalent. JPL facility safety surveys are intended to focus on laboratory-specific issues like ESD protection and use of protective goggles, rather than on building maintenance issues.

Figure 2 . General location of DAWN mishap

Figure 3 . Configuration of Dawn PPU/ion engine Digital Control & Interface Unit (DCIU) test lab during mishap It is an accepted practice to perform Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) to identify all potential failure modes that could be induced by ground support equipment. For example, the project seeks to assure that the power output of commercial test equipment cannot in any circumstance damage the flight equipment to which it is connected (Reference (12)). Similarly, system safety engineers at the launch site verify that the air conditioning routed to a launch shroud cannot serve as a source of payload contamination (Reference (13)). However, there is a demarcation of responsibility where testbed safety is evaluated by aerospace engineers while building utilities are vouchsafed by building construction and maintenance personnel. For example, FMEA is a specialized reliability engineering task that is not typically performed on building utilities.
sections.recommendation:
1. JPL System Safety should identify especially critical buildings where harm to their contents would pose a significant (i.e., possibly irrecoverable) setback to flight projects. (It is not uncommon for JPL facilities to be repurposed for critical tasks or storage that are not reflected on the JPL critical facilities list.) These buildings should be assessed for their vulnerability to a list of common (e.g., leaky roof, power outage) and not-so-common building structural and utility anomalies. Remedial action should be taken consonant with the risk.

2. Plans for new JPL building construction and for major modifications should include features that route water pipes away from areas that may house critical equipment.

2. “Water leak on ceiling in RCE lab on 7/2/2014,” JPL Problem/Failure Report No. 56641, July 8, 2014.

3. “July 2014 Testbed Mishap,” e-mail from Matthew Riley, May 11, 2016.

4. “Water leak in CETB lab,” JPL Problem/Failure Report No. 56630, July 7, 2014.

5. “Poor Coordination of Routine Maintenance Spoiled an Important Test,” NEN No. 10401, NASA Lesson Learned Information System (LLIS), August 11, 2014.

6. “Provide Adequate Maintenance and Hazard Response for UPS Units,” NEN No. 12101, NASA Lesson Learned Information System (LLIS), July 14, 2014.

7. JPL Mishap Report No. 0100 (Bldg. 318), November 11, 2002.

8. JPL Mishap Report No. 1995 (Bldg. 306), November 13, 2009.

9. JPL Mishap Report No. 2001 (Bldg. 306), November 24, 2009.

10. JPL Mishap Report No. 2365 (Bldg. 317), February 17, 2011.

11. JPL Mishap Report No. 1822 (Bldg. 179), February 14, 2009.

12. “Ensure Test Monitoring Software Imposes Limits to Prevent Overtest,” NEN No. 1529, NASA Lesson Learned Information System (LLIS), October 11, 2004.

Figure 2 . General location of DAWN mishap

Figure 3 . sections.abstract: Reuse of heritage facilities and equipment can save Programs and Projects substantial amounts of money but there is a risk that heritage systems can cause substantial budget and schedule impacts if their condition is not thoroughly assessed and required upgrades planned into the project budget and schedule. It is strongly recommended that a thorough condition assessment be conducted and documented during project formulation and that the assessments be updated if the schedule for bringing the systems online changes substantially.
sections.driving_event:
During the design and development phase of the Ground Systems Development and Operations (GSDO) Program there were a number of instances where unexpected costs and schedule delays resulted from discovering the following types of unexpected issues: Lead-based paint, the presence of asbestos, discovery of structural inadequacy of existing systems, and the discovery of hidden corrosion. Specific driving events:

1. During refurbishment of Kennedy Space Center Launch Pad 39B, unexpected corrosion was found in various locations including inside the water tank for the Pad water deluge system. This water tank is very large and the corrosion was a major impact.

2. During modifications to the work platforms in the Rotation Processing and Surge Facility (RPSF)

- Discovery of Lead-based paint resulted in schedule delays and cost increase

- Discovery of inadequacies in existing platforms during implementation of modifications resulted in cost and schedule impacts due to repair and reinforcement

- Unplanned disassembly of decking was required in order to paint the platforms

3. During modification of the Crawler Transporter, asbestos was found in the control room ceiling.

4. During the Vehicle Assembly Building refurbishment, the condition of elevator motors and Environmental Control System supply piping were not understood during budget estimation
sections.lesson_learned: Programs and Projects can be substantially impacted by unexpected additional work resulting from unforeseen issues with reuse of heritage facilities and systems. Thorough assessments of heritage systems need to be performed early, updated as required during the project life cycle and used as a Basis of Estimate for budget and schedule. The assessments should include thorough inspections and analyses.
sections.recommendation:
1. Program/Project Managers relying on the use of heritage hardware, facilities and infrastructure should perform a thorough assessment of the capabilities and condition of these assets early in the Program/Project.

2. Assessments should consider the following:

a) The extent of rework required to comply with changes in codes and regulations (OSHA, National Electrical Code, Pressure Vessel System Code, etc.)

b) Existing issues that will require mitigation; e.g., corrosion, environmental remediation, the presence of asbestos or lead based paint in facilities

c) Supportability and maintainability analyses, considering issues such as parts obsolescence.

d) The assessment should document all assumptions related to facility conditions, required maintenance, rework and supportability of facility systems (supportability of older systems is sensitive to project delays as obtaining repair parts becomes more difficult over time)

e) For systems including software, consideration should be given to the computing platform, operating system and maintaining of any COTS or custom applications

f) Address time sensitivity of this analysis (if the project incurs significant delays how the assessment will be changed)

3. The condition assessment should include physical inspections of visible as well as hard-to-access areas (e.g. hidden corrosion inside a tank or metal structure)

4. The assessment should be updated in the event that the need date for the heritage systems slips as this may invalidate the previous analysis

# [NASA LLIS #17501] Thorough Assessment of Facility Condition During Project Planning and Budgeting
- **Date:** 2016-09-27
- **Organization:** Kennedy Space Center (KSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Categories:** Configuration Management; Logistics; Program and Project Management; Logistics and maintenance; Configuration control and data management; Configuration Change Control
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/17501

## Abstract
Reuse of heritage facilities and equipment can save Programs and Projects substantial amounts of money but there is a risk that heritage systems can cause substantial budget and schedule impacts if their condition is not thoroughly assessed and required upgrades planned into the project budget and schedule. It is strongly recommended that a thorough condition assessment be conducted and documented during project formulation and that the assessments be updated if the schedule for bringing the systems online changes substantially.

## Driving Event / Background
During the design and development phase of the Ground Systems Development and Operations (GSDO) Program there were a number of instances where unexpected costs and schedule delays resulted from discovering the following types of unexpected issues: Lead-based paint, the presence of asbestos, discovery of structural inadequacy of existing systems, and the discovery of hidden corrosion. Specific driving events:

1. During refurbishment of Kennedy Space Center Launch Pad 39B, unexpected corrosion was found in various locations including inside the water tank for the Pad water deluge system. This water tank is very large and the corrosion was a major impact.

2. During modifications to the work platforms in the Rotation Processing and Surge Facility (RPSF)

- Discovery of Lead-based paint resulted in schedule delays and cost increase

- Discovery of inadequacies in existing platforms during implementation of modifications resulted in cost and schedule impacts due to repair and reinforcement

- Unplanned disassembly of decking was required in order to paint the platforms

3. During modification of the Crawler Transporter, asbestos was found in the control room ceiling.

4. During the Vehicle Assembly Building refurbishment, the condition of elevator motors and Environmental Control System supply piping were not understood during budget estimation

## Lesson Learned
Programs and Projects can be substantially impacted by unexpected additional work resulting from unforeseen issues with reuse of heritage facilities and systems. Thorough assessments of heritage systems need to be performed early, updated as required during the project life cycle and used as a Basis of Estimate for budget and schedule. The assessments should include thorough inspections and analyses.

## Recommendation
1. Program/Project Managers relying on the use of heritage hardware, facilities and infrastructure should perform a thorough assessment of the capabilities and condition of these assets early in the Program/Project.

2. Assessments should consider the following:

a) The extent of rework required to comply with changes in codes and regulations (OSHA, National Electrical Code, Pressure Vessel System Code, etc.)

b) Existing issues that will require mitigation; e.g., corrosion, environmental remediation, the presence of asbestos or lead based paint in facilities

c) Supportability and maintainability analyses, considering issues such as parts obsolescence.

d) The assessment should document all assumptions related to facility conditions, required maintenance, rework and supportability of facility systems (supportability of older systems is sensitive to project delays as obtaining repair parts becomes more difficult over time)

e) For systems including software, consideration should be given to the computing platform, operating system and maintaining of any COTS or custom applications

f) Address time sensitivity of this analysis (if the project incurs significant delays how the assessment will be changed)

3. The condition assessment should include physical inspections of visible as well as hard-to-access areas (e.g. hidden corrosion inside a tank or metal structure)

4. The assessment should be updated in the event that the need date for the heritage systems slips as this may invalidate the previous analysis

full_text:
# [NASA LLIS #5862] Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) Nomenclature
- **Date:** 2016-09-07
- **Organization:** Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Aeronautics Research; Human Exploration and Operations; Science
- **Categories:** Policy & Planning; Program and Project Management; Business processes; Program planning / development and management
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/5862

## Abstract
The WBS element nomenclature was not consistently used within the Constellation Program (CxP) Extravehicular Activity (EVA) Project Integrated Master Schedule (IMS) within a standard scheduling tool code field/data set. Since each Project Control Account Manager (P-CAM) was responsible for their schedule, several different variations of WBS numbering schemes were used by different P-CAMs. This situation made it very difficult to integrate the multiple P-CAM schedules and for non-project personnel to validate and ensure that all approved WBS elements were included in the IMS. It also made it difficult to use the WBS code field within the project’s scheduling tool to accurately summarize project schedule data for reporting.

## Driving Event / Background
A pilot effort was conducted on the CxP Extravehicular Activity (EVA) Project as part of the Agency’s Earned Value Management Capability Project. This pilot effort drove the identification of the issue regarding inconsistent WBS element nomenclature.

## Lesson Learned
NASA project organizations responsible for project planning and control of scheduling, budgeting, and implementing approved work scope must define documentation templates so that project data can be integrated among multiple organizations and users. One template within this documentation set should define specific instructions for code field usage and WBS nomenclature to be entered into the project’s schedule management tool. This will enable all tasks within the IMS to be uniquely and consistently mapped to the project’s approved WBS numbering scheme as established by the NASA Structure Management (NSM) system and reflected within the Agency’s Meta Data Manager (MdM) and the Financial Accounting System. The NSM numbering scheme is described and illustrated in the NASA Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) Handbook.

## Recommendation
Project Planning and Control (PP&C) organizations should develop standard product templates that allow for easy integration and summarization of project schedule and budget data and is traceable between the schedule and budget tools and documents. The templates must include, at a minimum, the approved project WBS coding as defined by the NSM system. All schedule tasks must uniquely map to a single WBS element. The PP&C organization should provide all project personnel the necessary training and guidance regarding correct and consistent referencing of the WBS numbering used within the IMS, the budget, or any other project documentation.

title: Schedule Integration Using Multiple Software Tools

sections.abstract: The Constellation Program (CxP) and the CxP Extravehicular Activity (EVA) Project used Primavera as the primary software schedule tool. The CxP EVA Project prime contractor and some Project Control Account Managers (P-CAM’s) used Microsoft Project as their software schedule tool. The automated interface to convert/integrate MS Project data into Primavera is not 100% reliable. This created a potential for errors and/or inaccuracies to occur in certain data fields within Primavera after the conversion from MS Project. This potential for conversion errors created additional work for schedulers to find and correct the errors and validate the converted data. The CxP EVA Project also tried another approach to recreate a subset of the detailed level MS Project schedules within Primavera to create the project level Integrated Master Schedule (IMS). Well-defined templates, data protocols, or interface and reporting requirements were not contained in the prime contractor Data Requirements Documents (DRDs) nor were there clearly defined schedule interface and reporting requirements for the P-CAMs. The lack of a well-defined schedule integration approach impacted the project's ability to efficiently and effectively perform schedule management and analysis and required the project schedulers to be trained and proficient with the different schedule tools.
sections.driving_event: The event driving this lesson learned is the pilot conducted on the CxP Extravehicular Activity (EVA) Project as part of the Agency’s Earned Value Management (EVM) Capability Project.
sections.lesson_learned: Without a clearly defined schedule integration approach, using multiple scheduling tools within a single project can impact efficient and effective schedule management and analysis.
sections.recommendation: While it is a best practice that all project partners use a common scheduling tool to support the total program or project Integrated Master Schedule (IMS), it may not be practical. Therefore, NASA contract proposals with schedule reporting requirements and NASA program and project agreements should contain language outlining software tool interface (IMS, EVMS cost engine, etc.) delivery requirements, standard code fields, and any restrictions on specific tool features that do not support the primary software tools to be used by the project. These requirements should be defined in the contractor Data Requirements Documents (DRDs) or appropriate program and project agreements.

full_text:
# [NASA LLIS #5861] Schedule Integration Using Multiple Software Tools
- **Date:** 2016-09-07
- **Organization:** Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Aeronautics Research; Human Exploration and Operations; Science
- **Categories:** Program and Project Management; Acquisition / procurement strategy and planning; Program planning / development and management
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/5861

## Abstract
The Constellation Program (CxP) and the CxP Extravehicular Activity (EVA) Project used Primavera as the primary software schedule tool. The CxP EVA Project prime contractor and some Project Control Account Managers (P-CAM’s) used Microsoft Project as their software schedule tool. The automated interface to convert/integrate MS Project data into Primavera is not 100% reliable. This created a potential for errors and/or inaccuracies to occur in certain data fields within Primavera after the conversion from MS Project. This potential for conversion errors created additional work for schedulers to find and correct the errors and validate the converted data. The CxP EVA Project also tried another approach to recreate a subset of the detailed level MS Project schedules within Primavera to create the project level Integrated Master Schedule (IMS). Well-defined templates, data protocols, or interface and reporting requirements were not contained in the prime contractor Data Requirements Documents (DRDs) nor were there clearly defined schedule interface and reporting requirements for the P-CAMs. The lack of a well-defined schedule integration approach impacted the project's ability to efficiently and effectively perform schedule management and analysis and required the project schedulers to be trained and proficient with the different schedule tools.

## Driving Event / Background
The event driving this lesson learned is the pilot conducted on the CxP Extravehicular Activity (EVA) Project as part of the Agency’s Earned Value Management (EVM) Capability Project.

## Lesson Learned
Without a clearly defined schedule integration approach, using multiple scheduling tools within a single project can impact efficient and effective schedule management and analysis.

## Recommendation
While it is a best practice that all project partners use a common scheduling tool to support the total program or project Integrated Master Schedule (IMS), it may not be practical. Therefore, NASA contract proposals with schedule reporting requirements and NASA program and project agreements should contain language outlining software tool interface (IMS, EVMS cost engine, etc.) delivery requirements, standard code fields, and any restrictions on specific tool features that do not support the primary software tools to be used by the project. These requirements should be defined in the contractor Data Requirements Documents (DRDs) or appropriate program and project agreements.

title: Facility Test Set-Up Not Fully Inspected Prior To Use / Heritage Panels Unintentionally Pressurized
categories: Integration and Testing; Systems Engineering and Analysis; Facilities; Ground Operations; Industrial Operations; Test & Verification; Ground support systems; Configuration Change Control

sections.abstract:
The Ground Systems Development and Operations (GSDO) Program was modifying subsystems in the Multi Payload Processing Facility (MPPF) at the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) to support processing of Exploration Mission 1 flight hardware. The modifications at the MPPF included the facility Gaseous Nitrogen (GN2) system.

On August 16^th, 2016 a pressurization test of the GN2 system was conducted. The intent of the test was to pressurize the new or modified parts of the GN2 system as part of Verification and Validation (V&V) but four panels that were part of the unmodified heritage portion of the GN2 system were also inadvertently pressurized.

Had there been any disconnected lines or leaks in the tubing assemblies, this condition could have caused an oxygen deficient atmosphere within the interstitial walls of the facility and /or the high bay and airlock areas. Engineering, the Systems Engineers and the NASA Chief Engineers agreed to classify this event as a “Close Call”. The Close Call was caused by inadequate understanding of the actual configuration of the system under test and communication of this organization between the organizations involved in system design and testing. The Test Readiness Review (TRR) did not adequately address the configuration of the system under test.

Communication between multiple organizations working on the same facility is imperative. Test Readiness Reviews need to question test/system configuration to ensure cross checking between drawings applicable to systems being tested, facility drawings, and other organizations
sections.driving_event:
During the course of GN2 V&V operations in the MPPF, personnel noted heritage panels labeled as “Gaseous Outlet Panels”. One such panel, located on the south wall had been previously opened and remained open enough to see inside, all of the gaseous lines were clearly capped/terminated, leading personnel to assume that all 6 of the similar GN2 panels shared the same configuration.

After testing was initiated and facility GN2 pressure was applied, another cabinet was opened and it was observed to still have valves, regulators, gages, etc. installed for both the GN2 and Gaseous Helium (Ghe) systems and that pressure was present. Further investigation identified that 4 of the 6 heritage panels had valves, regulators, and gages rather than capped lines.

Following discussions with GN2 Systems Engineers, Lead Design Engineers, Facility representatives, and Chief Engineers, the V&V work was halted until the panels could be more thoroughly evaluated and placed into a safe configuration.

KSC utilizes different organizations to operate and maintain different types of systems (e.g. Information Technology systems, facilities and facility systems, or Ground Support Equipment). The GSDO Program also used various organizations to do facility modifications and Ground Support Equipment. The situation is also complex because of the mixture of unmodified heritage systems and new/modified systems. The MPPF facility GN2 system is partly unmodified heritage and partly new/modified. The drawings for the heritage part of the system were created and maintained by an organization different than that designing and implementing the new/modified part of the system. This leads to multiple organizations with responsibilities in the same facility and different groups may be modifying or maintaining different parts of the same system.

Facility modification drawing (245G2200002) does not consistently identify supply lines, and the interior layout of the panels was unclear.
sections.lesson_learned: Communication between multiple organizations working on the same facility is imperative. Test Readiness Reviews must thoroughly address the configuration of the system under test to ensure cross checking between different organizational drawings applicable to systems being tested and facility drawings.
sections.recommendation:
Verify all panels not part of testing are capped and plugged. The capped lines need to be labeled with commodity and pressure. Conduct a walk downs of entire system configurations prior to Test Readiness Reviews (TRR) as well as two mandatory questions to answer at TRR:

1. For the configuration under test, are you only pressurizing/energizing the items/systems under test?

2. Did you cross check with other documents/drawings and other organizations?

Communication: Team communication is key to safety. All parties need to be instructed to come together immediately and discuss events whenever they are uncomfortable, or unsure of, moving forward.

# [NASA LLIS #17601] Facility Test Set-Up Not Fully Inspected Prior To Use / Heritage Panels Unintentionally Pressurized
- **Date:** 2016-08-16
- **Organization:** Kennedy Space Center (KSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Categories:** Integration and Testing; Systems Engineering and Analysis; Facilities; Ground Operations; Industrial Operations; Test & Verification; Ground support systems; Configuration Change Control
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/17601

## Abstract
The Ground Systems Development and Operations (GSDO) Program was modifying subsystems in the Multi Payload Processing Facility (MPPF) at the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) to support processing of Exploration Mission 1 flight hardware. The modifications at the MPPF included the facility Gaseous Nitrogen (GN2) system.

On August 16^th, 2016 a pressurization test of the GN2 system was conducted. The intent of the test was to pressurize the new or modified parts of the GN2 system as part of Verification and Validation (V&V) but four panels that were part of the unmodified heritage portion of the GN2 system were also inadvertently pressurized.

Had there been any disconnected lines or leaks in the tubing assemblies, this condition could have caused an oxygen deficient atmosphere within the interstitial walls of the facility and /or the high bay and airlock areas. Engineering, the Systems Engineers and the NASA Chief Engineers agreed to classify this event as a “Close Call”. The Close Call was caused by inadequate understanding of the actual configuration of the system under test and communication of this organization between the organizations involved in system design and testing. The Test Readiness Review (TRR) did not adequately address the configuration of the system under test.

Communication between multiple organizations working on the same facility is imperative. Test Readiness Reviews need to question test/system configuration to ensure cross checking between drawings applicable to systems being tested, facility drawings, and other organizations

## Driving Event / Background
During the course of GN2 V&V operations in the MPPF, personnel noted heritage panels labeled as “Gaseous Outlet Panels”. One such panel, located on the south wall had been previously opened and remained open enough to see inside, all of the gaseous lines were clearly capped/terminated, leading personnel to assume that all 6 of the similar GN2 panels shared the same configuration.

After testing was initiated and facility GN2 pressure was applied, another cabinet was opened and it was observed to still have valves, regulators, gages, etc. installed for both the GN2 and Gaseous Helium (Ghe) systems and that pressure was present. Further investigation identified that 4 of the 6 heritage panels had valves, regulators, and gages rather than capped lines.

Following discussions with GN2 Systems Engineers, Lead Design Engineers, Facility representatives, and Chief Engineers, the V&V work was halted until the panels could be more thoroughly evaluated and placed into a safe configuration.

KSC utilizes different organizations to operate and maintain different types of systems (e.g. Information Technology systems, facilities and facility systems, or Ground Support Equipment). The GSDO Program also used various organizations to do facility modifications and Ground Support Equipment. The situation is also complex because of the mixture of unmodified heritage systems and new/modified systems. The MPPF facility GN2 system is partly unmodified heritage and partly new/modified. The drawings for the heritage part of the system were created and maintained by an organization different than that designing and implementing the new/modified part of the system. This leads to multiple organizations with responsibilities in the same facility and different groups may be modifying or maintaining different parts of the same system.

Facility modification drawing (245G2200002) does not consistently identify supply lines, and the interior layout of the panels was unclear.

## Lesson Learned
Communication between multiple organizations working on the same facility is imperative. Test Readiness Reviews must thoroughly address the configuration of the system under test to ensure cross checking between different organizational drawings applicable to systems being tested and facility drawings.

## Recommendation
Verify all panels not part of testing are capped and plugged. The capped lines need to be labeled with commodity and pressure. Conduct a walk downs of entire system configurations prior to Test Readiness Reviews (TRR) as well as two mandatory questions to answer at TRR:

1. For the configuration under test, are you only pressurizing/energizing the items/systems under test?

2. Did you cross check with other documents/drawings and other organizations?

Communication: Team communication is key to safety. All parties need to be instructed to come together immediately and discuss events whenever they are uncomfortable, or unsure of, moving forward.
