# [NASA LLIS #8601] Reflight of Spacecraft Designs May be Inhibited by Inadequate Capture of Design Knowledge
- **Date:** 2013-12-03
- **Organization:** Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)
- **Mission Directorate:** Aeronautics Research; Human Exploration and Operations; Science
- **Categories:** Missions and Systems Requirements Definition; Program Management; Systems Engineering and Analysis; Flight Equipment; Hardware; Payloads; Spacecraft; Spacecraft and Spacecraft Instruments; Configuration control and data management; Configuration and data management; Engineering design and project processes and standards
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/8601

## Abstract
The JPL focus on primarily one-of-a-kind flight systems and missions may result in insufficient priority placed on design documentation and mission-centric knowledge retention. The OCO-2 project found the inherited Orbiting Carbon Observatory design to be poorly documented. Assure that the spaceflight project retains the design knowledge needed to duplicate a system design. Train employees at all levels to recognize the value of project-generated knowledge and to champion its retention, sharing, and reuse.

## Driving Event / Background
When NASA plans to refly existing system designs, it typically assumes that reuse of a tested or proven design will substantially reduce system development costs and mission risk.

Following the 2009 launch vehicle failure of the Orbiting Carbon Observatory (OCO), NASA funded the NASA/Caltech Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) to develop and fly an identical replacement spacecraft (OCO-2). Where the single instrument aboard OCO was designed by a contractor, OCO-2 was to be developed mostly by JPL. It became clear early in OCO-2 development, however, that key OCO design knowledge was not retained to the extent it might have been if JPL had possessed foreknowledge of an OCO-2 mission.

First, the OCO project had not formally updated system drawings and processes to account for all the corrections (i.e., “redlines”). This necessitated a substantial effort by the OCO-2 project to locate the redlined information and correlate the redlines with each component. The project then had to decide whether to (1) build the corrections into the new hardware (or processes), or (2) duplicate the successive design iterations made by OCO. In duplicating the OCO processes, for example, OCO-2 added graphite to a component, and then removed it; then, because of incomplete incorporation of redlines, the project found additional places where the graphite needed to be removed.

Second, the OCO design was poorly documented. The OCO contractor provided drawings to JPL in PDF format and without the redlines, and they had captured the design in disparate media (e.g., drawings, assembly and inspection data sheets, and test reports). In addition, much of the documentation (including proprietary data) had not been provided to JPL by the contractor, such as verification data at Level 3 and below. This incomplete documentation and transfer of design knowledge made it more difficult to accommodate required design changes (e.g., due to obsolescence or in response to failures on other missions) since the rationale for the original OCO design was not always manifest. As a result, JPL may have foregone some opportunities for risk reduction or cost reduction that might otherwise have followed from the reuse of a tested or proven design.

## Lesson Learned
1. Reflight of a system design is becoming a more common JPL practice. For example, the Mars 2020 mission concept under study by NASA would duplicate the successful design of the Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) rover. (If the prospective Mars 2020 flight system is not designed as an exact copy of MSL, it would likely retain major MSL elements like the Descent Stage; Entry, Descent, and Landing (EDL) design; and Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (MMRTG)). In addition, NASA is supporting the use of common spacecraft buses (e.g., LADEE, Cubesats) that will facilitate reflight of a standard flight system design.

2. The JPL focus on primarily one-of-a-kind flight systems and missions may result in insufficient priority placed on design documentation and mission-centric knowledge retention. However, much technical knowledge gained over the course of a JPL project is reusable, and the actual reflight of a spacecraft design is not uncommon (e.g., Mars Polar Lander/Mars Phoenix, Jason-1/Jason-2/Jason-3, OCO/OCO-2, Mars Science Laboratory/proposed Mars 2020 mission). Even modest efforts to husband technical knowledge may reduce the cost of future projects, even ones that are not planned as build-to-print, by making the knowledge reusable.

## Recommendation
1. Assure that the spaceflight project retains the design knowledge needed to duplicate a system design at an unspecified future time. Subcontracts should clearly specify the design documentation to be delivered by the subcontractor. Knowledge retention by the project should be verified by a process such as the (multi-stage) certification of flight readiness (COFR).

2. Declare the capture and sharing of project and mission-related design knowledge, and retention for possible reuse, to be an objective of all spaceflight projects. Train employees at all levels to recognize the value of project-generated knowledge and to champion its retention, sharing, and reuse.

title: Pay Attention to the Weather

sections.abstract: The delivery of the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) Core Observatory from the Goddard Space Flight Center to the launch site in Japan was delayed when weather conditions forced the flight from the US to Japan to make an unplanned refueling stop, with additional weather delays and complications potentially increasing risks to the observatory.
sections.driving_event:
The GPM Core Observatory left NASA Goddard on November 19, 2013 and arrived at its destination in Japan on November 24^, 2013. The 7,300 mile journey started at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, with the observatory being transported by truck to Andrews Air Force Base where the container was loaded onto an Air Force C-5 transport aircraft. The next step was expected to be a 15-hour flight, followed by a journey on a barge to reach the island of Tanegashima in Southern Japan and a last stretch by truck to the launch pad.

While the launch happened as expected and GPM performed well, the journey from Goddard to the launch site was not without obstacles. One such obstacle was the weather. Unanticipated headwinds prevented the planned in-flight refuel. The flight was forced to land for refueling in Anchorage, Alaska. A wind storm turned what could have been a two-hour stopover into two days. Given the complexity of the transport, the delay has significant impacts on preparations in Japan.

Resources:

- GPM Ships Out to Japan for Launch, November 25, 2013. https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/11424

- New Video Shows GPM’s Journey to Japan. https://pmm.nasa.gov/articles/new-video-shows-gpms-journey-japan
sections.lesson_learned: Pay attention to the weather ahead of time. The team should have anticipated the potential impact of headwinds and could have planned for more fuel for refueling in the air or for two refueling events in the air. This could have prevented the few days of delay on the ground in Alaska.
sections.recommendation:
1. Make weather planning and forecasting an integral part of project planning, especially during transport of the spacecraft, so that any potential weather can be mitigated to avoid mission delays.

2. When planning a highly complex transport (launch in foreign country, multiple modes of transportation, etc...), develop contingency plans in case of bad weather.

# [NASA LLIS #18401] Pay Attention to the Weather
- **Date:** 2013-11-19
- **Organization:** Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Science
- **Categories:** Logistics; Transportation; International partner coordination
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/18401

## Abstract
The delivery of the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) Core Observatory from the Goddard Space Flight Center to the launch site in Japan was delayed when weather conditions forced the flight from the US to Japan to make an unplanned refueling stop, with additional weather delays and complications potentially increasing risks to the observatory.

## Driving Event / Background
The GPM Core Observatory left NASA Goddard on November 19, 2013 and arrived at its destination in Japan on November 24^, 2013. The 7,300 mile journey started at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, with the observatory being transported by truck to Andrews Air Force Base where the container was loaded onto an Air Force C-5 transport aircraft. The next step was expected to be a 15-hour flight, followed by a journey on a barge to reach the island of Tanegashima in Southern Japan and a last stretch by truck to the launch pad.

While the launch happened as expected and GPM performed well, the journey from Goddard to the launch site was not without obstacles. One such obstacle was the weather. Unanticipated headwinds prevented the planned in-flight refuel. The flight was forced to land for refueling in Anchorage, Alaska. A wind storm turned what could have been a two-hour stopover into two days. Given the complexity of the transport, the delay has significant impacts on preparations in Japan.

Resources:

- GPM Ships Out to Japan for Launch, November 25, 2013. https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/11424

- New Video Shows GPM’s Journey to Japan. https://pmm.nasa.gov/articles/new-video-shows-gpms-journey-japan

## Lesson Learned
Pay attention to the weather ahead of time. The team should have anticipated the potential impact of headwinds and could have planned for more fuel for refueling in the air or for two refueling events in the air. This could have prevented the few days of delay on the ground in Alaska.

## Recommendation
1. Make weather planning and forecasting an integral part of project planning, especially during transport of the spacecraft, so that any potential weather can be mitigated to avoid mission delays.

2. When planning a highly complex transport (launch in foreign country, multiple modes of transportation, etc...), develop contingency plans in case of bad weather.

sections.abstract: Three employees were exposed and two additional employees were potentially exposed to hypergolic oxidizer Nitrogen Tetroxide/Nitrogen Dioxide (N2O4/NO2) and experienced some degree of nasal and/or skin irritation. The hypergolic oxidizer leaked from a flex hose (F/H), one of 12 Hypergolic Propellant Servicing System (HPSS) F/Hs at the Water Waste Support Building (WWSB) outdoor storage area located in the KSC Industrial Area.
sections.driving_event: The set of six contaminated flex hoses that were found to have been damaged by the Ares I-X launch required field flushing because they contained residual hypergolic propellant. Employees were potentially exposed to hypergolic oxidizer [Nitrogen Tetroxide/Nitrogen Dioxide (N2O4/NO2)]. An employee was conducting cleanup operations pursuant to a Standing Work Order (SWO) and verbal direction from the supervisor. The cleanup was part of a management initiative to improve working conditions, efficiencies, and appearances at the Waste and Water Support Building (WWSB). As an employee moved a flexible stainless steel braided hose stored on the east side of the WWSB, a strong odor, similar to chlorine, and a hissing noise were noted. The employee noticed an unidentified orange-colored vapor cloud being released from one of the F/H flanged ends, which were both capped with a metal blanking flange. 1. Affix hazard warnings / identifications on contaminated components.

2. Designate work orders as hazardous if tasks involve hazards.

3. Safety training videos should include details for identification and handling of hypergolic propellants.

4. Train employees on requirements for hazardous waste storage.

# [NASA LLIS #8016] Residual Oxidizer in Flex Tubing High Visibility Close Call
- **Date:** 2013-10-18
- **Organization:** Kennedy Space Center (KSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Categories:** Mission Operations and Ground Support Systems; Safety and Mission Assurance; Disposal; Hazardous / Toxic Waste / Materials; Advanced planning of safety systems; Early requirements and standards definition; Maintenance
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/8016

## Abstract
Three employees were exposed and two additional employees were potentially exposed to hypergolic oxidizer Nitrogen Tetroxide/Nitrogen Dioxide (N2O4/NO2) and experienced some degree of nasal and/or skin irritation. The hypergolic oxidizer leaked from a flex hose (F/H), one of 12 Hypergolic Propellant Servicing System (HPSS) F/Hs at the Water Waste Support Building (WWSB) outdoor storage area located in the KSC Industrial Area.

## Driving Event / Background
The set of six contaminated flex hoses that were found to have been damaged by the Ares I-X launch required field flushing because they contained residual hypergolic propellant. Employees were potentially exposed to hypergolic oxidizer [Nitrogen Tetroxide/Nitrogen Dioxide (N2O4/NO2)]. An employee was conducting cleanup operations pursuant to a Standing Work Order (SWO) and verbal direction from the supervisor. The cleanup was part of a management initiative to improve working conditions, efficiencies, and appearances at the Waste and Water Support Building (WWSB). As an employee moved a flexible stainless steel braided hose stored on the east side of the WWSB, a strong odor, similar to chlorine, and a hissing noise were noted. The employee noticed an unidentified orange-colored vapor cloud being released from one of the F/H flanged ends, which were both capped with a metal blanking flange. Initially, the employee attempted to mitigate the situation by applying water to the flanged end of the F/H with a garden hose.

## Lesson Learned
Clean up technicians were unaware of the contaminated hypergolic flex hose and were not the correct personnel to be performing the pickup.

## Recommendation
1. Affix hazard warnings / identifications on contaminated components.

2. Designate work orders as hazardous if tasks involve hazards.

3. Safety training videos should include details for identification and handling of hypergolic propellants.

4. Train employees on requirements for hazardous waste storage.

title: Verify That Test Equipment Cannot be Interrupted by Extraneous Computer Processes
categories: Integration and Testing; Computers; Configuration Management; Facilities; Ground Equipment; Ground Operations; Hardware; Information Technology / Systems; Software; Spacecraft; Test and Verification; Test Facility; Advanced planning of safety systems

sections.abstract: Thermal-vacuum testing of a Ka-side frequency multiplier for the Juno Small Deep Space Transponder (SDST) was interrupted in mid-performance when a desktop computer running the test unexpectedly sought to download an update of an installed software package. While the flight hardware and test equipment were not harmed, eight hours of test data were lost. Verify that test support equipment critical to tests or experiments cannot be interrupted by extraneous computer processes or external commands.
sections.driving_event:
The sole scheduled thermal-vacuum (T-V) test of a Juno spacecraft telecommunications component was being conducted in September 2008 at a facility under contract to the NASA/Caltech Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) when the test was unexpectedly interrupted (References (1) and (2)). The commercial component under test (Figure 1) was a X4 Frequency Multiplier, a small mechanical part with one internal diode on the Ka-band side of the Juno Small Deep Space Transponder (SDST). The Ka-band side of the Juno telecommunication subsystem is used for gravity science uplink and downlink via the Juno High Gain Antenna. Throughout the T-V test, data on the levels of radio frequency (RF) power flowing into and out of the X4 were being monitored by a data acquisition computer in the test facility.

| |
| --- |
| Figure 1. Juno Radio Frequency Instrument Subsystem (RFIS) components located in the spacecraft radiation vault. (A red oval marks the label pointing to the X4 Frequency Multiplier component.) |

The data acquisition computer was a typical desktop computer employing a very common commercial operating system. The test failure during the hot soak portion of the test was traced to the computer autonomously initiating contact over the computer network with the manufacturer of the computer’s operating system to obtain a software update. Activating this process extraneous to the flight hardware test caused a conflict that resulted in the shutdown of the computer and the immediate termination of the test in mid-performance. Neither the flight hardware nor the support equipment controlling the environmental test were affected by the failure, but about eight hours of test data were lost due to the test interruption. This test ran for approximately one week prior to the failure, and the pre-hot soak and post-hot soak data matched. Hence, the loss of eight hours of test data was not deemed significant, and the test was not repeated.

References :

1. “SDST x4 STE: Data Acquisition System Auto Off,” JPL Problem/Failure Report No. 13512, September 10, 2008.

2. “SDST x4: T-Vac Missing Data,” JPL Problem/Failure Report No. 13513, September 10, 2008.
sections.lesson_learned: Many computers used for specialized purposes in test facilities are general purpose computers that may also be configured to perform office functions. Processes extraneous to flight system testing (e.g., code updates, scheduled file backups, e-mail downloads, and security scans) may occur intermittently on these units without user interaction or knowledge, particularly when they are connected to institutional networks. Should an extraneous process interrupt an active test, significant test time may be lost and the test article or support equipment may be damaged.
sections.recommendation: Test conductors should verify that the operation of test support equipment critical to tests or experiments cannot be interrupted by extraneous computer processes or external commands. Before initiating a test, either (1) disable extraneous processes that are not essential to the test or (2) verify that the extraneous processes cannot interfere with the test. If the extraneous processes are to be disabled, take appropriate action to assure that essential services (e.g., managing critical security patches) are maintained. (For example, if the connection to the institutional network is to be severed, a local system administrator can manually install updates and patches at a safe time.)

While the flight hardware and test equipment were not harmed, eight hours of test data were lost. ## Driving Event / Background
The sole scheduled thermal-vacuum (T-V) test of a Juno spacecraft telecommunications component was being conducted in September 2008 at a facility under contract to the NASA/Caltech Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) when the test was unexpectedly interrupted (References (1) and (2)). The commercial component under test (Figure 1) was a X4 Frequency Multiplier, a small mechanical part with one internal diode on the Ka-band side of the Juno Small Deep Space Transponder (SDST). Throughout the T-V test, data on the levels of radio frequency (RF) power flowing into and out of the X4 were being monitored by a data acquisition computer in the test facility.

| |
| --- |
| Figure 1. Juno Radio Frequency Instrument Subsystem (RFIS) components located in the spacecraft radiation vault. (A red oval marks the label pointing to the X4 Frequency Multiplier component.) |

The data acquisition computer was a typical desktop computer employing a very common commercial operating system. The test failure during the hot soak portion of the test was traced to the computer autonomously initiating contact over the computer network with the manufacturer of the computer’s operating system to obtain a software update. Activating this process extraneous to the flight hardware test caused a conflict that resulted in the shutdown of the computer and the immediate termination of the test in mid-performance. Neither the flight hardware nor the support equipment controlling the environmental test were affected by the failure, but about eight hours of test data were lost due to the test interruption. This test ran for approximately one week prior to the failure, and the pre-hot soak and post-hot soak data matched. References :

1. “SDST x4 STE: Data Acquisition System Auto Off,” JPL Problem/Failure Report No. 13512, September 10, 2008.

2. “SDST x4: T-Vac Missing Data,” JPL Problem/Failure Report No. 13513, September 10, 2008.

## Lesson Learned
Many computers used for specialized purposes in test facilities are general purpose computers that may also be configured to perform office functions. Processes extraneous to flight system testing (e.g., code updates, scheduled file backups, e-mail downloads, and security scans) may occur intermittently on these units without user interaction or knowledge, particularly when they are connected to institutional networks. Should an extraneous process interrupt an active test, significant test time may be lost and the test article or support equipment may be damaged.

## Recommendation
Test conductors should verify that the operation of test support equipment critical to tests or experiments cannot be interrupted by extraneous computer processes or external commands. Before initiating a test, either (1) disable extraneous processes that are not essential to the test or (2) verify that the extraneous processes cannot interfere with the test. If the extraneous processes are to be disabled, take appropriate action to assure that essential services (e.g., managing critical security patches) are maintained. (For example, if the connection to the institutional network is to be severed, a local system administrator can manually install updates and patches at a safe time.)

title: Proper Use of MIL-A-8625 Type II Anodize on 2000 and 7000 Series Aluminum Alloys
mission_directorate: Aeronautics Research; Human Exploration and Operations; Science
categories: Flight Equipment; Hardware; Parts; Materials; & Processes; Payloads; Spacecraft; Spacecraft and Spacecraft Instruments

sections.abstract: Following thermal-vacuum bakeout/testing, various Mars Science Laboratory aluminum parts exhibited flaking of the black anodize coating. The flaking was traced to a known problem with Type II anodization of 2000 and 7000 series aluminum alloys. Although these coating failures were not significant for MSL, contamination from such debris poses a potentially significant mission impact. Use of Type III anodize or paint instead of Type II anodization is recommended on series 2000 and 7000 aluminum.
sections.driving_event: Following thermal-vacuum bakeout/testing, various Mars Science Laboratory aluminum parts exhibited flaking of the black anodize coating. The flaking was traced to a known problem with Type II anodization of 2000 and 7000 series aluminum alloys. Although these coating failures were not significant for MSL, contamination from such debris poses a potentially significant mission impact. Use of Type III anodize or paint instead of Type II anodization is recommended on series 2000 and 7000 aluminum.
sections.lesson_learned:
1. Type II black anodization of aluminum is commonly performed by JPL and by industry to provide a durable coating for corrosion control or to minimize glint for cameras. Although anodizing aluminum alloys by this technique is usually successful, the compatibility of certain aluminum alloys with the Type II anodize process is unpredictable. Although the coating failures caused no damage to MSL, contamination from the resulting debris can potentially have serious mission consequences.

2. There is some evidence that factors such as exposure of the anodized surface to extreme low-side temperature cycles (e.g., to -130C), and the deep thermal cycling associated with planetary protection measures, may affect the tendency of the coating to spall. For component surfaces that experience relatively benign total thermal variations, or for missions that do not require planetary protection bakeout, it may be feasible to specify and deliver a reliable Type II black anodize coating on 2000 and 7000 series aluminum alloys for a given flight project.
sections.recommendation:
1. When parts will be exposed to elevated temperatures such as planetary protection bakeouts and/or deep thermal cycling, avoid MIL-A-8625 Type II anodization of 2000 and 7000 series aluminum.

2. Employ either paint or MIL-A-8625, Type III anodization for 2000 and 7000 series aluminum. Testing performed at JPL, including thermal cycling from -130°C to 50°C after a simulated planetary protection bakeout at 120°C, indicated that Type III coatings will not spall/flake.

3. For parts that require a Type II black anodized surface, 6000 series aluminum is recommended. Testing of both MIL-A-8625, Type II and Type III coatings on the 6000 series aluminum that is used most commonly at JPL-- 6061-T6-- did not result in any spalling failures.

title: Small, Diverse Operations Teams Produce Efficient and Innovative Operations Solutions
categories: Flight Operations; Payloads; Spacecraft; Organizational Planning

sections.abstract: A “skunk works” approach to mission operations, in which the operations group is given a high degree of autonomy and unhampered by standard rules and procedures, may be appropriate when a rapid response to serious flight system anomalies is required.
sections.driving_event: Lesson Learned occurred over an extended period of time during K2 mission development; date shown is around the period of maximum activity as documented in the attached paper
sections.lesson_learned: During Phase C/D it is prudent to bring in as much expertise as the program can afford to design the spacecraft/mission and also to verify that the design is good. In Phase E programs are typically much more constrained with both time and money. The Kepler operations team had only a few months to develop the K2 mission, and if it had been constrained by the same level of oversight, documentation and formal reviews that normally are placed on a mission development effort, the team would not have succeeded. Giving the small team more authority to develop the mission quickly and use its own judgment about which processes to adhere to and which ones to set aside was absolutely essential to completing the K2 mission development and in-flight testing on time.
sections.recommendation:
- When facing problems in flight, it should never be assumed that using more people will lead to a more robust outcome.

- In all mission phases a “tiger team” of uninhibited, focused technical specialists is often used to solve a problem quickly without spending a lot of money. # [NASA LLIS #25506] Small, Diverse Operations Teams Produce Efficient and Innovative Operations Solutions
- **Date:** 2013-07-31
- **Organization:** Ames Research Center (ARC)
- **Categories:** Flight Operations; Payloads; Spacecraft; Organizational Planning
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/25506

## Abstract
A “skunk works” approach to mission operations, in which the operations group is given a high degree of autonomy and unhampered by standard rules and procedures, may be appropriate when a rapid response to serious flight system anomalies is required.

## Driving Event / Background
Lesson Learned occurred over an extended period of time during K2 mission development; date shown is around the period of maximum activity as documented in the attached paper

## Lesson Learned
During Phase C/D it is prudent to bring in as much expertise as the program can afford to design the spacecraft/mission and also to verify that the design is good. In Phase E programs are typically much more constrained with both time and money. The Kepler operations team had only a few months to develop the K2 mission, and if it had been constrained by the same level of oversight, documentation and formal reviews that normally are placed on a mission development effort, the team would not have succeeded. Giving the small team more authority to develop the mission quickly and use its own judgment about which processes to adhere to and which ones to set aside was absolutely essential to completing the K2 mission development and in-flight testing on time.

## Recommendation
- When facing problems in flight, it should never be assumed that using more people will lead to a more robust outcome.

- In all mission phases a “tiger team” of uninhibited, focused technical specialists is often used to solve a problem quickly without spending a lot of money. While not appropriate in all cases, K2 has demonstrated that this approach can be used for mission operations in general with great success.

sections.driving_event:
SLS Program Preliminary Design Review (PDR)

The SLS Program conducted a PDR in June and July of 2013. The review focus was on meeting the success criteria for the review per MPR 7123.1B. Review item discrepancies (RIDs) for the SLS PDR were written against success criteria versus prior programs which focused on writing RIDs against specific documents under review. The review approach included a combined technical and safety review, the use of MPR 7123.1B milestone success criteria, and eleven discipline review teams. Success criterion 9 was tailored for safety and mission assurance to guide the combined technical and safety assessments.

Data package documents were mapped to success criteria to support the review approach of writing RIDs against the PDR success criteria rather than against documentation. For example, multiple data items, which were mapped to a success criterion, could be used to support a success criteria RID.

The planning process of the PDR included development of a review plan that detailed the review process which included review team lead, review member, Tabletop/Pre-screening lead, LSE, Pre-Board, and Board responsibilities, the scope of the PDR, the review schedule, the documentation maturity matrices, document mapping to entrance criteria to support the PDR readiness assessment, document mapping to success criteria to support development of pre-RIDs and comments, and the PDR data package listing that also included reference documentation. The implementation and execution process of the PDR review plan included review training, logistics for rooms, parking, review and Tabletop/Pre-screening team scheduling, web portal and review team dashboard development to support review communication, review team lead and review team member selection, and conduction of the review. Review conduction included review of products and development of pre-declared RIDs, discipline team and Tabletop/Pre-screening reviews , screening, dispositioning of RIDS which included negotiating the terms of RID closure, the compilation of the review results, and the presentation of the review results to decisional authorities for approval.

Post PDR Review Success Evaluation

Following the completion of the PDR, a PDR Pause and Learn (PaL) activity and review effectiveness survey were administered to the participants of the review. The PaL assessment included a survey, focus groups, interviews, and a quantitative data assessment of the pre-RID flow through discipline team and Tabletop/Pre-screening . Lessons learned gained from the PaL and survey are described below.

The PaL and survey covered a quantitative assessment of the Pre-RID and RID process, the PDR training, and included a PaL interview and a PaL focus group exercise. The objective of the PaL activity was to gain knowledge from the experience of conducting this review and to learn and apply the lessons gained to the next review cycles. The PaL activity included all information gathering methods: survey, interview, and focus groups. PaL activities focused on gathering constructive feedback about the reviews rather than developing specific solutions for the next review.

A Likert scale survey was conducted to determine if the review was planned and executed well in regards to the review process, logistics, customer service, information management, and the MSFC RID System. The survey was designed to be conducive to constructive feedback and easy results compilation. The training provided leading up to the review was surveyed as well through MSFC ‘s training organization for additional constructive feedback.

Focus groups for Review Team Leads, planning, logistics, RID initiator, developers of corrective actions, and internal EV71 planning were conducted to gather constructive feedback not solutions. The focus groups were facilitated by persons without a direct link to the review. In addition, semi-structured interviews of several Review Team Leads were also conducted to gather more detailed qualitative data.

All focus group and interview notes were compiled and assessed for common themes. The common repetitive themes were condensed into recommended results, goals, and areas to improve by review topic area (planning, review process, logistics, customer service, information management, and the MSFC RID System). The condensed qualitative data was further condensed into a PaL top ten list. Quantitative observations were used in order to understand the acceptance rate of pre-RIDs between the discipline review, tabletop review( prescreening), and screening. All results, goals, and areas to improve were validated by Chief Engineer, Program, and S&MA peer review.

The team evaluated the utility and flow of using the RID tool and they gained insight into the logistics, support, and scheduling of reviews that can aid future milestone review planners. The PaL also looked at the SLS Review Portal page which was used as the main communication gateway for key review activities, contacts, review data package links, training packages and videos, as well as other key review links.

Summary of Post-PDR Execution Evaluation

The PaL and open ended-question survey observances suggested that the portal page needed to be decluttered in order to become more user friendly. The Review Team Lead dashboard accessed via the SLS Review Portal was used for Review Director and Cross-Review Team communication. The dashboard was observed to have been used by half of the review team leads. The discussion board capability for the review was used infrequently. Minor restructuring of the portal page and review team lead dashboard has the potential to improve reviewer usability. More training on the importance of use of the dashboard and discussion board also has the potential to ultimately improve the review communication process.

The specific survey topic areas were:

a. The PDR Review Process

b. Logistics

c. Review Customer Service

d. Information Management

e. MSFC RID System (RID Tool)

f. Review training (review process, RID Tool, and limited data rights)

Overall, the data showed that the PDR was well executed in all areas. The recommendations for changes are relatively minor. The training survey indicated that training was satisfactorily conducted, with a few refining recommendations provided. In short, the PDR was considered successful.

End Result : A successful review. The overall Likert scale survey for planning and review execution results indicated the review was planned and conducted satisfactorily with a median of 3.7. The mean and median minus the planning and logistics team inputs resulted in a rating of 3.9. Neutral and agree were 3 and 4 respectively on the Likert scale survey for planning and review execution. The overall training survey result was a median of 2 which corresponds to “agree” indicating training was conducted satisfactorily.
sections.lesson_learned:
1. Milestone reviews are first and foremost about Data, Communication, Collaborative Team work, team leadership, and organization of work tasks and products. Organizers of milestone review events must plan to enable a smooth flow of activity and data throughout the event.

Roles, Responsibilities, and Commitments

2. In some review areas, planning team roles and responsibilities were not clearly defined.

3. The external reviewer process and expectations were not clearly defined.

4. In some cases, discipline points of contact and /or document developers were difficult to locate for support during the screening process due to events such as planned vacations.

Tabletops

5. Success criteria tabletops or prescreening did not significantly reduce the number of pre-RIDs going to screening.

6. Pre-Declared RID actionees were not assigned prior to kickoff. Pre-Declared RID actionees were assigned toward the end of the screening process. This resulted in the developer/assignee of the corrective action having less time to develop a corrective action response.

7. The SE Success Criteria Tabletop carried 51% of the pre-RID load. This was an indicator that for future reviews additional support would be required for the systems engineering discipline.

8. The Tabletop/Pre-screening activity had an acceptance rate of Pre-RIDS of 90%. This is a high percentage of Pre-RIDs that were sent forward to screening indicating that the Tabletop/Pre-screening process was not working as well as expected to reduce the number of Pre-RIDs going into screening.

Screening

9. A screening schedule for RID Discussion at the beginning of the screening meetings would have been helpful and kept the first days of screening time focused.

MSFC RID System and Data Access Issues

10. The MSFC RID System would benefit from additional fields for comments, expected closure date, and, and a final corrective action.

11. The data access process was a complicated lengthy process due to items such as NASA identity requirements in IDmax if you did not have a NASA ID, RID Tool IDmax requirement to access the MSFC RID System, and training requirements for the RID Tool and Limited Data Rights.

12. The review portal page contained a lot of review information on one page. Some reviewers had difficulty locating the desired data links due to the amount of information on the page.

Logistical Support Issues

1. Customer service rooms were not fully utilized. The use of fewer Customer Service rooms should be considered for CDR.

2. Conducting table top reviews across disparate and physically dislocated personnel was a challenge. The team used WebEx telecons, but not video teleconferencing.

The prescreening review location(s) were distributed in two primary buildings in the same building complex. As a result, it was difficult to easily walk to other prescreening/tabletop locations since they were distributed on different floors in two different buildings. Some people needed to be in multiple prescreening locations at the same time.
sections.recommendation:
Summary

1. Reevaluate the use of Success Criteria Tabletops/Prescreening.

2. Clarify planning team roles and responsibilities to reduce any overlap or task confusion.

3. Define process and expectations for external reviewers.

4. Consider data access process improvement.

5. Assign Pre-Declared RID actionees prior to Kickoff.

6. Develop a backup discipline point of contacts and a backup document developer list.

7. Assess if a central location for CDR is possible.

8. Reformat portal page to be more user friendly.

9. Add additional fields for comments, expected closure date, and a final corrective action in the MSFC RID System.

10. Develop detailed RID discussion schedules to improve time management during screening and/or dispositioning meetings.

Detailed

1. Logistics:

a. Avoid holidays and school vacations (Fall and Spring Break).

b. Limit vacation time during a milestone review.

c. Have a goal to balance the success criteria review team workload.

d. The pre-Board (final approval) should have a template and it should be available early in the review process to allow the secretariats to populate the pre-Board agenda as they go. This would level the work load needed to prepare pre-Board charts, which eventually become Board charts.

e. It is preferable to lock down documents at least 6 months prior to the review, or in accordance with the approved schedule. Late documentation throws the planned work load off balance.

f. Work out all issues with the data access process prior to review kick off.

g. Agendas, room lists, all logistical information that would help participants know what is going on over the entire review should be available online. More than one avenue of communication of the logistics is preferable.

i. Co-Locating the Review Participants is Highly Recommended.

1. Planning Review Events:

2. Planners should evaluate the use of Tabletops/Pre-screening versus other forums for reviewing and discussing technical data in a technical milestone review.

i. Planners should consider the need and benefit of Tabletop review of RIDs. All three screening process steps may be able to be collapsed to one.

ii. Concurrent Tabletops may overload some reviewers who cannot attend all relevant tabletops.

1. The timing of the review should be in conjunction with the readiness for the review, and should consider the SRB schedule in mind, as well as the timing between element and vehicle reviews.

2. Allow more time for development of corrective actions.

i. Corrective action assignees were pressed to try to get corrective actions into the RID tool prior to discipline review team disposition.

1. Dispositioning time should be at least one week.

2. On Comments:

i. The RID Tool needs to have a comment graphical interface button added during each major RID Tool step to capture comments. Currently comments can only be captured at screening using the “cancel as comment” feature.

ii. Comments should be established as formal comments prior to screening.

1. Team Leader Roles

2. Team Leader roles and responsibilities need to be clear and distinct.

3. A greater focus on Team leader roles and responsibilities should be provided in review training.

4. Assign Actionees to pre-declared RIDs prior to kick off.

5. Tabletop review agendas should include a schedule of the pre-RIDs to be discussed.

i. The agenda should be available to other Review Team Leads.

1. Team Leads should know the review schedule and when products/results are due.

i. Team Leads should evaluate and plan their team activities to coordinate with the overall schedule.

ii. Team Leads should communicate the planned schedule to all team members and the review director.

1. All Team Leads should provide criteria assessments.

2. Team Leads need to be proactive.

3. Transferring RIDs between teams was difficult and had to be done offline. Team Leads did not always coordinate with each other.

4. Pre-Board charts should be pre-reviewed by all the Team Leads if possible.

1. Training

2. Team may have needed more training on what criteria based reviews are versus the traditional document based reviews.

3. Team leaders and deputy team leaders need to be trained in the scope and execution of their roles and responsibilities, including the hands-on use of the RID tool.

4. Limited Rights Data training may need to be adapted to the roles of 1) reviewer and 2) document developer.

1. Approach, Criteria

2. For technical reviews, the leading authority needs to state whether or not programmatic material is under review.

3. If programmatic material or considerations are under review, the programmatic success criteria must be provided.

4. If it is a technical review, focus on the technical criteria, and not on programmatic criteria.

5. Clearly define the process and expectations for external reviewers.

1. Communication

2. IT Issues

i. Do not schedule server maintenance during a review.

ii. Data access (see Limited Rights data access comment above)

1. Access had too many gates.

2. There was a lack of access to some documents, such as Level III documents.

iii. On the RID tool:

1. RID numbers should remain consistent and traceable throughout the process.

iv. Make portal page or central location for information user friendly.

1. Review Team Members should work with the Developer if possible prior to submitting comments via a spreadsheet or putting comments into the RID tool.

2. DLEs can help keep the developers informed about changes and comments made to their documents.

If the RID changes after the developer has entered the corrective action into the RID tool, those responsible for the change need to coordinate with the developer to ensure proper handling and traceability of the CA.

sections.driving_event:
The Kepler mission was specifically designed to discover Earth-size planets in or near the habitable zone and assess how common such exoplanets may be in our galaxy. Because the Kepler instrument required exceptional pointing stability, the spacecraft design incorporated a fixed (i.e., non-deployable) solar array (Figure 1).

| |
| --- |
| Figure 1. Kepler employed a fixed solar array that was partially wrapped around the photometer instrument |

Shortly following the March 2009 launch of Kepler, spacecraft fault protection responded to an over-voltage condition caused by the battery exceeding the specified voltage. Kepler’s solar panels were hard mounted on three sides of the spacecraft. During a roll, the panels went in and out of the sunlight; this resulted in an anticipated periodicity in battery charging while the spacecraft tumbled following separation from the launch vehicle. The battery charge control algorithm was designed to adjust for the nominal roll rate during science operations. However, the over-voltage anomaly occurred because the battery charge control algorithm was not designed to manage the anticipated higher roll rate during launch operations, combined with the anticipated detumble that Kepler experienced post-separation.

A Subsystem Interface Box (SIB) swap recovery contingency procedure had been vetted by an independent review team, and exercised on a testbed during operational readiness testing prior to launch. The procedure was successful in restoring the spacecraft configuration, and the battery voltage readings were nominal once detumble was completed.

References :

1. Peg Frerking, “Kepler SIB Swap Contingency following Auto-Initiation,” March 18, 2009.

full_text:
# [NASA LLIS #8402] Assure Flight Control Algorithms Can Cope With All Mission Phases
- **Date:** 2013-07-23
- **Organization:** Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations; Science
- **Categories:** Flight Operations; Ground Equipment; Ground Operations; Software; Spacecraft; Power; Software Engineering; Spacecraft and Spacecraft Instruments; Level II/III requirements definition; Mission definition and planning
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/8402

## Abstract
An in-flight anomaly occurred because the Kepler battery charge control algorithm was not designed to cope with the changes in the roll rate that the spacecraft experienced, nor was the dynamic behavior of the spacecraft adequately modeled. Assure that flight control algorithms have adequate margin to deal with all mission phases and operational scenarios.

## Driving Event / Background
The Kepler mission was specifically designed to discover Earth-size planets in or near the habitable zone and assess how common such exoplanets may be in our galaxy. Because the Kepler instrument required exceptional pointing stability, the spacecraft design incorporated a fixed (i.e., non-deployable) solar array (Figure 1).

| |
| --- |
| Figure 1. Kepler employed a fixed solar array that was partially wrapped around the photometer instrument |

Shortly following the March 2009 launch of Kepler, spacecraft fault protection responded to an over-voltage condition caused by the battery exceeding the specified voltage. Kepler’s solar panels were hard mounted on three sides of the spacecraft. During a roll, the panels went in and out of the sunlight; this resulted in an anticipated periodicity in battery charging while the spacecraft tumbled following separation from the launch vehicle. The battery charge control algorithm was designed to adjust for the nominal roll rate during science operations. However, the over-voltage anomaly occurred because the battery charge control algorithm was not designed to manage the anticipated higher roll rate during launch operations, combined with the anticipated detumble that Kepler experienced post-separation.

A Subsystem Interface Box (SIB) swap recovery contingency procedure had been vetted by an independent review team, and exercised on a testbed during operational readiness testing prior to launch. The procedure was successful in restoring the spacecraft configuration, and the battery voltage readings were nominal once detumble was completed.

References :

1. Peg Frerking, “Kepler SIB Swap Contingency following Auto-Initiation,” March 18, 2009.

## Lesson Learned
When designing flight control algorithms, such as battery control algorithms, the design must cover all phases of the mission, including post-separation detumble. For Kepler, this constituted a failure to (1) model dynamic spacecraft behavior during all operational phases so that they could impose the proper flow-down of requirements to the power system, and (2) test-as-you-fly and demonstrate margin.

## Recommendation
1. Model the spacecraft dynamic behavior for launch and all operational phases.

2. Assure that spacecraft flight control algorithms, such as battery charge control algorithms, are designed for all mission phases and operational scenarios, with margin, including the detumble that occurs immediately post launch.

categories: Integration and Testing; Program Management; Ground Equipment; Information Technology / Systems; Test and Verification; Ground support systems; Configuration control and data management; Science integration

sections.abstract: The Orbiting Carbon Observatory project was unable to generate simulated science data that covered all critical operational modes, which impacted the completeness of system testing. Early in the project lifecycle, project management should define which science datasets, both simulated and captured, will be required for use during system testing. Project management should also require the Project Element Managers to collaborate in defining these needs.
sections.driving_event:
A Science Data Processing System (SDPS) is typically developed for a NASA project to accommodate the huge quantities of raw science data downlinked from instruments or experiments over the course of a mission. Sometimes referred to as a Science Data System (SDS), the SDPS converts telemetry into higher level science data products provided to the science community for research and applications. The SDPS is centered at the NASA/Caltech Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) on JPL-managed missions, where JPL is responsible for processing and distributing data products in a timely manner as required to meet mission objectives. Figure 1 depicts the science data flow to and from the science data processing function. One critical task in SDPS development is data simulation, a technique that provides visualizations of the extremely large and complicated science datasets and permits verification of the system.

| |
| --- |
| Figure 1. The science data processing function is depicted within the context of the entire Mission Operations System (MOS) for the Orbiting Carbon Observatory mission Legend : OSC– Orbital Sciences Corp; GSFC– NASA Goddard Space Flight Center |

The Orbiting Carbon Observatory (OCO), an Earth orbiting satellite mission managed by JPL, was designed to make precise, time-dependent, global measurements of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO_2). In developing the SDPS for OCO, The Ground Data System (GDS) Team (which is responsible for spacecraft and instrument monitoring and operations) did a good job of leveraging the Instrument and Observatory thermal-vacuum test output to generate datasets for system testing (Reference (1)). The team generated multiple sets of data that represented varying conditions. These data provided a good basis for OCO system testing.

Unfortunately, the GDS Team was unable to generate simulated data that covered all critical operational modes. The team only generated Attitude Control System (ACS) data for the Nadir mode, and was unable to generate ACS data in the Glint or Target modes. Further, the team was not able to generate data that could run through Level 2. The Instrument thermal-vacuum tests recorded only direct solar observations, rather than solar light reflected off the surface of the Earth. The science retrieval algorithms could not work with direct solar observations. It should be noted that, despite the best efforts of the team that plans and performs an SDPS test, it is not uncommon for the SDPS test configuration and environment to be unable to generate certain characters of test data. In such cases, certain simulated data sets are generated by the science instrument during system-level testing (e.g., thermal-vacuum test), while other types of simulated data are generated by an algorithm scientist and inserted into the processing chain to exercise and validate certain science data product software executables.

The Algorithm Team generated a partial orbit of spectra that simulated the spectra that they expected to see in flight. The GDS obtained that dataset, manipulated it into an OCO L1B (registered radiance at the sensor product dataset) file, and gathered the ancillary data needed to run the dataset through the Level 2 AOPD (Agent-Oriented Program & Design algorithm) PGE (Product Generation Executive). Even at launch, however, that dataset had not yet been diffused into the system testing process.

For OCO, the full set of required test cases was not identified soon enough to conduct the additional planning needed for their generation. For the OCO-2 follow-on project, the full set of simulated test cases was known, and the GDS Team began early to determine which sets should be implemented and which sets the project could omit as an acceptable risk.

References :

1. P.J. Guske, “OCO (Orbiting Carbon Observatory) Project Lessons Learned Document (Final),” JPL Document No. D-26172, July 7, 2009, Paragraph 3.7.6.
sections.lesson_learned: Simulated science data is needed by multiple groups within a project team to test their respective SDPS elements. Even though the specific needs of each group may vary, a cooperative effort among the different groups may reduce the amount of time required to generate an adequately complete set of simulated data for system test. If the project fails to plan the timely generation of a complete set of simulated data, system testing may be unable to verify and validate all critical operational modes.
sections.recommendation:
1. Early in the project lifecycle, project management should define which science datasets, both simulated and captured, will be required for use during system testing. Schedules should allocate adequate time to ensure that all required simulated datasets are generated and validated in time for system testing.

2. Project management should also require the various Project Element Managers (PEMs) to collaborate in this effort. Early in Phase C/D and well before the thermal-vacuum test cycles, PEMs should document their specific data simulation needs and their plans to simulate the required datasets. Based on these brief documents, the project team can collectively determine how the members can most efficiently generate all of the requisite simulated datasets.

- **Date:** 2013-06-25
- **Organization:** Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)
- **Mission Directorate:** Science
- **Categories:** Integration and Testing; Program Management; Ground Equipment; Information Technology / Systems; Test and Verification; Ground support systems; Configuration control and data management; Science integration

## Abstract
The Orbiting Carbon Observatory project was unable to generate simulated science data that covered all critical operational modes, which impacted the completeness of system testing. Early in the project lifecycle, project management should define which science datasets, both simulated and captured, will be required for use during system testing. Project management should also require the Project Element Managers to collaborate in defining these needs.

## Driving Event / Background
A Science Data Processing System (SDPS) is typically developed for a NASA project to accommodate the huge quantities of raw science data downlinked from instruments or experiments over the course of a mission. Sometimes referred to as a Science Data System (SDS), the SDPS converts telemetry into higher level science data products provided to the science community for research and applications. | |
| --- |
| Figure 1. The science data processing function is depicted within the context of the entire Mission Operations System (MOS) for the Orbiting Carbon Observatory mission Legend : OSC– Orbital Sciences Corp; GSFC– NASA Goddard Space Flight Center |

The team generated multiple sets of data that represented varying conditions. These data provided a good basis for OCO system testing.

Unfortunately, the GDS Team was unable to generate simulated data that covered all critical operational modes. References :

Simulated science data is needed by multiple groups within a project team to test their respective SDPS elements. ## Recommendation
1. Early in the project lifecycle, project management should define which science datasets, both simulated and captured, will be required for use during system testing. 2. Project management should also require the various Project Element Managers (PEMs) to collaborate in this effort. Early in Phase C/D and well before the thermal-vacuum test cycles, PEMs should document their specific data simulation needs and their plans to simulate the required datasets. Based on these brief documents, the project team can collectively determine how the members can most efficiently generate all of the requisite simulated datasets.

title: Systems Engineering Management Plan (SEMP) Development for the Space Launch System (SLS) Program
categories: Systems Engineering and Analysis; Program and Project Management; DDT/E; Program planning / development and management; Engineering design and project processes and standards; Mission definition and planning; Planning of requirements verification processes
categories_list: Engineering design and project processes and standards

sections.abstract:
On October 11, 2010, the United States Congress authorized NASA to design, develop, operate and retire a Space Launch System (SLS) that can deliver crew and cargo to low Earth orbit and to enable missions beyond earth orbit. [1] The SLS is a single-project program [2] managed from the Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC). The goal of the SLS program is to provide a heavy launch capability for NASA. SLS provides the propulsion stages to lift a variety of anticipated payloads. The SLS is to be capable of lifting astronauts and supplies to near-Earth destinations such as asteroids, the moon, Mars, and most of Earth’s Lagrangian points. SLS may provide launch capability for payloads to the International Space Station. The SLS program approved their draft SEMP on December 2, 2011 before they conducted a Block 1 System Requirements Review (SRR)/System Design Review (SDR) in February to March 2012. The MSFC Center Director’s designee (the Center Management Council) formally approved the SEMP on May 13, 2013 before the SLS Program’s Block 1 Preliminary Design Review (PDR) in June to July 2013. A timeline of events is given. Lessons learned from the drafting, review, and approval processes of the SEMP are described.

[1] United States Public Law 111-267 “National Aeronautics and Space Administration Authorization Act of 2010”. The U.S. Government Printing Office link = http://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/PLAW-111publ267/pdf/PLAW-111publ267.pdf [2] Single-project program is defined in NPR 7120.5, NASA Space Flight Program and Project Management Requirements and SLS-PLAN-001, SLS Program Plan section 3.3 Program Architecture.
sections.driving_event:
MSFC EV71 is the Technical Management Branch in the Systems Engineering and Integration Division of the Spacecraft and Vehicle Systems Department in the MSFC Engineering Directorate. EV71 started writing the SLS Program’s SEMP under the direction of the SLS Lead Systems Engineer (LSE) in October 2010. As step number one, EV71 and the SLS LSE wrote down and agreed upon the following guiding principles for development of the SLS SEMP:

- Keep SEMP as short and concise as possible by focusing tightly on MPR 7123.1.

- Help readers see the big picture.

- Make the SEMP modular and flexible. See Recommendation #2d on page 4.

- Avoid duplication.

The Developer of the SLS Program’s SEMP then wrote and revised six drafts before the SLS LSE and SLS Program Control Board (PCB) agreed to internally baseline the draft SEMP (prior to Center approval) on December 3, 2011. The SLS PCB was challenged with a lack of agreements on the philosophical approach for systems engineering management; the SLS Program Integration Office non-concurred and presented the following concerns:

- “SEMP may not provide enough specific details for how the SLS Program will integrate the technical effort…”

- “SEMP may not meet Center and Agency requirements.”

- “SEMP may not pass external review…”

- “Missing content may require development of additional documents…”

- “Pointer documents (MPRs, MPDs, MWIs, etc.) may need to be provided and could be put under scrutiny by external reviewers.”

Some stakeholders wanted the SEMP to be “perfect” but program plans and SEMP are never perfect. The SLS PCB listened to the non-concurrence and then decided to move forward with approval of the draft SEMP. The PCB acknowledged that they might have to update the SEMP in the future to reflect new developments as the Program matures.

Another issue that persisted throughout the writing of the SEMP was that decisions were not always made and communicated in open forums. The closed forums-approach precluded the SEMP writer from capturing some decisions first hand and in context. The context of the decision can be as important as the decision itself.

The first Engineering Management Council (EMC) was held on January 2012, and the draft SEMP was approved. Afterward, the SLS Program Manager decided to postpone the SEMP’s presentation to the MSFC Program/Project Management Advisory Committee (PPMAC) and the MSFC Center Management Council (CMC) until after the SLS Program’s combined System Requirements Review (SRR)/System Design Review (SDR). The SLS Program Manager felt that it would be advantageous to allow the draft SEMP be reviewed at SRR/SDR first so that SRR/SDR Review Item Discrepancies (RIDs) and SRR/SDR Standing Review Board (SRB) Requests for Action (RFAs) could be incorporated in the SEMP before asking the Center Director to approve it. The SLS Program’s Block 1 SRR/SDR was conducted in February to March 2012.

After SRR/SDR when the draft SEMP was updated, the October 2012 review of the SEMP by the PCB went much smoother. The Program approved the updated draft SEMP on 4 October 2012.

The SLS SEMP was finally approved by the MSFC Center Director in May of 2013 in the CMC, just weeks prior to the kickoff of the SLS Program’s Preliminary Design Review (PDR). The sequence of events from first draft to final approval highlighted some successful areas and other areas for improvement.

Final approval timeline of events:

4 October 2012 SLS Program Control Board approved the Post-SRR/SDR updates to the SEMP.

23 April 2013 Engineering Management Council (EMC)

2 May 2013 Program Project Management Advisory Committee (PPMAC); PPMAC approved

13 May 2013 Modified EMC SEMP presentation presented to Marshall Space Flight Center Management Council (CMC); CMC approved/Center Director approved

30 May 2013 SLS Program Control Board (PCB); PCB accepted the Center’s modifications (they did not elect to reclama any of the changes).

18-19 June 2013 SLS Preliminary Design Review Kick Off

At the EMC meeting on 23 April 2013, the Engineering Management Council, chaired by the Deputy Manager of Engineering agreed to the SLS Program’s request that the Center Director delegate authority to the Program Manager (PM) to approve future revisions to the SEMP with the Chief Engineer’s (CE) concurrence. The SLS Program also requested that the SLS Program would request for the CMC's approval if a future SEMP revision proposes any further tailoring of Center-level requirements. The SLS Program recognizes that the SEMP must comply with MPR 7123.1. If the SEMP changes do not affect the tailoring of the SEMP, the changes can be approved by the Program Manager.

Note: Tailoring refers to the compliance of the plan to meeting all the requirements from MPR 7123.1 which are traceable to the requirements of NPR 7123.1. Customization of a SEMP, which is not tailoring, refers to the choices of methods, tools, and processes for complying with the MPR requirements. Tailoring refers to adjusting the requirements to meet specific program or project needs, and necessarily involves seeking relief from some aspect of the requirement (i.e. a deviation or waiver). Customization refers to how a requirement (which may or may not have been tailored) is met.

The SEMP arrived at the PPMAC on 2 May 2013. The PPMAC only addressed comments to the SEMP, and approved the SEMP on 2 May 2013. The CMC then approved the SEMP on 13 May 2013.

End Result : Success

Additional Information & Comments:

The SLS Program released revision A of their SEMP on December 5, 2013. The SEMP now has zero To Be Determined (TBD) items. The SEMP’s Forward Work Plan (Appendix C) is to make updates prior to each lifecycle review to reflect Program maturity, if necessary ; and to close any Review Item Discrepancies or Standing Review Board Requests for Action after those lifecycle reviews, if the SEMP receives any .
sections.lesson_learned:
1. Good practice – The Developer/Book Manager and the SLS LSE wrote down and agreed upon a set of guiding principles for development of the SEMP before they began writing the SEMP. The guiding principles were very beneficial and a positive for the Program. See Recommendation #2

2. Observation – SEMPs will never be perfect, and that’s okay.

3. Good practice – Given that a plan is simply a collection of decisions, the Developer/Book Manager of the SEMP actively collaborated with the SLS Lead Systems Engineer and others to help them make those decisions. The Developer did not passively sit and wait for other people to come to him.

4. Observation - Document change processes and review times were not fully developed through most of the SEMP development.

5. Improvement - Include the SEMP author in all meetings where decisions relevant to SEMP content are made, and include context for the decision made.
sections.recommendation:
1. From the beginning, write down the guiding principles to be used for the SEMP’s development and seek agreement from key decision makers.

2. For example, here are the guiding principles that we adopted for the development of the SLS Program’s SEMP:

1. Keep the SEMP as short and concise as possible by focusing tightly on the MPR 7123.1 requirements (center requirements for systems engineering).

2. Help readers see the big picture

1. Focus on the forest, not the trees

2. Focus on how the Chief Engineer and the Lead System Engineer will manage their day-to-day system engineering and integration efforts

1. Make the SEMP modular and flexible

1. Point to other documents and plans

2. By analogy, follow a software-like model

1. Small, central core

2. Call subroutines (in our case, existing MSFC processes and other SLS plans) to perform detailed instructions

3. Subroutines (the other plans) can be upgraded without affecting the core

1. Avoid Duplication

1. Do not quote verbatim what is written in higher level documents

2. Do not duplicate details in lower level documents; reference and point to them

1. SEMP Writers:

1. SEMP writers need to have good people skills and emotional intelligence to persuade and influence others to make the decisions that a SEMP is required to document.

2. It would be very beneficial for a SEMP developer to be a Chief Engineer or Lead systems Engineer at one point in their career so that they have the a) experience, b) know the ground rules, c) know the standpoint or view of the CE, and d) are able to write short, concise requirements. The SLS Program’s SEMP Developer served in both of those roles at one point in his career.

1. Training

1. SEMP writers should take the Center-recommended class in “Developing and Implementing a SEMP” BEFORE they are tasked with writing a SEMP

2. Look for examples to emulate good practices; don’t emulate poor practices

1. The Review and Approval Process

1. Plan adequate time for review of the documents prior to major reviews.

2. Plan for delays due to changes, or other extenuating circumstances

3. The SEMP approval presentation preparer should include charts in back up that described decisions or recommendations made at earlier approval meetings.

4. Identify options for release (e.g. the PCB may have been an effective alternative)

2 May 2013 Program Project Management Advisory Committee (PPMAC); PPMAC approved

13 May 2013 Modified EMC SEMP presentation presented to Marshall Space Flight Center Management Council (CMC); CMC approved/Center Director approved

30 May 2013 SLS Program Control Board (PCB); PCB accepted the Center’s modifications (they did not elect to reclama any of the changes).

18-19 June 2013 SLS Preliminary Design Review Kick Off

At the EMC meeting on 23 April 2013, the Engineering Management Council, chaired by the Deputy Manager of Engineering agreed to the SLS Program’s request that the Center Director delegate authority to the Program Manager (PM) to approve future revisions to the SEMP with the Chief Engineer’s (CE) concurrence. The SLS Program also requested that the SLS Program would request for the CMC's approval if a future SEMP revision proposes any further tailoring of Center-level requirements. The SLS Program recognizes that the SEMP must comply with MPR 7123.1. If the SEMP changes do not affect the tailoring of the SEMP, the changes can be approved by the Program Manager.

Note: Tailoring refers to the compliance of the plan to meeting all the requirements from MPR 7123.1 which are traceable to the requirements of NPR 7123.1. Customization of a SEMP, which is not tailoring, refers to the choices of methods, tools, and processes for complying with the MPR requirements. Tailoring refers to adjusting the requirements to meet specific program or project needs, and necessarily involves seeking relief from some aspect of the requirement (i.e. a deviation or waiver). Customization refers to how a requirement (which may or may not have been tailored) is met.

The SEMP arrived at the PPMAC on 2 May 2013. The PPMAC only addressed comments to the SEMP, and approved the SEMP on 2 May 2013. The CMC then approved the SEMP on 13 May 2013.

End Result : Success

Additional Information & Comments:

The SLS Program released revision A of their SEMP on December 5, 2013. The SEMP now has zero To Be Determined (TBD) items. The SEMP’s Forward Work Plan (Appendix C) is to make updates prior to each lifecycle review to reflect Program maturity, if necessary ; and to close any Review Item Discrepancies or Standing Review Board Requests for Action after those lifecycle reviews, if the SEMP receives any .

## Lesson Learned
1. Good practice – The Developer/Book Manager and the SLS LSE wrote down and agreed upon a set of guiding principles for development of the SEMP before they began writing the SEMP. The guiding principles were very beneficial and a positive for the Program. See Recommendation #2

2. Observation – SEMPs will never be perfect, and that’s okay.

3. Good practice – Given that a plan is simply a collection of decisions, the Developer/Book Manager of the SEMP actively collaborated with the SLS Lead Systems Engineer and others to help them make those decisions. The Developer did not passively sit and wait for other people to come to him.

4. Observation - Document change processes and review times were not fully developed through most of the SEMP development.

5. Improvement - Include the SEMP author in all meetings where decisions relevant to SEMP content are made, and include context for the decision made.

## Recommendation
1. From the beginning, write down the guiding principles to be used for the SEMP’s development and seek agreement from key decision makers.

2. For example, here are the guiding principles that we adopted for the development of the SLS Program’s SEMP:

1. Keep the SEMP as short and concise as possible by focusing tightly on the MPR 7123.1 requirements (center requirements for systems engineering).

2. Help readers see the big picture

1. Focus on the forest, not the trees

2. Focus on how the Chief Engineer and the Lead System Engineer will manage their day-to-day system engineering and integration efforts

1. Make the SEMP modular and flexible

1. Point to other documents and plans

2. By analogy, follow a software-like model

1. Small, central core

2. Call subroutines (in our case, existing MSFC processes and other SLS plans) to perform detailed instructions

3. Subroutines (the other plans) can be upgraded without affecting the core

1. Avoid Duplication

1. Do not quote verbatim what is written in higher level documents

2. Do not duplicate details in lower level documents; reference and point to them

1. SEMP Writers:

1. SEMP writers need to have good people skills and emotional intelligence to persuade and influence others to make the decisions that a SEMP is required to document.

2. It would be very beneficial for a SEMP developer to be a Chief Engineer or Lead systems Engineer at one point in their career so that they have the a) experience, b) know the ground rules, c) know the standpoint or view of the CE, and d) are able to write short, concise requirements. The SLS Program’s SEMP Developer served in both of those roles at one point in his career.

1. Training

1. SEMP writers should take the Center-recommended class in “Developing and Implementing a SEMP” BEFORE they are tasked with writing a SEMP

2. Look for examples to emulate good practices; don’t emulate poor practices

1. The Review and Approval Process

1. Plan adequate time for review of the documents prior to major reviews.

2. Plan for delays due to changes, or other extenuating circumstances

3. The SEMP approval presentation preparer should include charts in back up that described decisions or recommendations made at earlier approval meetings.

4. Identify options for release (e.g. the PCB may have been an effective alternative)

sections.abstract:
2010 was a significant year for NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope Program. The National Academy of Sciences Astronomy Decadal Survey reaffirmed that completing the Webb Telescope was the nation’s top astronomy priority. At nearly the same time, Senator Barbara Mikulski, a long-time Webb advocate, requested an independent review of the successor to the Hubble Space Telescope, as the JWST Program was beginning a replan due to its continual budget troubles.

When an independent panel of experts published its review of the Program in October of 2010, its members recommended the Project shift from focusing on technology development to managing the Webb’s life cycle cost and launch readiness date, with the Project getting more visibility inside NASA by reporting directly to the Goddard Center Director and the Program reporting directly to the Agency’s Associate Administrator. This lesson describes changes in the JWST Program Office's approach to management and the resulting positive outcomes, recognizing that the telescope still has years of fabrication, integration, assembly and test ahead.
sections.driving_event:
JWST had a prolonged technology development period following the selection of the prime contractor in 2002. It is difficult to predict how long it will take to develop a new technology, and during the period from 2002 to 2008, JWST struggled with several cutting-edge developments. These developments took longer, and consequently cost more, than forecast during formulation. Since commitment, telescope development has faced continual budget problems. An independent review panel assessing the JWST Program in 2010 concluded that the problems causing cost growth and schedule delays were associated with budgeting and program management, not technical performance, as the budget baseline accepted at the confirmation review did not reflect the most probable cost with adequate reserves in each year of project execution. This resulted in a project that was simply not executable within the budgeted resources.

James Webb Space Telescope Artists Concept
sections.recommendation: Projects experience challenges that are not limited to pushing technology to the limits or using existing technologies in entirely new ways. When replanning or rebaselining a project, consider program and project management and how it is helping the project to succeed or may be causing it to fail. In the case of the James Webb Space Telescope, it took management changes at several levels to finally put the project on a solid foundation -- the changes went beyond putting new people in place and included taking new approaches to Program/project management. Success for this successor to the Hubble Space Telescope may ultimately be due to a combination of technical excellence and a new management approach.
