# [NASA LLIS #1391] Detection of Steam Pipe Wall Thinning Due to Corrosion
- **Date:** 2003-09-11
- **Organization:** Johnson Space Center (JSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Aeronautics Research; Human Exploration and Operations; Science
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1391

## Abstract
Systemic management and technical failures led to the catastrophic rupture of a test system. 3 lessons are published regarding this specific incident; this lesson addresses problems with the detection of pipe wall thinning due to corrosion and the selection of inadequate test methods.

## Driving Event / Background
On September 11, 2003, at approximately 2:16 PM, the steam line on the Large Altitude Simulation System (LASS) suffered a catastrophic failure of the 24-inch expansion loop located adjacent to the Test Stand 401 steam ejector exhaust duct. The LASS was being operated to verify its readiness to support an altitude firing of the 4th stage of a Minuteman ICBM scheduled for September 25, 2003. The failure occurred approximately 16 seconds after the LASS was commanded to go to full steam, and resulted in a rupture of a portion of the line that dislocated several pieces of the 24-inch pipe in various directions away from the test stand. The proximate cause of the event was pipe wall corrosion that led to selective thinning of the wall, which resulted in the pipe rupture under pressure. The following observations came from the investigation:

1. During the mishap investigation, evidence of rust scale deposits around steam line drains (or “exhaust ducts”) was observed. This is an indicator that internal corrosion and erosion is taking place in the system.

External corrosion products on the pipes were also observed, especially where external insulation trapped water from environmental sources.

1. In piping subject to corrosion, it is difficult to determine the location of old pipe wall thinning in complex installations without 100% surveying.

2. At the same time, Non-Destructive Evaluation techniques for determining steam pipe wall thickness were found to be inconclusive due to the detritus from internal corrosion remaining in place primarily on the inside of pipe walls.

3. In this particular case, an alternative method to assess system integrity - hydrostatic pressure testing of old or modified fluid handling lines - was not an effective means of verification of long-term pressure integrity.

## Lesson Learned
Methods of evaluating critical system parameters must be verified as sufficiently reliable to support risk assessment

## Recommendation
1. Contingent on system design life requirements, develop and implement a corrosion survey plan for all of the steam lines and ejector duct that includes documenting the results and location of pipe inspections, comparing results from year to year, documenting any trends that may develop, and stating clearly the minimum passing criteria for each inspection.

2.

sections.abstract: Systemic management and technical failures led to the catastrophic rupture of a test system. 3 lessons are published regarding this specific incident; this lesson addresses contingency planning and assuring that risk controls remain in place throughout a system's life.
sections.driving_event:
On September 11, 2003, at approximately 2:16 PM, the steam line on the Large Altitude Simulation System (LASS) suffered a catastrophic failure of the 24-inch expansion loop located adjacent to the Test Stand 401 steam ejector exhaust duct. The LASS was being operated to verify its readiness to support an altitude firing of the 4th stage of a Minuteman ICBM scheduled for September 25, 2003. The failure occurred approximately 16 seconds after the LASS was commanded to go to full steam, and resulted in a rupture of a portion of the line that dislocated several pieces of the 24-inch pipe in various directions away from the test stand. The proximate cause of the event was pipe wall corrosion that led to selective thinning of the wall, which resulted in the pipe rupture under pressure. The investigation resulted in the following conclusions and observations:

1. Piping containing high mass flow rates must be examined for the capacity to withstand the forces generated during a pipe wall failure, and potential moment arms must be kept short enough that the pipe strength is not exceeded during a failure.

2. Piping designed to “leak-before-burst” capability that has experienced wall thinning will ultimately transition to a “burst-before-leak” situation if the wall thinning is not arrested.

3. Instrumentation data sample rate and data quality must be high enough to catch the possible events that the transducer might measure, not just the expected events.

4. System operational capability, such as design life, must be established and documented at the initial design to allow appropriate decisions as the system approaches its capability limits.

1. Assure that the system contains voids, supports, guides, and restraints that would allow the steam lines to handle thermal expansion and thrust loading.

2.

3. Implement remote safing capability for facility systems.

1. Assess the availability of PPE and atmospheric monitoring equipment in manned test monitoring facilities such as blockhouses.

2. Assess the human factors design of control room console layouts, and facility system status displays to aid personnel in assessing facility conditions.

3. Implement measures to renew the appreciation of the hazards associated with high energy systems, and to the importance of understanding all aspects of high energy facility systems condition, among design, test, and maintenance personnel.

7. Ensure that the integrity of design principles such as “leak before burst” are preserved throughout the system life cycle and verified by hard data (as a complement to standards and code compliance).

sections.abstract: A mechanical technician came into contact with an energized electrical circuit at the LC-39, Pad A Oxidizer Storage Area. A control cabinet had been removed and the circuit breaker feeding the bare conductors had been locked out in the electrical switchboard. Another contractor was modifying the electrical distribution system. The LOTO device was improperly removed and the circuit was later re-energized.
sections.driving_event: On July 10, 2003, a mechanical technician came into contact with an energized electrical circuit at the LC-39, Pad A Oxidizer Storage Area. A control cabinet had been removed and the circuit breaker feeding the bare conductors had been locked out in the electrical switchboard. Another contractor was modifying the electrical distribution system. The LOTO device was improperly removed and the circuit was later re-energized.
sections.lesson_learned:
1. Hazardous situations can be created if LOTO devices are improperly removed.

2.

3. During construction, it is critical to understand the proper placement of LOTO devices.

4. Hazardous situations can be created if bare conductors are not properly secured.

5. During electrical system modification, it is critical to involve all affected users.

6. After electrical system modification, it is critical for affected users to revalidate their systems.
sections.recommendation:
1. Do not improperly remove LOTO devices.

2.

3. Understand system configuration to ensure proper placement of LOTO devices.

4. Adequately guard or ground exposed conductors when working on electrical systems, even if the circuit has been de-energized or LOTO has been applied.

5. Ensure all users affected by an electrical system modification are aware of configuration changes.

6. Ensure all affected users revalidate their systems after electrical system modifications are complete.

# [NASA LLIS #1365] Lock out/Tag out Procedure Not Followed
- **Date:** 2003-09-08
- **Organization:** Kennedy Space Center (KSC)
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1365

## Abstract
A mechanical technician came into contact with an energized electrical circuit at the LC-39, Pad A Oxidizer Storage Area. A control cabinet had been removed and the circuit breaker feeding the bare conductors had been locked out in the electrical switchboard. Another contractor was modifying the electrical distribution system. The LOTO device was improperly removed and the circuit was later re-energized.

## Driving Event / Background
On July 10, 2003, a mechanical technician came into contact with an energized electrical circuit at the LC-39, Pad A Oxidizer Storage Area. A control cabinet had been removed and the circuit breaker feeding the bare conductors had been locked out in the electrical switchboard. Another contractor was modifying the electrical distribution system. The LOTO device was improperly removed and the circuit was later re-energized.

## Lesson Learned
1. Hazardous situations can be created if LOTO devices are improperly removed.

2.

3. During construction, it is critical to understand the proper placement of LOTO devices.

4. Hazardous situations can be created if bare conductors are not properly secured.

5. During electrical system modification, it is critical to involve all affected users.

6. After electrical system modification, it is critical for affected users to revalidate their systems.

## Recommendation
1. Do not improperly remove LOTO devices.

2.

3. Understand system configuration to ensure proper placement of LOTO devices.

4. Adequately guard or ground exposed conductors when working on electrical systems, even if the circuit has been de-energized or LOTO has been applied.

5. Ensure all users affected by an electrical system modification are aware of configuration changes.

6. Ensure all affected users revalidate their systems after electrical system modifications are complete.

title: Transporting Tools for Overhead Work
mission_directorate: Aeronautics Research; Human Exploration and Operations; Science

sections.abstract: Overhead work requires special precautions and safe behavior practices to ensure that equipment does not fall on personnel and equipment underneath.
sections.driving_event: A maintenance worker was ascending a fixed ladder when one of the tools he was carrying fell to the ground. The worker needed multiple specialty tools requiring multiple trips on the ladder to do some overhead work. In this particular case, the worker tried to carry all the tools he needed on one trip. Not all the tools were secured, such as in a tool bag or tied-off to the worker.
sections.lesson_learned: Use safe procedures in accordance with behavior-based safety principles when transporting and operating tools during overhead work.
sections.recommendation: Before going up the ladder, remove all loose items from upper shirt pockets. Do not carry tools or hardware up a ladder; have them hoisted up to the work site. While at the overhead work site tether your tools and/or hardware as applicable. Since even under the best circumstances tools can still fall while doing overhead work, establish safety barriers below the work site to establish a "drop-zone" safety area so people don't run the risk of being struck by falling objects.

full_text:
# [NASA LLIS #1364] Transporting Tools for Overhead Work
- **Date:** 2003-09-03
- **Organization:** Johnson Space Center (JSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Aeronautics Research; Human Exploration and Operations; Science
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1364

## Abstract
Overhead work requires special precautions and safe behavior practices to ensure that equipment does not fall on personnel and equipment underneath.

## Driving Event / Background
A maintenance worker was ascending a fixed ladder when one of the tools he was carrying fell to the ground. The worker needed multiple specialty tools requiring multiple trips on the ladder to do some overhead work. In this particular case, the worker tried to carry all the tools he needed on one trip. Not all the tools were secured, such as in a tool bag or tied-off to the worker.

## Lesson Learned
Use safe procedures in accordance with behavior-based safety principles when transporting and operating tools during overhead work.

## Recommendation
Before going up the ladder, remove all loose items from upper shirt pockets. Do not carry tools or hardware up a ladder; have them hoisted up to the work site. While at the overhead work site tether your tools and/or hardware as applicable. Since even under the best circumstances tools can still fall while doing overhead work, establish safety barriers below the work site to establish a "drop-zone" safety area so people don't run the risk of being struck by falling objects.

title: Space Network (SN) Ka-band Infrastructure - Design, Integration, and Test Issues

sections.abstract: A Ka-band return infrastructure was implemented for NASA's Space Network under the GSFC Ka-Band Transition Project (KaTP). Throughout the requirements development, design, implementation, and testing activities for this ground terminal, there were a number of events or circumstances that caused lessons to be learned. These events and lesson learned are listed below.
sections.driving_event:
The KaTP was instituted at the White Sand Complex by December 2002 and consisted of two major functions: Modify the existing 225 MHz Ku-band downconverters to support the Ka-band Space Network Interoperability Plan (SNIP) frequencies and install a Ka-band wideband architecture consisting of waveguide equalizers, downconverters and IF Switch. Associated software and firmware changes were also required. A demonstration test was conducted to validate the overall performance of the KaTP infrastructure using high data rate technologies that could support future NASA near-earth missions.

1. System Requirements Document (SRD) Development

The SRD encompassed too many requirements, some of which were not directly applicable to the immediate KaTP.

1. Analysis

The WSC KaTP team spent unscheduled resources performing analysis on the “RF solution” Waveguide Equalizer. The vendor produced simulation results based on group delay, while the KaTP SRD had results in deviation from best-fit phase (phase nonlinearity). The KaTP team also spent considerable unscheduled time performing analysis on the effects of phase non-linearity on system performance.

1. Vendor Delivery

The KaTP was adversely affected by the late delivery of vendor-developed equipment. The downconverter vendor has originally proposed a 6-month delivery schedule that extended to 19 months. The vendor had difficulty meeting several downconverter specifications and had spent several months redesigning modules. The IF Switch delivery was also extended from 6 months to 10 months based on vendor inexperience with developing the product.

1. Equipment Procurement

The KaTP contractor team underestimated the time and effort to initiate procurements through the GSFC Consolidated Logistics Facility (CLF). The KaTP contractor accounted for the time required to perform RFP technical reviews, however processes required for large-ticket items (i.e. downconverters) require additional vendor paperwork that was not accounted for by the team. While the KaTP contractor team set up communications with the buyer at the CLF to speed the procurement process, the schedule estimates were far too optimistic (usually assuming 1 week) to get vendors under contract.

1. Project Budget

The KaTP team exceeded the initial budget estimate allocated for the project. The KaTP provided many unique design challenges that were magnified by the limited funds available for the task. The KaTP team was required to modify a total of 28 downconverters (225 MHz), and install a Ka-band architecture consisting of 650 MHz downconverters, waveguide equalizers in multiple equipment chains interfaced to a common IF Switch. Some of the budgetary problems encountered can be attributed to the growth of the project and additional testing required by the customer.

1. Waveguide Equalizer Equipment Definition

The KaTP team initially focused on the Waveguide Equalizer operating at the IF frequency similar to the legacy design The KaTP Waveguide Equalizer procurement was delayed while a vendor performed a feasibility study. There were considerable additional amounts of time (approximately 9 months) and money ($47,000) before the IF solution was scrapped in favor of an RF solution.

1. 225 MHz Downconverter Modifications

The KaTP project called for the modification of an existing set of unique downconverter chassis'. These units were not consistent in their implementation when initially manufactured a decade earlier. There were unanticipated differences in the original implementation between each chassis such as cable routing and parts supplied by different vendors. This caused some additional “lost time” in having to deal with these subtle differences, and realignments.

1. Interference with TDRS Telemetry Signal

During KaTP Demonstration tests interference of the TDRS telemetry signal was noted while a CW signal was present on the Ka- wideband channel. The KaTP attempted to support the SNIP wideband frequency plan where the downlink signal of 13.720 GHz was shifted to 13.725 GHz. It was the view of the KaTP team that sufficient isolation existed between the Ka-band downlink signal on one polarization and the TDRS telemetry signal at 13.725 GHz on the opposite polarization. The KaTP team did not account for the potential for a user spacecraft going to CW mode.

1. SN Demonstration

During the KaTP 600 Mbps demonstration, a high end-to-end implmentation loss was measured. This high implementation loss occurred as a result of using non-optimum test equipment to test the channel. The test transmitter, receiver, upconverter, downconverter and high-powered amplifier (HPA) all contributed to the channel distortions that degraded performance. The KaTP demonstration tram spent unscheduled resourced performing analyses and simulations in order to determine the reason for the high end-to-end implementation loss.
sections.lesson_learned:
1. System Requirements Document (SRD) Development

2.

The SRD development task unnecessarily grew in scope and began to encompass future follow-on work. In addition to Ka-band IF requirements, several versions of the SRD included performance issues related to CCSDS data routing. Considerable time and effort was expended on reviewing documentation that was not pertinent to the task at hand. The SRD should have focused on the function and performance requirements of the Ka-band IF implementation task

1. Analysis

The WSC KaTP team did not originally allocate any labor costs or schedule impacts associated with performing analysis to the waveguide and phase nonlinearity issues. Delays to the KaTP project were incurred while a contractor team was called on to perform additional “impact to system performance” analysis. An example of this was experienced during the decision on total amounts of phase nonlinearity allowable for the KaTP infrastructure during the Waveguide Equalizer procurement. On a project with the scope, complexity and challenges of the KaTP, the team must consider budgeting additional hours for these unforeseen problems.

1. Vendor Delivery

While the KaTP implementation schedule was aggressive, one could not account for the large delays encountered from the vendors. The contractor team spent considerable time and energy working with the vendor and pushing for delivery. In future large procurements, the contractor team should account for some vendor delays when forecasting schedule and there should be some way of enforcing vendors to deliver hardware on time (either through incentives or penalties incorporated into the contract). The procurement office should have been involved earlier and they may have worked the delivery issues since they control the payments and have more clout with the vendor. Additional time in schedule should be allocated to do more work on vendor surveys and “requests for information” from prospective vendors. This may have given the KaTP team a better feel for aggressive specifications and alternative architectures. In some cases the team received one vendor quote, which implies
the specifications may have been too restrictive.

1. Equipment Procurement

The KaTP contractor team has learned to project more time into a schedule to account for RFP technical evaluations, initiating procurements through the CLF, and getting vendors under contract. For large acquisitions, this process can take four to eight weeks.

1. Project Budget

The size and complexity of the KaTP presented several unique challenges. From the onset, NASA project management stated the project had limited funds, however, they wanted to accomplish all of the goals of the project. The KaTP team attempted to achieve a system that met all the requirements with a minimal amount of risk to the project budget and schedule. This approach drove the team to implement an architecture similar to the legacy design and in the future the team should evaluate the critical parameters that impact system performance and choose an architecture that would minimize this risk.

1. Waveguide Equalizer Equipment Definition

The KaTP team focused on an IF frequency Waveguide Equalizer too quickly without weighing other options. This decision was based somewhat on the legacy equipment design using an IF-based equalizer. The team should have explored other possibilities concurrently but the time and effort was not allocated into the schedule.

1. 225 MHz Downconverter Modifications

The legacy 225 MHz downconverters were built as custom units and the implementation varied from chassis to chassis. This problem could not have been foreseen, a realistic schedule should allot additional time to handle unforeseen problems.

1. Interference with TDRSS Telemetry Signal

The KaTP team should have contacted the NASA spacecraft engineering group charged with the development of the TDRS- HIJ series spacecraft to determine the rationale for their frequency plan. The spacecraft manufacturer chose to design a specific frequency plan for the TDRS-HIJ series satellites that was not compatible with the SNIP frequency plan. The KaTP team should have researched this issue more thoroughly during the design and implementation of the ground infrastructure.

1. SN Demonstration

The KaTP was hindered during the SN Demonstration tests by test equipment that exhibited higher than expected implementation losses. A considerable amount of time was spent verifying the test equipment, understanding and characterizing the losses inherent in the various test configurations. It is recommended that test receivers should be optimized for the data rate under test. Future testing should incorporate test equipment that meets or exceeds the fidelity one is trying to demonstrate. Suspect test equipment reduces the confidence in the test results and impacts the schedule and budget.
sections.recommendation: Recommendations are provided above as part of the lesson learned for each topic.

sections.abstract: Throughout the requirements development, design, implementation, integration and testing activities for this ground terminal, there were a number of events and/or circumstances that caused lessons to be learned. These events and lessons are listed below.
sections.driving_event:
A Ka-band demonstration ground terminal was implemented for NASA»s Ground Network under the GSFC Ka-Band Transition Project (KaTP). This ground terminal is intended to function as a demonstration terminal to demonstrate the feasibility of Ka-band services, and to aid the testing of Ka-band and high data rate technologies that could support future NASA near-earth missions. a. System Requirements Document (SRD) The SRD encompassed too many requirements that were not directly related to the performance and capability of the Ka band portion of the ground terminal. b. High Data Rate Receiver The performance of the high data rate demodulator/bit synchronizer used during the demonstration testing did not perform as well as desired. The unit was tunable from 50 to 600 Mbps. Performance was acceptable up to 450 Mbps, but the unit seemed very susceptible to channel distortions at higher rates. c. Boresite Antenna The boresite system used for testing the KaTP GN ground terminal consisted of a test modulator, upconverter and one meter dual band S, Ka parabolic antenna mounted at the top of an antenna tower. The one meter boresite antenna provided adequate S-band and Ka-band gain, however, the beamwidth at Ka was too narrow for testing purposes. Movement of the boresite antenna tower due to wind caused problems during error gradient testing of the Ka-band autotrack system.

Also, a different antenna was used on the boresite tower than the one used for factory testing of the GN Ka-band antenna autotrack system. This resulted in test results on-site that varied from factory test results making problem resolution difficult with the antenna vendor. d. Channel Distortions The Ka-band ground terminal system was purchased in several subsystems (antenna, downconverter, fiber optics, etc) and integrated together at Wallops Flight Facility. Once the system was fully configured, the channel distortion levels were greater than anticipated. e. Radome The radome leaked considerably after installation. All seams had to eventually be caulked. f. Antenna axis configuration A Ka-band ground terminal antenna was required that could track low-earth orbiting spacecraft, including tracking support of spacecraft through zenith. Three axis (azimuth/elevation/tilt mount) antennas have been used in the recent past by NASA's Ground Network to support these type of spacecraft orbits, but some reliability and maintenance issues with this configuration have been encountered. g. Ka Feed components Performance problems encountered with the Ka feed considerably impacted delivery and installation.
sections.lesson_learned: a. System Requirements Document (SRD) In addition to Ka-band requirements, the SRD also included S band transmit and receive requirements for the system since the antenna was dual band. However, S band requirements should have been stated at a higher level. Much effort went into justifying and verifying S band equipment performance specs. Nearly 75% of the SRD requirements were related to S band. The SRD should have focused less on the S band requirements, since the intent of the system was primarily to demonstrate the Ka performance. The S band subsystems utilized standard, proven equipment that were already in use in the GN. b. High Data Rate Receiver For bit error rate (BER) testing, it is recommended to use receivers that have been optimized for the data rates under test. Although the unit used during demonstration testing was very flexible and useful for general lab support, the receiver performance in terms of implementation loss at the higher data rates of interest was not adequate to support the objectives of the test. The implementation loss of the test receiver was higher than expected and created difficulties in obtaining useful BER test data. It would also be recommended that a receiver manufacturer take into account the system channel magnitude and phase response to optimally match the receiver filter for best ISI performance. c. Boresite Antenna The use of a smaller boresite antenna, or separate antennas for S and Ka band would provide better performance during boresite testing, particularly in high wind situations. For example, a WR-34 horn was used during the latter portion of the demonstration testing, and it provided improved performance compared to the one meter parabolic antenna for this test scenario. It is also recommended to use the same boresite antenna for on-site testing that is used for factory testing. When problems were encountered on-site that did not appear at the factory, the local boresite antenna was blamed for the problems. Using the same boresite antenna would eliminate any finger pointing in a similar situation. d. Channel Distortions It is recommended that system requirements be levied on one vender that is responsible for the entire ground terminal design, integration, and test. For example, the magnitude and phase response for the entire channel should be specified from RF input to IF output, and the vendor should perform an allocation of theses end-to-end system requirements to individual components. Distortion measurements through the whole system should be verified at the factory prior to delivery. Also it is recommended that the receiver be mounted close to antenna, and transfer the IF signal in digital format via fiber optic cable rather than at the intermediate frequency. Cable runs should be minimized, and the use very low loss cable is recommended. e. Radome The vendor should demonstrate water tightness of radome prior to delivery and installation on-site. f. Antenna axis configuration The X-Y axis configuration is the recommended approach for a ground terminal that is required to track low-earth orbiting spacecraft. This configuration precludes the use of a third tilt axis to handle high elevation passes. The X-Y axis system is less complex, improving maintenance and reliability. g. Ka Feed components Nearly all problems encountered with the feed were the result of low quality cables and adapters. Recommend in the future that reliability be considered more than cost for the feed subsystem components.
sections.recommendation: Recommendations are provided above as part of the lesson learned for each topic.

sections.abstract: Even though NASA may be able to provide goods and services more effectively and economically, an investigation board may use outside contractors to ensure a perception of "independence."
sections.driving_event: There was concern at NASA over the role of the Columbia Accident Investigation Board's procurement of goods and services through a support contractor. NASA and other government agencies have the ability on occasion to provide services much cheaper. Procurement decisions were often made on the basis of the perception of independence rather than cost efficiency or effectiveness.
sections.lesson_learned: In general, an independent accident investigation board may use outside contractors on the basis of “independence” even if that function can be provided more effectively by the NASA center or another government agency.
sections.recommendation:
- Draft language in the Contingency Action Plan (CAP) that enables full use of existing governmental (e.g. FEMA, NTSB, DOD, DOJ) resources for investigation purposes. Services provided to the investigation groups will require 24/7 support at startup with the appropriate organizational functions in place as required.

- Consult with pre-identified onsite experts to purchase products need (e.g. high resolution camera, recording devices, software system), so (1) the users of the product can be properly trained or a professional can be provided, and (2) the hardware/software can be utilized by that provider at the end of the project.

# [NASA LLIS #1435] Accident Investigations/Procurement of Goods and Services
- **Date:** 2003-08-31
- **Organization:** Johnson Space Center (JSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1435

## Abstract
Even though NASA may be able to provide goods and services more effectively and economically, an investigation board may use outside contractors to ensure a perception of "independence."

## Driving Event / Background
There was concern at NASA over the role of the Columbia Accident Investigation Board's procurement of goods and services through a support contractor. NASA and other government agencies have the ability on occasion to provide services much cheaper. Procurement decisions were often made on the basis of the perception of independence rather than cost efficiency or effectiveness.

## Lesson Learned
In general, an independent accident investigation board may use outside contractors on the basis of “independence” even if that function can be provided more effectively by the NASA center or another government agency.

## Recommendation
- Draft language in the Contingency Action Plan (CAP) that enables full use of existing governmental (e.g. FEMA, NTSB, DOD, DOJ) resources for investigation purposes. Services provided to the investigation groups will require 24/7 support at startup with the appropriate organizational functions in place as required.

- Consult with pre-identified onsite experts to purchase products need (e.g. high resolution camera, recording devices, software system), so (1) the users of the product can be properly trained or a professional can be provided, and (2) the hardware/software can be utilized by that provider at the end of the project.

For the Columbia accident investigation, investigators initially had to purchase their own tape recorders for witness interviews conducted in the field.

title: Accident Investigations/Configuration Management of Data

sections.abstract: Strong support to the CM organization is required to develop a fully functional action/request process and as quickly as possible and minimize the impact to the conduct of the investigation.
sections.driving_event: For the Columbia accident investigation, the end-to-end CM process for actions/requests for information took significantly longer than expected to be established and begin running smoothly. A manual, paper-based signoff process further hampered it.
sections.lesson_learned: To develop a fully functioning action/request for information process to support an accident investigation will take several weeks. Assure strong support to the CM organization because until it is working, the investigation will be hampered.
sections.recommendation:
- Designate CM specialists to analyze and tune the various CM processes and sub-processes for improvements and efficiencies. The start-up phase for the full end-to-end CM process to support an accident investigation may take 4-6 weeks. Additional CM personnel would probably speed up that startup inefficiency. After the start-up phase, the end-to-end CM process for a single action may still take on average around 3 weeks.

- Designate a Board support member to ensure that Board members understand the CM processes, so as to not create management issues.

- Use electronic OR manual concurrence for the CM process (not both). The process must avoid multiple entries and differing status.

## Abstract
Difficulty in contacting the IT support person and getting issues resolved, necessitates in situ, resident IT specialists, at least for investigation start-up activities.

## Driving Event / Background
While the Johnson Space Center - Mission Operations Directorate provided an IT support person for Columbia Task Force hardware, that person was not co-located with the Task Force. As it was often difficult to contact this person, it was difficult to get IT issues resolved.

## Lesson Learned
At least during startup, the resident IT specialists need to be in situ with the Board and with the Task Force and support available 24/7.

## Recommendation
- Make IT support specialists responsible for generating all NASA Service Requests (SRs) and working personnel computer configuration issues. Do not make the Task Force submit SRs for everything they need.

- Consider blanket SR's.

- For contractor support, put a Level of Effort (LOE) task in the current IT contract to support this type of function ahead of time. This person should not be the same person responsible for administering the action tracking and documentation management system. Suggest documenting this planning in an appendix to the CAP

title: Accident Investigations/Information Technology (IT) Support Requirements for Major Mishap Investigation

sections.abstract: An in-place, operational web-based Mishap Investigation Support System on hot standby, and a designated management team ready to support operational requirements and customization are needed to support accident investigation/information technology requirements for a major mishap.
sections.driving_event: There was no single NASA system on February 1 that could meet the requirements set for the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) and Columbia Task Force (CTF). The Process Based Mission Assurance - Enhanced Security (PBMA-ES) system, using a proven COTS "engine" was rapidly deployed within a dedicated stand-alone hardware/software environment to provide a high level of security, including 2-factor strong user authentication. The system provided immediate secure, web-based operability of key functionality to support a mobile, in-the-field, investigation activity including, action tracking, calendar, document management, and database capabilities. Neither the CAIB, the CTF, nor the PBMA management team could reasonably anticipate or identify all of the requirements at the beginning of the investigation (both functional and interface) needed to support the investigation. The requirements "critical needs" continued to evolve from the initial request for “action tracking,” i.e., customization of JSC form 564, to web links, to full text search, to advanced library support capabilities. In addition, particularly early-on, there existed a continuous, often tension-filled negotiation process between the needs of the multi-headed customer(s) (CAIB) and the IT-security community. The absence of clear IT security policies exacerbated the requirements change process. Finally, the degree and complexity of library management requirements, as driven by Department of Justice (DOJ), did not emerge until a month after implementation of the PBMA-ES. This real-time customization with “on-the-fly” changes constantly in-work, resulted in a major hw/sw configuration management challenge, organizational policy disconnects, and ultimately frustrated customers who were looking for immediate implementation of their desired changes.
sections.lesson_learned: Real-time, crisis-mode systems engineering can never capture all potential future requirements. You do the best that you can and make the best decisions you can with the information you have at the time. The overarching lesson learned is that NASA needs to have a web-based, Mishap Investigation Support System (MISS) in-place and operational, "locked and loaded" on hot standby to support major mishaps. The system must fulfill the requirement set identified in the next section. It is equally important to have a designated (hot standby) management team ready to support the myriad of operational requirements and customization needs that one can expect to emerge. In the final analysis, the experienced PBMA management team provided the necessary support to implement the dynamically evolving CAIB requirements.
sections.recommendation:
Establish a NASA baseline information technology Mishap Investigation Requirements Set (MIRS) to include the following elements:

- MISS Management Team: Experience dictates that a management team be available to quickly respond to a major mishap and be able to quickly implement mishap-specific plans and procedures such as: Configuration management IT Security Plan modifications On-site user orientation/training 24x7 technical support during the early phase of an investigation Data backup and archival activities Work group administration

- Financial/resource management

- Sustaining engineering and operations

- Collaborative Environment: Use a web-based, fully integrated, COTS knowledge management system application to provide immediate field support for the investigation team (i.e., members, contacts, calendars, task management, web-links, etc.). A COTS product will ensure best-available, market-driven capabilities are available to support mishap investigation teams.

- Independence/Portability: Expect to confront the issue of accident board independence and ensure that the MISS is established as a stand-alone hardware/software infrastructure behind a NASA firewall but portable so that it can be easily moved to any NASA Center.

- IT Security: A well-defined and documented NASA IT security policy applicable to all systems is essential. Recommend baselining NASA system host-center firewalls, secure socket layer encryption, and a secure but usable single factor user-authentication policy. A generic but tailorable IT security plan should be in place for the hot standby system.

- Hardware/Software Infrastructure: Use a commercial-like, multiple-web server front-end to ensure a high level of reliability and operability.

- Interfaces: Identify mandatory interfaces for compatibility with other support tool sets. Establish interface control agreements as part of MISS development. Interface control testing should verify interoperability.

- Library Services / Massive File Manipulation and Data Archiving: Co-locate the web servers with standalone archive/library servers if it is deemed necessary to perform frequent massive file upload, download, and manipulation. It is inefficient and time consuming to transfer massive files via the internet.

- Expect to Customize/Change Management: Experience suggests that no system can meet all potential requirements that may evolve during an investigation. Anticipating the need to customize, the MISS management team must have in-place: a baseline configuration management plan and process a change process with clear roles and responsibilities for requirements management and change approval a dedicated beta-test server to conduct verification testing for hw/sw changes

# [NASA LLIS #1463] Accident Investigations/Information Technology (IT) Support Requirements for Major Mishap Investigation
- **Date:** 2003-08-31
- **Organization:** Johnson Space Center (JSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1463

## Abstract
An in-place, operational web-based Mishap Investigation Support System on hot standby, and a designated management team ready to support operational requirements and customization are needed to support accident investigation/information technology requirements for a major mishap.

## Driving Event / Background
There was no single NASA system on February 1 that could meet the requirements set for the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) and Columbia Task Force (CTF). The Process Based Mission Assurance - Enhanced Security (PBMA-ES) system, using a proven COTS "engine" was rapidly deployed within a dedicated stand-alone hardware/software environment to provide a high level of security, including 2-factor strong user authentication. The system provided immediate secure, web-based operability of key functionality to support a mobile, in-the-field, investigation activity including, action tracking, calendar, document management, and database capabilities. Neither the CAIB, the CTF, nor the PBMA management team could reasonably anticipate or identify all of the requirements at the beginning of the investigation (both functional and interface) needed to support the investigation. The requirements "critical needs" continued to evolve from the initial request for “action tracking,” i.e., customization of JSC form 564, to web links, to full text search, to advanced library support capabilities. In addition, particularly early-on, there existed a continuous, often tension-filled negotiation process between the needs of the multi-headed customer(s) (CAIB) and the IT-security community. The absence of clear IT security policies exacerbated the requirements change process. Finally, the degree and complexity of library management requirements, as driven by Department of Justice (DOJ), did not emerge until a month after implementation of the PBMA-ES. This real-time customization with “on-the-fly” changes constantly in-work, resulted in a major hw/sw configuration management challenge, organizational policy disconnects, and ultimately frustrated customers who were looking for immediate implementation of their desired changes.

## Lesson Learned
Real-time, crisis-mode systems engineering can never capture all potential future requirements. You do the best that you can and make the best decisions you can with the information you have at the time. The overarching lesson learned is that NASA needs to have a web-based, Mishap Investigation Support System (MISS) in-place and operational, "locked and loaded" on hot standby to support major mishaps. The system must fulfill the requirement set identified in the next section. It is equally important to have a designated (hot standby) management team ready to support the myriad of operational requirements and customization needs that one can expect to emerge. In the final analysis, the experienced PBMA management team provided the necessary support to implement the dynamically evolving CAIB requirements.

## Recommendation
Establish a NASA baseline information technology Mishap Investigation Requirements Set (MIRS) to include the following elements:

- MISS Management Team: Experience dictates that a management team be available to quickly respond to a major mishap and be able to quickly implement mishap-specific plans and procedures such as: Configuration management IT Security Plan modifications On-site user orientation/training 24x7 technical support during the early phase of an investigation Data backup and archival activities Work group administration

- Financial/resource management

- Sustaining engineering and operations

- Collaborative Environment: Use a web-based, fully integrated, COTS knowledge management system application to provide immediate field support for the investigation team (i.e., members, contacts, calendars, task management, web-links, etc.). A COTS product will ensure best-available, market-driven capabilities are available to support mishap investigation teams.

- Independence/Portability: Expect to confront the issue of accident board independence and ensure that the MISS is established as a stand-alone hardware/software infrastructure behind a NASA firewall but portable so that it can be easily moved to any NASA Center.

- IT Security: A well-defined and documented NASA IT security policy applicable to all systems is essential. Recommend baselining NASA system host-center firewalls, secure socket layer encryption, and a secure but usable single factor user-authentication policy. A generic but tailorable IT security plan should be in place for the hot standby system.

- Hardware/Software Infrastructure: Use a commercial-like, multiple-web server front-end to ensure a high level of reliability and operability.

- Interfaces: Identify mandatory interfaces for compatibility with other support tool sets. Establish interface control agreements as part of MISS development. Interface control testing should verify interoperability.

- Library Services / Massive File Manipulation and Data Archiving: Co-locate the web servers with standalone archive/library servers if it is deemed necessary to perform frequent massive file upload, download, and manipulation. It is inefficient and time consuming to transfer massive files via the internet.

- Expect to Customize/Change Management: Experience suggests that no system can meet all potential requirements that may evolve during an investigation. Anticipating the need to customize, the MISS management team must have in-place: a baseline configuration management plan and process a change process with clear roles and responsibilities for requirements management and change approval a dedicated beta-test server to conduct verification testing for hw/sw changes

IT issues became backlogged and personnel were frustrated when their issues with the key CM software and Board management tool were not addressed in a timely fashion.
sections.lesson_learned: Do not assume that a single CM/electronic library tool will meet needs of all investigation participants.
sections.recommendation:
- Preplan the capabilities needed and the current tools available to quickly and easily begin Board and Task Force operations. Widespread long-term buy-in and use by the investigation and support teams of a single on-line CM/electronic library capability for action tracking and document search & retrieval may not be attainable.

- Test the interfacing capabilities of the tools annually.

- Avoid unknown tools. Complex tools will create backlogs of issues and training nightmares.

- Do not under-estimate the constant care and feeding required to address IT availability, access control, and security issues. IT availability, access control, and security issues were numerous during startup and although less frequent later on, still were persistent. When these issues arose, everyone's issue becomes priority 1, which is understandable but difficult to manage. On-site, adequate co-located support will catch some of these before they became larger issues.

title: Accident Investigations/Software Tool Selection

sections.abstract: A criteria-based software tool selection process should have been implemented. Advanced software tools with which most people are unfamiliar delay investigation initiation.
sections.driving_event: A criteria-based software tool selection process was not used for support of the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB). As a result, the primary Board and Task Force users procured a software tool without fully understanding the capabilities and limitations of the software. In addition, investigation personnel were required to learn new software tools (e.g., databases), adding inefficiencies in Board and Task Force startup time.
sections.lesson_learned: A criteria-based tool selection process should have been implemented, and it should have been kept in mind that advanced software tools that most people are unfamiliar with, such as databases, cause delays in initiating an investigation. Further, the use of multiple software tools implemented to satisfy specific needs cause additional startup delays and tax the IT support staff.
sections.recommendation:
- Develop an appendix/annex to the Contingency Action Plan (CAP) and annually update the definition of critical tool requirements based on established selection criteria.

- Develop a clear set of functional requirements for use in the criteria-based tool selection. In particular, consider early on that all investigation data will have to be archived.

- (NASA should) identify in advance software tools for data management that can be implemented quickly to support future investigations. Factors to consider include meeting anticipated software system availability, data security, firewall requirements, data capacity, and on-site/off-site access requirements for supporting a major mishap investigation.

- Implement software solutions that are proven and that local Center IT and CM personnel are familiar with to minimize coordination, expedite implementation, and reduce potential system/transmission interface issues.

- Avoid significant modification or customized software development. When necessary, develop specific software system requirements so that support contractors have clear guidance and can implement requirements appropriately.

- Separate database administration and general Task Force IT support functions (e.g., service requests, user configuration and set-up, etc.).

- Avoid multiple software solutions and multiple data repositories as data will diverge making configuration management difficult.

- Provide a start up kit and appropriate training for the Board Chairman and Board members upon arrival.

- Discourage investigation board and support staff recommendations from implementing new software solutions that have to be “force-fit” with systems defined in the CAP that have been approved, tested, and accepted by NASA's IT administration.

## Abstract
A criteria-based software tool selection process should have been implemented. Advanced software tools with which most people are unfamiliar delay investigation initiation.

## Driving Event / Background
A criteria-based software tool selection process was not used for support of the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB). As a result, the primary Board and Task Force users procured a software tool without fully understanding the capabilities and limitations of the software. In addition, investigation personnel were required to learn new software tools (e.g., databases), adding inefficiencies in Board and Task Force startup time.

## Lesson Learned
A criteria-based tool selection process should have been implemented, and it should have been kept in mind that advanced software tools that most people are unfamiliar with, such as databases, cause delays in initiating an investigation. Further, the use of multiple software tools implemented to satisfy specific needs cause additional startup delays and tax the IT support staff.

## Recommendation
- Develop an appendix/annex to the Contingency Action Plan (CAP) and annually update the definition of critical tool requirements based on established selection criteria.

- Develop a clear set of functional requirements for use in the criteria-based tool selection. In particular, consider early on that all investigation data will have to be archived.

- (NASA should) identify in advance software tools for data management that can be implemented quickly to support future investigations. Factors to consider include meeting anticipated software system availability, data security, firewall requirements, data capacity, and on-site/off-site access requirements for supporting a major mishap investigation.

- Implement software solutions that are proven and that local Center IT and CM personnel are familiar with to minimize coordination, expedite implementation, and reduce potential system/transmission interface issues.

- Avoid significant modification or customized software development. When necessary, develop specific software system requirements so that support contractors have clear guidance and can implement requirements appropriately.

- Separate database administration and general Task Force IT support functions (e.g., service requests, user configuration and set-up, etc.).

- Avoid multiple software solutions and multiple data repositories as data will diverge making configuration management difficult.

- Provide a start up kit and appropriate training for the Board Chairman and Board members upon arrival.

- Discourage investigation board and support staff recommendations from implementing new software solutions that have to be “force-fit” with systems defined in the CAP that have been approved, tested, and accepted by NASA's IT administration.

title: Accident Investigations/Action Request System

sections.abstract: Complex Action/Request for Information Forms require numerous iterations to implement cross-organizationally and may cause the authorization process to break down.
sections.driving_event: For the Columbia accident investigation, the Action/Request for Information Form format took a long time to establish, which caused many investigators to use obsolete and discontinued formats. A significant amount of time was spent backtracking and cataloging actions and responses/data that were created prior to selecting a specific format.
sections.lesson_learned: Complex forms will take endless iterations to implement evenly across all organizations and may cause the action authorization process to break down.
sections.recommendation:
- Establish the Action Request process within the first days of Board arrival.

- Have all action/information requests screened by Task Force technical leads to ensure the requests are detailed enough to be accurately interpreted during initial review by NASA data providers and specifically germane to the investigation. Forms, tracking logs, and files/database must accommodate sensitive/proprietary (legal, medical, contractual, national security, export control (ITAR)) data and generic/public data required by the Investigative Board as well as unsolicited data provided by the public, private industry, and/or political sector.

- Establish an authoritative lead immediately for sensitive/secure data to determine what data should be evaluated and marked (export controlled, sensitive, proprietary, etc.) or whether all documentation should be protected with a global/generic statement.

- Inform the Board early on known sensitive data process requirements. Ensure that this authority reviews any data that are to be released to the public.

- Audit the system process regularly.

Board and TF CM leads must:

- Create an action tracking form immediately that captures actions and closure response processes tailored to the accident specifics (recommend the attached).

sections.abstract: Ground rules, methods, and equipment for witness interview transcription, review, and revision should be established up front to preclude subsequent issues.
sections.driving_event: The Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) experimented with different methods to record private witness interviews creating problems with transcriptions.
sections.lesson_learned: For accident investigations, ground rules, processes and equipment necessary for review and revision of transcribed interviews should be established prior to the first interview.
sections.recommendation:
- Assign a Support Staff member to pre-test recording equipment under a variety of circumstances (e.g. where interviews will actually take place) to make certain it will accomplish the task it is intended to accomplish.

- Address room logistics, including room size, access control, and documentation control.

- Use analog tape (not digital) for electronic recorders; it is easier to copy and duplicate, and the files are in a standard format unlike some digital devices. Laptop-based recording did not work for this investigation.

title: Accident Investigations/Software Tool Selection

sections.abstract: A set of prioritized requirements should be considered in the decision process for selecting an accident investigation software tool, or tools, to meet the varying needs of users.
sections.driving_event: Due to the urgent need to quickly select and implement a software tool to support the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB), the tool designated to be the single interface to the Board was selected based on brief demonstrations of the key features of various tools, including a generic collaborative environment tool already in use within the NASA community for non-sensitive data, and a NASA-developed mishap investigation specific tool. At the time, the collaborative environment tool was in the process of being expanded to include enhanced security for storing sensitive data, namely, two-factor- strong authentication. Two-factor-strong authentication was identified as an IT requirement, and it allowed remote access to sensitive data over the Internet - a feature not offered by other alternative software solutions. The collaborative environment tool was selected because of the enhanced security with remote access, the built-in generic database capability, and the overall ease of use. A best- effort approach was undertaken to implement the enhanced security features ahead of schedule to meet the needs of the board. However, implementing the enhanced security features caused initial problems with normal operation of the tool, which resulted in delays in implementing the library and action tracking databases. In addition, while the ease of use of the tool was attractive, this came at the expense of advance functionality required by the CM and library support staff, which required custom software engineering to meet their needs causing delays in functionality and frustration on behalf of the end users.
sections.lesson_learned: Different levels of software functionality are required by members of the investigation board and support staff (e.g., top-level board members vs. library support staff). A thorough review of software alternatives based on a clear set of functional requirements should precede selection of a tool. Criteria, such as having a single user interface, ease of use, remote access, security, etc., should be prioritized and considered in the decision-making process to select a tool, or set of tools, to meet the needs of the users.
sections.recommendation:
Have representative members of an investigation board and representative end users of critical functionality (e.g., library support staff) review criteria for selection of a software tool, and the associated advantages and disadvantages, before tool selection. Specifically, consider the following “must have” requirements when selecting a library/data management software tool to support large-scale accident investigations:

- implements IT security (e.g., single-factor vs. two-factor strong authentication) that is consistent with the level of safeguarding required and the investigations need for simplicity and rapid startup,

- allows for easy storage and retrieval of very large data files that are an order of magnitude larger than what would currently be considered a big data file for every day use (e.g., by todays standard, allow for 100 to 300MB PowerPoint files),

- allows for secure remote access (consistent with an accident investigation board's needs) to stored files for download to local PCs by investigation board members while on travel or in a dispersed location environment,

- has strong keyword search capability, preferably full text search capability,

- has advanced capability adaptable to new functional requirements on-the-fly without requiring customized software engineering, yet still be easy to learn, easy to use, and compatible with other software applications,

- is comprised of proven COTS software solutions (when possible),

- incorporates the functional capability to store, read, and manipulate all flavors of detailed 3-D engineering models/drawings in use at NASA, and

- is adequately tested and implemented prior to future investigations for full buy-in by representative investigation board and support staff members.

# [NASA LLIS #1467] Accident Investigations/Software Tool Selection
- **Date:** 2003-08-31
- **Organization:** Johnson Space Center (JSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1467

## Abstract
A set of prioritized requirements should be considered in the decision process for selecting an accident investigation software tool, or tools, to meet the varying needs of users.

## Driving Event / Background
Due to the urgent need to quickly select and implement a software tool to support the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB), the tool designated to be the single interface to the Board was selected based on brief demonstrations of the key features of various tools, including a generic collaborative environment tool already in use within the NASA community for non-sensitive data, and a NASA-developed mishap investigation specific tool. At the time, the collaborative environment tool was in the process of being expanded to include enhanced security for storing sensitive data, namely, two-factor- strong authentication. Two-factor-strong authentication was identified as an IT requirement, and it allowed remote access to sensitive data over the Internet - a feature not offered by other alternative software solutions. The collaborative environment tool was selected because of the enhanced security with remote access, the built-in generic database capability, and the overall ease of use. A best- effort approach was undertaken to implement the enhanced security features ahead of schedule to meet the needs of the board. However, implementing the enhanced security features caused initial problems with normal operation of the tool, which resulted in delays in implementing the library and action tracking databases. In addition, while the ease of use of the tool was attractive, this came at the expense of advance functionality required by the CM and library support staff, which required custom software engineering to meet their needs causing delays in functionality and frustration on behalf of the end users.

## Lesson Learned
Different levels of software functionality are required by members of the investigation board and support staff (e.g., top-level board members vs. library support staff). A thorough review of software alternatives based on a clear set of functional requirements should precede selection of a tool. Criteria, such as having a single user interface, ease of use, remote access, security, etc., should be prioritized and considered in the decision-making process to select a tool, or set of tools, to meet the needs of the users.

## Recommendation
Have representative members of an investigation board and representative end users of critical functionality (e.g., library support staff) review criteria for selection of a software tool, and the associated advantages and disadvantages, before tool selection. Specifically, consider the following “must have” requirements when selecting a library/data management software tool to support large-scale accident investigations:

- implements IT security (e.g., single-factor vs. two-factor strong authentication) that is consistent with the level of safeguarding required and the investigations need for simplicity and rapid startup,

- allows for easy storage and retrieval of very large data files that are an order of magnitude larger than what would currently be considered a big data file for every day use (e.g., by todays standard, allow for 100 to 300MB PowerPoint files),

- allows for secure remote access (consistent with an accident investigation board's needs) to stored files for download to local PCs by investigation board members while on travel or in a dispersed location environment,

- has strong keyword search capability, preferably full text search capability,

- has advanced capability adaptable to new functional requirements on-the-fly without requiring customized software engineering, yet still be easy to learn, easy to use, and compatible with other software applications,

- is comprised of proven COTS software solutions (when possible),

- incorporates the functional capability to store, read, and manipulate all flavors of detailed 3-D engineering models/drawings in use at NASA, and

- is adequately tested and implemented prior to future investigations for full buy-in by representative investigation board and support staff members.

sections.abstract: NASA needs to understand that a human space flight accident field recovery operation will involve many organizations at various levels of Government.
sections.driving_event: NASA mishap personnel were surprised at the number of organizations, which managed and participated in the field debris collection effort.
sections.lesson_learned: A manned space flight accident will involve many national, state, local/regional emergency organizations in many phases of the investigation, especially debris recovery.
sections.recommendation:
- Identify national, state and local (and possibly international) organizations and agencies which are likely to take part in the debris collection in the Contingency Action Plan (CAP). Outline roles and responsibilities, and identify points of contact.

- Pre-establish the interagency processes and interfaces to organize the efforts and what the authority hierarchy will be (who is in charge over what and when).

- Establish the likely kinds of equipment, personnel, and facility support needed. These plans should not be so detailed/accident specific as to be administratively burdensome to maintain.

title: Accident Investigations/Investigation Organizer (IO)/IO Utilization for Major Mishap Investigations

sections.abstract: The "Investigation Organizer" management and modeling tool was the primary investigation management tool for the Columbia accident investigation; however, acceptance of the tool was not consistent across investigative groups because some investigators considered it a developmental tool rather than an operational tool.
sections.driving_event:
Investigation Organizer (IO) - is a Web-based pre-decisional collaborative information management and modeling tool designed to support mishap investigation teams. IO provides a centralized information repository that can be used by a distributed team of investigators to store digital products relevant to an ongoing mishap investigation. It was used by the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) to connect data from various sources to the storyboard that the Board used to guide its investigation. IO was developed, maintained and hosted at NASA Ames Research Center (ARC). IO maintainers, Ames Research Center civil servants and contractors, pull required data electronically from the NASA-provided Process Based Mission Assurance (PBMA) database to populate the IO fault tree. IO representatives were placed within each investigation group of the CAIB. Documents, digital photographs/video, links were uploaded to the IO database to support the engineering/management investigation
logic tree. The logistics “footprint” of IO-trained personnel was extensive.
sections.lesson_learned: Although Investigation Organizer was the primary investigation management tool for the Columbia accident investigation, it was not initially utilized across all investigative groups within the CAIB. It had been previously used on only one other investigation, the loss of the CONTOUR spacecraft. Acceptance of the tool was not consistent across groups. Some investigators complained that the Board was being forced to use a developmental tool in an operational environment.
sections.recommendation:
- Move the IO tool from a development environment to an operational environment to gain acceptance as the primary investigative tool across the Agency. This will require continued IO development and training across the NASA investigative community. The ARC IO personnel should expect to support logistics/training during investigations unless the tool can be made easier to use.

- Codify IO use in the NASA Mishap Investigation Plan, NPG 8621.

## Abstract
The "Investigation Organizer" management and modeling tool was the primary investigation management tool for the Columbia accident investigation; however, acceptance of the tool was not consistent across investigative groups because some investigators considered it a developmental tool rather than an operational tool.

## Driving Event / Background
Investigation Organizer (IO) - is a Web-based pre-decisional collaborative information management and modeling tool designed to support mishap investigation teams. IO provides a centralized information repository that can be used by a distributed team of investigators to store digital products relevant to an ongoing mishap investigation. It was used by the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) to connect data from various sources to the storyboard that the Board used to guide its investigation. IO was developed, maintained and hosted at NASA Ames Research Center (ARC). logic tree. The logistics “footprint” of IO-trained personnel was extensive.

## Lesson Learned
Although Investigation Organizer was the primary investigation management tool for the Columbia accident investigation, it was not initially utilized across all investigative groups within the CAIB. It had been previously used on only one other investigation, the loss of the CONTOUR spacecraft. Acceptance of the tool was not consistent across groups. Some investigators complained that the Board was being forced to use a developmental tool in an operational environment.

## Recommendation
- Move the IO tool from a development environment to an operational environment to gain acceptance as the primary investigative tool across the Agency. This will require continued IO development and training across the NASA investigative community. The ARC IO personnel should expect to support logistics/training during investigations unless the tool can be made easier to use.

- Codify IO use in the NASA Mishap Investigation Plan, NPG 8621.

It is unlikely, however, that a software system for action item tracking and investigative data configuration management can be selected that will be wholly satisfactory to the entire board.
sections.driving_event: For the Columbia accident investigation, the PBMA tool was oversold to rapidly assembled Board and Task Force members and did not deliver capabilities as expected. For example, record keeping, cataloging, tracking/status, search & retrieval, and metrics data were not immediately available in PBMA, resulting in an overall frustration and delays with the capability for getting data out of PBMA into the hands of the users. sections.lesson_learned: For large accident investigation support, is unlikely that you can select a software system for action item tracking and configuration management of investigative data that will make everyone happy at the same time.
sections.recommendation:
Consider the following criteria when selecting a software management system for accident investigation support:

- allows for the easy upload and download of very large files 100 to 300MB.

- is flexible and compatible enough to adapt to new requirements

- the advantages and disadvantages are sufficiently vetted by the Board

- the system can be adequately tested in the Board's environment before full buy-in

- is not overly complex, so that investigators don't have to spend many hours training

- remote access consistent with the Board's organization and nothing more

- factor of security is consistent with investigations need for simplicity and rapid startup

# [NASA LLIS #1446] Accident Investigations/Database/Collaborative Tool PBMA (Process Based Mission Assurance)
- **Date:** 2003-08-31
- **Organization:** Johnson Space Center (JSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1446

## Abstract
Experience with PBMA indicates that it was oversold and it did not deliver expected capabilities. It is unlikely, however, that a software system for action item tracking and investigative data configuration management can be selected that will be wholly satisfactory to the entire board.

## Driving Event / Background
For the Columbia accident investigation, the PBMA tool was oversold to rapidly assembled Board and Task Force members and did not deliver capabilities as expected. For example, record keeping, cataloging, tracking/status, search & retrieval, and metrics data were not immediately available in PBMA, resulting in an overall frustration and delays with the capability for getting data out of PBMA into the hands of the users. This tool was often found to be incompatible with other tools and its security system was overly complex.

## Lesson Learned
For large accident investigation support, is unlikely that you can select a software system for action item tracking and configuration management of investigative data that will make everyone happy at the same time.

## Recommendation
Consider the following criteria when selecting a software management system for accident investigation support:

- allows for the easy upload and download of very large files 100 to 300MB.

- is flexible and compatible enough to adapt to new requirements

- the advantages and disadvantages are sufficiently vetted by the Board

- the system can be adequately tested in the Board's environment before full buy-in

- is not overly complex, so that investigators don't have to spend many hours training

- remote access consistent with the Board's organization and nothing more

- factor of security is consistent with investigations need for simplicity and rapid startup

- has good keyword search capability

- avoid systems that will immediately require customization

- use a Commercial Off the Shelf (COTS) solution when possible

- electronic tools must be able to store and manipulate 3-D engineering models.
