title: Accident Investigations/Document Management, Retention, and Archival Policy for an Independent Investigation

sections.abstract: The lack of early adoption of a document management and archival policy made it difficult for the document management staff to obtain Investigation Board generated documents for inclusion in the database server.
sections.driving_event: Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) investigators were initially reluctant to submit documents to the document management staff (Department of Justice and their contract, Aspen Systems)) for inclusion to the CAIB Database Server; they expressed a desire to receive guidelines and direction directly from the Board before providing sensitive documents and work product.
sections.lesson_learned:
1. Early in the investigation, the Board did not adopt a document management and archival policy. Consequently, it was difficult for document management staff to obtain CAIB generated documents from the investigators and members of the Board.

2.

3. Investigators considered document management, archiving, and designating documents for release to the public as analogous processes. This made it considerably difficult for the document management staff to obtain documents from investigators for inclusion into the CAIB Database Server.
sections.recommendation:
- Have the General Counsel and/or document management support staff establish written guidelines for document management, retention, and archiving at the beginning of an independent investigation. Present these guidelines to the investigation board for approval and then circulate them to the investigators and support staff for action.

- Place document management support staff within each investigative group at the beginning of the investigation. The representatives may be able to assist the investigators in understanding and adhering to the document management, retention, and archiving policies, thus reducing concerns about sensitive documents becoming part of the public record.

full_text:
# [NASA LLIS #1470] Accident Investigations/Document Management, Retention, and Archival Policy for an Independent Investigation
- **Date:** 2003-08-31
- **Organization:** Johnson Space Center (JSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1470

## Abstract
The lack of early adoption of a document management and archival policy made it difficult for the document management staff to obtain Investigation Board generated documents for inclusion in the database server.

## Driving Event / Background
Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) investigators were initially reluctant to submit documents to the document management staff (Department of Justice and their contract, Aspen Systems)) for inclusion to the CAIB Database Server; they expressed a desire to receive guidelines and direction directly from the Board before providing sensitive documents and work product.

## Lesson Learned
1. Early in the investigation, the Board did not adopt a document management and archival policy. Consequently, it was difficult for document management staff to obtain CAIB generated documents from the investigators and members of the Board.

2.

3. Investigators considered document management, archiving, and designating documents for release to the public as analogous processes. This made it considerably difficult for the document management staff to obtain documents from investigators for inclusion into the CAIB Database Server.

## Recommendation
- Have the General Counsel and/or document management support staff establish written guidelines for document management, retention, and archiving at the beginning of an independent investigation. Present these guidelines to the investigation board for approval and then circulate them to the investigators and support staff for action.

- Place document management support staff within each investigative group at the beginning of the investigation. The representatives may be able to assist the investigators in understanding and adhering to the document management, retention, and archiving policies, thus reducing concerns about sensitive documents becoming part of the public record.

title: Accident Investigations/Transition Process/Integration Functions

sections.abstract: As evidenced by the fact that the Columbia Task Force was often required to be a major integration function between CAIB investigation teams, an independent accident investigation board may require NASA help integrating itself.
sections.driving_event: Columbia Task Force (CTF) was often required to be the major integration function between the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) Group/Subgroup investigation teams.
sections.lesson_learned: An Independent Accident Board is composed of many diverse members and may not be capable of integrating itself without help from NASA.
sections.recommendation:
- Establish an internal integration function to ensure that groups and teams integrate their goals, responsibilities, data requests, etc.

- Select a leader for Each Group/Team within the Board's organization to regulate Group discussion.

- Define roles and/or areas of investigative responsibility for each Group/Sub-Group member.

- Identify any overlap of responsibilities for the entire Board.

- Anticipate when warranted, but it may not be possible to predict an independent investigation Board's structural organization because of a Chairman's personal style, or what flight or ground phase the accident occurred in.

- **Date:** 2003-08-31
- **Organization:** Johnson Space Center (JSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1464

## Abstract
Clear IT security policies, consistent across all NASA Centers, need to be in place for care and management of ITAR, export control, and investigation sensitive information to avoid complications, cost, and delay.

## Driving Event / Background
On February 1, 2003 there was a NASA policy void concerning IT security requirements for web-based systems hosting ITAR and export controlled data. The NASA CIO deferred the policy to each Center CIO (in apparent contradiction of the “One NASA” vision), creating an inconsistent and confusing rule-set. The NASA CIO declined to clarify the need for two-factor-strong user authentication. Applications held to the higher standard of two-factor-strong user authentication requirements resulted in administrative burdens, hardware and software complications, cost, and delay.

## Lesson Learned
It is critical that NASA has in-place, clear and consistent IT security policies across all NASA centers as it relates to the care and management of ITAR, export control and investigation sensitive information.

## Recommendation
NASA must:

- Implement clear and consistent IT security policies across all NASA Centers as it relates to the care and management of ITAR, export control, and investigation sensitive information.

sections.abstract: Because some investigation board members may have minimal knowledge of space flight systems, NASA needs to anticipate this and be better prepared with technical and procedural materials to increase the board members learning curve.
sections.driving_event: Some Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) members arrived with minimal knowledge of Space Shuttle systems. Subsequently, the action/request for information system was flooded with informational and data requests to come up to speed, slowing down the NASA technical investigation/analysis.
sections.lesson_learned: NASA needs to be better prepared to handle the independent investigators in terms of technical and procedural materials that will increase the learning curve of Board members.
sections.recommendation:
- Anticipate and prepare for an educational process for an independent accident investigation board. Readily available data such as drawing databases and existing websites that an independent Board can have immediate access to should be kept up-to-date and more user friendly.

- Create a directory or cheat sheet with pointers to existing databases, websites, etc. NASA contingency planning should maintain basic documentation procedures that will always be scrutinized in a major investigation (e.g. maintenance, facilities, safety programs, contracts, training).

- Improve archival system to provide the most rapid possible recovery and delivery of documentation that shows vehicle histories, problems, etc.

- Assign this background function to NASA's on-site library system or to the flight program offices.

## Abstract
Because some investigation board members may have minimal knowledge of space flight systems, NASA needs to anticipate this and be better prepared with technical and procedural materials to increase the board members learning curve.

## Driving Event / Background
Some Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) members arrived with minimal knowledge of Space Shuttle systems. Subsequently, the action/request for information system was flooded with informational and data requests to come up to speed, slowing down the NASA technical investigation/analysis.

## Lesson Learned
NASA needs to be better prepared to handle the independent investigators in terms of technical and procedural materials that will increase the learning curve of Board members.

## Recommendation
- Anticipate and prepare for an educational process for an independent accident investigation board. Readily available data such as drawing databases and existing websites that an independent Board can have immediate access to should be kept up-to-date and more user friendly.

- Create a directory or cheat sheet with pointers to existing databases, websites, etc. NASA contingency planning should maintain basic documentation procedures that will always be scrutinized in a major investigation (e.g. maintenance, facilities, safety programs, contracts, training).

- Improve archival system to provide the most rapid possible recovery and delivery of documentation that shows vehicle histories, problems, etc.

- Assign this background function to NASA's on-site library system or to the flight program offices.

title: Accident Investigations/Archiving of Data & Library Requirements

sections.abstract: All data and documentation should be handled with the understanding that it will ultimately be archived.
sections.driving_event: For the Columbia accident investigation, handling, destination and formats of archival documentation were not fully considered in initial startup of library requirements.
sections.lesson_learned: For accident investigations, handle all data and documentation with the understanding that it will eventually be officially archived.
sections.recommendation:
- Be aware that most data collected and archived by the accident investigation board and NASA task force will be sent to the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) and will be consider public information unless directed otherwise.

- Segregate and mark all export controlled, sensitive, and proprietary data accordingly before sending data to NARA.

- Brief all investigators and staff on handling of proprietary and privileged information, specifically in the context of what we can and cannot put in the final report (public domain) and also in the context of archives and how they are handled.

- Do not permit various IT formats to be delivered. Have the NASA Archivist recommend formats for delivering data (to include formats for photos). Native format (not PDF) may be best because it allows cutting and pasting. If PDF, documents must be text searchable (i.e., OCR or other).

- Pre-establish e-mail archiving policy.

title: Accident Investigations/Public Inputs to the Investigation/Utilization of a Public Website & Toll-Free Number

sections.abstract: The Accident Investigation Board received valuable submissions from the public--both average citizens and experts--through its public website and 800 number and should be considered for all future large accident investigations.
sections.driving_event:
The Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) launched a public website ( http://caib.us/ ) in late February 2003 to inform the public about the activities of the CAIB. A Website link allowed the public to submit information directly to the CAIB through a pop-up form with document attachment capability. An 800 number was also offered as an alternative means to submit information. In concert with the launching of the Website, a public submission database was developed to receive and review public inputs. This database eventually was expanded to receive submissions from the Website, toll-free number, faxed messages, digital emails, and mail received by the CAIB. Over a period of two months, the functionality of the database increased incrementally. The first functions served to enable categorization of the submissions by priority and an ability to print records. These were then hand-carried directly to relevant group for action. Excel spreadsheets were used to review and track the database. Later, review and submission of actions to groups was automated. Finally added was the ability of groups to manage their actions and close them in a collaborative environment. The Process: Submission Entry: Public submissions come from several sources and are placed in the database through automatic Website entry or through a CAIB data entry support person. The Public website allows anyone to submit a message, as much information on themselves as they wish, and to attach any relevant electronic document. Those submitting information through the Website receive a message of thanks and a note that they will be contacted if their information needs additional follow-up. Toll-free phone messages are transcribed and then uploaded into the database with its audio file. Mail submissions are logged at the CAIB in Houston, and then scanned into the database in a PDF file form. Finally, any other hard copy information including emails is copied into the database and given its own unique record. Data Record Review and Action Assignment: Throughout each day, data records are read in entirety to determine relevance for action to one or more CAIB groups. A knowledgeable reviewer with senior management and aerospace technical expertise assigns a data record for action if, in his opinion, one or more of the CAIB working groups should see it. Every data record that has no action assigned is given a second review to make sure that there have been no accidental omissions of a useful submission. If the second review agrees no action is needed, the record is considered closed. Open records with actions assigned are immediately available to the working groups for disposition. A group manager can assign data records for action to other members of their group. When complete, the comments and action taken can be appended to the data records. Multiple group members can add comments to an action, which also becomes part of the data record. Statistics: Statistics about each group and the collective database are automatically and continuously updated as data records are received, reviewed, assigned for action, or closed. These statistics are reviewed each day to help manage the CAIB internal processes for reviewing and closing actions. Public Submission Information Statistics The Public Input Database contains over 3000 records, which were submitted in a little over 75 days. Out of this number over 750 records or 25% were deemed to be important enough for follow-on action by one or more CAIB groups. Surprisingly, given the highly public nature of the CAIB, an overwhelmingly high percentage of the submissions were well-intentioned comments to help the CAIB in its work. As of May 15, 2003 the following depicts numbers of records submitted to working groups for action. (Many submissions were assigned for action to more than one group. Therefore, total actions approach 1,000):

| CAIB Subgroup | Number of Public Submission Actions |
| --- | --- |
| Group 1- Materials, Management, Preflight | 138 |
| Group 2 -Flight Operations, Safety | 76 |
| Group 3 -Technology | 291 |
| Group 4 -History and Culture | 50 |
| Independent Analysis Team | 137 |
| Columbia Task Force | 105 |
| Public Affairs | 67 |
| Legal | 36 |
| Other | 52 |

The number of database records increased consistently on a daily basis. After press releases or public hearings, there was usually a large increase in the number of public submissions. Of particular note, many experts would provide their submissions after noting a particular public discussion. At other times, the public information would joggle the memory of former Shuttle or NASA workers about their direct experience and result in a useful submission. The weekly growth of the number of records is shown in the chart below: The percentage of submissions, which required action, also changed as the Board progressed. Early in the investigation, there were many avenues that were still in the exploration phase, as well as requests for debris sightings. Consequently, an early wave of theories, opinions, and potentially useful information was categorized as an action. As the Board investigation progressed and possibilities were narrowed, the number of submissions deemed actionable decreased and remained relatively flat. However, there continues to be very useful submissions provided to the CAIB. As the investigation avenues narrow and public information is released, the number of action items should decrease over the rest of May and into June. Submitters The following highlights some of the categories of people submitting information through the Website. General Public Press and other Media Scientists and Engineers Current and former Military Experts Current and former Shuttle contractor employees Current and former Shuttle Workers Current and Former NASA employees Former Astronauts In addition, many anonymous submissions were provided. These tended to be people with direct knowledge of the history of Columbia's design, construction, and NASA operations. Included with these submissions were several documents containing information that the submitters wanted the CAIB Board to investigate or consider. Nature of Submissions All database records were reviewed and categorized as being technical in nature, a comment, suggestion, request for information, offer of support, debris sighting, first-hand witness account, or other. Among these categories, there were several topics or themes that evolved during the course of the CAIB investigation. The nature of the submissions also changed as new information was presented in press briefings or public hearings. In fact, the public hearings, which were broadcast and viewable live or delayed through the Website, generated a number of post-hearing submissions with relevant follow-up information and leads. Themes and topics of submissions included: Photo and video of the last minutes of Columbia's flight Debris sightings with pictures attached Suggestions on ways to find debris Space physics issues to be explored for contributing factors in accident Identification of experts and facilities in specialty fields relevant to the investigation History of Columbia construction and operation Safety and Quality Assurance issues NASA Management and Culture issues Technical issues and insights with engineering, materials, or design of Shuttle system Theories and opinions on cause of accident Suggestions for improving the Shuttle and return to flight Hoaxes and Grievances As with any public access, there were also several categories of submissions that were clearly not helpful to the CAIB, yet were valuable to know. For example, several weeks into the investigation, a widely dispersed Internet hoax claiming Israeli spy pictures were available of Columbia's destruction was promulgated throughout the world. The CAIB public submissions started as a trickle of questions asking if these pictures were real. Several people submitted these pictures through the Website. The CAIB was able to quickly determine they were photos from the movie “Armageddon.” When the volume of inquiries to the CAIB website began to escalate, CAIB Public Affairs agreed to place a statement on the Website stating that the only authorized photos from the investigation would be released by the CAIB. This statement quickly resulted in a marked decrease in these hoax picture inquiries. Some submitters also felt compelled to submit the same information to the CAIB each day hoping for a direct response. Eventually, the provision for an email reply sharply decreased the number of duplicate and follow up submissions.
sections.lesson_learned:
1. Future public investigations should not hesitate to seek information from the public. There will be many valuable submissions from not only the average person, but also from many former experts who wish to contact the Board.

2.

3. A complete submission response plan is required to utilize appropriately the valuable information that might come in. This would include

a. The ability to evaluate, prioritize, and categorize multiple submissions.

b. Single place for various formats-letters, web, fax, email to be stored in a common record format.

c. Single individual with full knowledge of the areas of investigation, the subject matter, and history of submissions to make sound judgments on disposition of submissions.

d. A second independent review of all submissions for correct disposition.

e. A collaborative environment for subject matter experts or investigators to transfer, evaluate and act upon submissions.

1. The use of public submissions and follow-up by investigators is dependent on the commitment of the investigation leaders to review submissions in a timely manner and treat them as an important source of information. This must be conveyed to the investigating team.

2. Policy decisions should be made early in an investigation to determine to what extent all public submissions, in whatever form, should be responded to; either personally, or by automatic reply.

3. The Public Database should be web-based and secure.

4. It is important to make progress in reviewing submissions daily in order not to fall behind in review.

a. If there are functions to be tailored, created, or developed, find a mechanism to review and evaluate actions in parallel with development.

b. Excel is valuable decision tools to keep the momentum in reviewing submissions- make sure the database elements can be downloaded to Excel.

1. It would be helpful if the reviewer of actions has access to the latest thinking and activities of each group. This would have precluded a number of actions for the groups to work on due to the activity already being under consideration.

2. Responses to the actions were not consistent within each group. It is important to set an early framework for the expectations and degree of response to each action. For example- some closed actions without comments, others detailed at least a reason why the action was closed.
sections.recommendation: The use of a website and toll free number for public inputs should be considered for all future large accident investigations. full_text:
# [NASA LLIS #1474] Accident Investigations/Public Inputs to the Investigation/Utilization of a Public Website & Toll-Free Number
- **Date:** 2003-08-31
- **Organization:** Johnson Space Center (JSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1474

## Abstract
The Accident Investigation Board received valuable submissions from the public--both average citizens and experts--through its public website and 800 number and should be considered for all future large accident investigations.

## Driving Event / Background
The Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) launched a public website ( http://caib.us/ ) in late February 2003 to inform the public about the activities of the CAIB. A Website link allowed the public to submit information directly to the CAIB through a pop-up form with document attachment capability. An 800 number was also offered as an alternative means to submit information. In concert with the launching of the Website, a public submission database was developed to receive and review public inputs. This database eventually was expanded to receive submissions from the Website, toll-free number, faxed messages, digital emails, and mail received by the CAIB. Over a period of two months, the functionality of the database increased incrementally. The first functions served to enable categorization of the submissions by priority and an ability to print records. These were then hand-carried directly to relevant group for action. Excel spreadsheets were used to review and track the database. Later, review and submission of actions to groups was automated. Finally added was the ability of groups to manage their actions and close them in a collaborative environment. The Process: Submission Entry: Public submissions come from several sources and are placed in the database through automatic Website entry or through a CAIB data entry support person. The Public website allows anyone to submit a message, as much information on themselves as they wish, and to attach any relevant electronic document. Those submitting information through the Website receive a message of thanks and a note that they will be contacted if their information needs additional follow-up. Toll-free phone messages are transcribed and then uploaded into the database with its audio file. Mail submissions are logged at the CAIB in Houston, and then scanned into the database in a PDF file form. Finally, any other hard copy information including emails is copied into the database and given its own unique record. Data Record Review and Action Assignment: Throughout each day, data records are read in entirety to determine relevance for action to one or more CAIB groups. A knowledgeable reviewer with senior management and aerospace technical expertise assigns a data record for action if, in his opinion, one or more of the CAIB working groups should see it. Every data record that has no action assigned is given a second review to make sure that there have been no accidental omissions of a useful submission. If the second review agrees no action is needed, the record is considered closed. Open records with actions assigned are immediately available to the working groups for disposition. A group manager can assign data records for action to other members of their group. When complete, the comments and action taken can be appended to the data records. Multiple group members can add comments to an action, which also becomes part of the data record. Statistics: Statistics about each group and the collective database are automatically and continuously updated as data records are received, reviewed, assigned for action, or closed. These statistics are reviewed each day to help manage the CAIB internal processes for reviewing and closing actions. Public Submission Information Statistics The Public Input Database contains over 3000 records, which were submitted in a little over 75 days. Out of this number over 750 records or 25% were deemed to be important enough for follow-on action by one or more CAIB groups. Surprisingly, given the highly public nature of the CAIB, an overwhelmingly high percentage of the submissions were well-intentioned comments to help the CAIB in its work. As of May 15, 2003 the following depicts numbers of records submitted to working groups for action. (Many submissions were assigned for action to more than one group. Therefore, total actions approach 1,000):

| CAIB Subgroup | Number of Public Submission Actions |
| --- | --- |
| Group 1- Materials, Management, Preflight | 138 |
| Group 2 -Flight Operations, Safety | 76 |
| Group 3 -Technology | 291 |
| Group 4 -History and Culture | 50 |
| Independent Analysis Team | 137 |
| Columbia Task Force | 105 |
| Public Affairs | 67 |
| Legal | 36 |
| Other | 52 |

The number of database records increased consistently on a daily basis. After press releases or public hearings, there was usually a large increase in the number of public submissions. Of particular note, many experts would provide their submissions after noting a particular public discussion. At other times, the public information would joggle the memory of former Shuttle or NASA workers about their direct experience and result in a useful submission. The weekly growth of the number of records is shown in the chart below: The percentage of submissions, which required action, also changed as the Board progressed. Early in the investigation, there were many avenues that were still in the exploration phase, as well as requests for debris sightings. Consequently, an early wave of theories, opinions, and potentially useful information was categorized as an action. As the Board investigation progressed and possibilities were narrowed, the number of submissions deemed actionable decreased and remained relatively flat. However, there continues to be very useful submissions provided to the CAIB. As the investigation avenues narrow and public information is released, the number of action items should decrease over the rest of May and into June. Submitters The following highlights some of the categories of people submitting information through the Website. General Public Press and other Media Scientists and Engineers Current and former Military Experts Current and former Shuttle contractor employees Current and former Shuttle Workers Current and Former NASA employees Former Astronauts In addition, many anonymous submissions were provided. These tended to be people with direct knowledge of the history of Columbia's design, construction, and NASA operations. Included with these submissions were several documents containing information that the submitters wanted the CAIB Board to investigate or consider. Nature of Submissions All database records were reviewed and categorized as being technical in nature, a comment, suggestion, request for information, offer of support, debris sighting, first-hand witness account, or other. Among these categories, there were several topics or themes that evolved during the course of the CAIB investigation. The nature of the submissions also changed as new information was presented in press briefings or public hearings. In fact, the public hearings, which were broadcast and viewable live or delayed through the Website, generated a number of post-hearing submissions with relevant follow-up information and leads. Themes and topics of submissions included: Photo and video of the last minutes of Columbia's flight Debris sightings with pictures attached Suggestions on ways to find debris Space physics issues to be explored for contributing factors in accident Identification of experts and facilities in specialty fields relevant to the investigation History of Columbia construction and operation Safety and Quality Assurance issues NASA Management and Culture issues Technical issues and insights with engineering, materials, or design of Shuttle system Theories and opinions on cause of accident Suggestions for improving the Shuttle and return to flight Hoaxes and Grievances As with any public access, there were also several categories of submissions that were clearly not helpful to the CAIB, yet were valuable to know. For example, several weeks into the investigation, a widely dispersed Internet hoax claiming Israeli spy pictures were available of Columbia's destruction was promulgated throughout the world. The CAIB public submissions started as a trickle of questions asking if these pictures were real. Several people submitted these pictures through the Website. The CAIB was able to quickly determine they were photos from the movie “Armageddon.” When the volume of inquiries to the CAIB website began to escalate, CAIB Public Affairs agreed to place a statement on the Website stating that the only authorized photos from the investigation would be released by the CAIB. This statement quickly resulted in a marked decrease in these hoax picture inquiries. Some submitters also felt compelled to submit the same information to the CAIB each day hoping for a direct response. Eventually, the provision for an email reply sharply decreased the number of duplicate and follow up submissions.

## Lesson Learned
1. Future public investigations should not hesitate to seek information from the public. There will be many valuable submissions from not only the average person, but also from many former experts who wish to contact the Board.

2.

3. A complete submission response plan is required to utilize appropriately the valuable information that might come in. This would include

a. The ability to evaluate, prioritize, and categorize multiple submissions.

b. Single place for various formats-letters, web, fax, email to be stored in a common record format.

c. Single individual with full knowledge of the areas of investigation, the subject matter, and history of submissions to make sound judgments on disposition of submissions.

d. A second independent review of all submissions for correct disposition.

e. A collaborative environment for subject matter experts or investigators to transfer, evaluate and act upon submissions.

1. The use of public submissions and follow-up by investigators is dependent on the commitment of the investigation leaders to review submissions in a timely manner and treat them as an important source of information. This must be conveyed to the investigating team.

2. Policy decisions should be made early in an investigation to determine to what extent all public submissions, in whatever form, should be responded to; either personally, or by automatic reply.

3. The Public Database should be web-based and secure.

4. It is important to make progress in reviewing submissions daily in order not to fall behind in review.

a. If there are functions to be tailored, created, or developed, find a mechanism to review and evaluate actions in parallel with development.

b. Excel is valuable decision tools to keep the momentum in reviewing submissions- make sure the database elements can be downloaded to Excel.

1. It would be helpful if the reviewer of actions has access to the latest thinking and activities of each group. This would have precluded a number of actions for the groups to work on due to the activity already being under consideration.

2. Responses to the actions were not consistent within each group. It is important to set an early framework for the expectations and degree of response to each action. For example- some closed actions without comments, others detailed at least a reason why the action was closed.

## Recommendation
The use of a website and toll free number for public inputs should be considered for all future large accident investigations. The process used by the CAIB should be used as a starting point to document this process. Consideration should be given to documenting this in the Contingency Action Plan (CAP).

## Abstract
Reorganization of an independent investigation board or supporting NASA investigation structure in mid-stream as was required in the case of the Columbia accident is destabilizing and should be avoided when possible.

## Driving Event / Background
The NASA Accident Investigation Team (NAIT) structure was forced to reorganize to be more compatible organizationally with the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB).

## Lesson Learned
Re-organizing an independent investigation board or NASA investigation structures in mid-stream is inherently destabilizing and should be avoided as much as possible.

## Recommendation
- Re-organize the NASA investigative teams into an interface structure consistent with the Board's as soon as independent Board's organization is firmly established (usually within 10 days of startup).

title: Accident Investigations/Web-based Mishap Investigation Support System (MISS) Hardware and Software Infrastructure

sections.abstract: To reduce service outages, a Mishap Investigation Support System hardware and software infrastructure fully tested and ready to support a full range of perceived and anticipated operational needs is required.
sections.driving_event: Several service outages occurred early in the implementation. The first case involved expiration of a software license associated with the Neoterris box (February 14 - 48 hours). The second involved failure of a mother-board on the Dell application server (March 5 - 2 hours). Unknown cause (March 13 - 3 hours). GRC firewall outage (March 18 - 1.5 hours). Inadvertent cable disconnect (April 2 - 15 minutes). A separate hardware issue involved large-file load time from certain web-browser applications. Considering all of the above, from February 13 to May 13, 2003 the system total downtime was approximately 90 hours - this includes 24 hours for scheduled maintenance and upgrades and a “down time penalty” to account for less than optimum performance. This represents an operational availability of approximately 96%.
sections.lesson_learned: As a result of problems encountered, lessons were learned quickly and changes implemented just as quickly. Only limited time was available for system testing and under only limited conditions. The systems engineering life-cycle was compressed into a virtual real-time requirements analysis/design/test/implementation. Lessons include the need for traditional multi-functional, end-to-end testing of all system components over the full range of operational scenarios, including different internet routing and NASA firewall configurations. Again the need exists to have a system ready to support the full range of perceived and anticipated operational needs based on the CAIB experience (see #1).
sections.recommendation:
- Implement multiple web-servers in parallel to maximize system availability for critical web-based applications. Duplicate, to the extent possible, a commercial implementation configuration to ensure greatest possible system reliability.

- Implement the application software on a separate server from the database server. This approach allows routine large file backup activity to take place on the database server without slowing down the web server.

full_text:
# [NASA LLIS #1465] Accident Investigations/Web-based Mishap Investigation Support System (MISS) Hardware and Software Infrastructure
- **Date:** 2003-08-31
- **Organization:** Johnson Space Center (JSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1465

## Abstract
To reduce service outages, a Mishap Investigation Support System hardware and software infrastructure fully tested and ready to support a full range of perceived and anticipated operational needs is required.

## Driving Event / Background
Several service outages occurred early in the implementation. The first case involved expiration of a software license associated with the Neoterris box (February 14 - 48 hours). The second involved failure of a mother-board on the Dell application server (March 5 - 2 hours). Unknown cause (March 13 - 3 hours). GRC firewall outage (March 18 - 1.5 hours). Inadvertent cable disconnect (April 2 - 15 minutes). A separate hardware issue involved large-file load time from certain web-browser applications. Considering all of the above, from February 13 to May 13, 2003 the system total downtime was approximately 90 hours - this includes 24 hours for scheduled maintenance and upgrades and a “down time penalty” to account for less than optimum performance. This represents an operational availability of approximately 96%.

## Lesson Learned
As a result of problems encountered, lessons were learned quickly and changes implemented just as quickly. Only limited time was available for system testing and under only limited conditions. The systems engineering life-cycle was compressed into a virtual real-time requirements analysis/design/test/implementation. Lessons include the need for traditional multi-functional, end-to-end testing of all system components over the full range of operational scenarios, including different internet routing and NASA firewall configurations. Again the need exists to have a system ready to support the full range of perceived and anticipated operational needs based on the CAIB experience (see #1).

## Recommendation
- Implement multiple web-servers in parallel to maximize system availability for critical web-based applications. Duplicate, to the extent possible, a commercial implementation configuration to ensure greatest possible system reliability.

- Implement the application software on a separate server from the database server. This approach allows routine large file backup activity to take place on the database server without slowing down the web server.

title: Accident Investigations/Formulation of an E-mail Retention and Archival Policy for an Independent Investigation

sections.abstract: There is a need for an independent Accident Investigation Board to establish and adopt a formal policy for use, retention, and archiving of investigation-related e-mail to minimize inadvertent transmittal and archiving of sensitive data.
sections.driving_event: The Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) relied upon JSC for e-mail and network access. During a conference call with National Archive and Records Administration (NARA) representatives, JSC IT personnel, and NASA Archivists, the CAIB support staff was advised that all accident related e-mail, including CAIB e-mail accounts, were being backed up and retained as “permanent records” by NASA (See 19 March 2003 memo from Scott N. Pace, NASA HQ re: Ensuring Retention of Mishap-Related E-Mail on NASA Systems). NASA Archivists further stated that they planned to treat all accident related e-mail as records for consideration when submitting archival documents to NARA. This will likely include CAIB e-mail unless the CAIB creates its own e-mail policy and conveys that policy to NASA and NARA.
sections.lesson_learned:
1. During the investigation, the Board did not adopt a formal policy for use, retention, and archiving of investigation e-mail. Consequently, e-mail was used to transmit CAIB generated investigative materials and analysis. Approximately two months after the investigation began, the General Counsel and DOJ/Aspen began researching NASA and NARA e-mail retention and archival policies for guidance.

2.

3. E-mail generated by CAIB members may be subject to NASA e-mail and document retention policies because the applications and data reside on the JSC network
sections.recommendation:
- Adopt a written policy for use, retention, and archiving of investigation-generated e-mail, consistent with the charge and responsibilities of the investigating entity at the beginning of an independent investigation.

- Use an independent e-mail system separate from NASA to minimize inadvertent transmittal and archiving of sensitive data on NASA networks and systems.

- Establish an independent server with a shared file system to reduce the use of e-mail by investigators for file sharing and document transmittal.

- Make E-mail archival policies part of the Contingency Action Plan (CAP)

# [NASA LLIS #1471] Accident Investigations/Formulation of an E-mail Retention and Archival Policy for an Independent Investigation
- **Date:** 2003-08-31
- **Organization:** Johnson Space Center (JSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1471

## Abstract
There is a need for an independent Accident Investigation Board to establish and adopt a formal policy for use, retention, and archiving of investigation-related e-mail to minimize inadvertent transmittal and archiving of sensitive data.

## Driving Event / Background
The Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) relied upon JSC for e-mail and network access. During a conference call with National Archive and Records Administration (NARA) representatives, JSC IT personnel, and NASA Archivists, the CAIB support staff was advised that all accident related e-mail, including CAIB e-mail accounts, were being backed up and retained as “permanent records” by NASA (See 19 March 2003 memo from Scott N. Pace, NASA HQ re: Ensuring Retention of Mishap-Related E-Mail on NASA Systems). NASA Archivists further stated that they planned to treat all accident related e-mail as records for consideration when submitting archival documents to NARA. This will likely include CAIB e-mail unless the CAIB creates its own e-mail policy and conveys that policy to NASA and NARA.

## Lesson Learned
1. During the investigation, the Board did not adopt a formal policy for use, retention, and archiving of investigation e-mail. Consequently, e-mail was used to transmit CAIB generated investigative materials and analysis. Approximately two months after the investigation began, the General Counsel and DOJ/Aspen began researching NASA and NARA e-mail retention and archival policies for guidance.

2.

3. E-mail generated by CAIB members may be subject to NASA e-mail and document retention policies because the applications and data reside on the JSC network

## Recommendation
- Adopt a written policy for use, retention, and archiving of investigation-generated e-mail, consistent with the charge and responsibilities of the investigating entity at the beginning of an independent investigation.

- Use an independent e-mail system separate from NASA to minimize inadvertent transmittal and archiving of sensitive data on NASA networks and systems.

- Establish an independent server with a shared file system to reduce the use of e-mail by investigators for file sharing and document transmittal.

- Make E-mail archival policies part of the Contingency Action Plan (CAP)

title: Accident Investigations/Transition Process from NASA-led to Independent Board-led Investigation

sections.abstract: To avoid team leadership and public image concerns, NASA should recognize that it will not be the lead public investigative entity in a human space flight mishap.
sections.driving_event: Initially, NASA took a strong lead in organizing the Columbia accident investigation only to be required to allow the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) to take the lead causing team leadership and public image concerns.
sections.lesson_learned: NASA should recognize from the beginning that NASA will not be the lead public investigative entity of a manned spaceflight mishap.
sections.recommendation:
- Expand the charters of the NASA Accident Investigation Team (NAIT), the Columbia Task Force (CTF) and the [Columbia] Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) more clearly in the NASA Contingency Action Plan (CAP).

- Replace NASA managers who led the initial phases of the investigation and who were responsible for vehicle and mission operations with senior manager who were not directly involved in day-to-day decisions.

- Assign point(s) of contact for releasing reports (including interim and final), video imagery, public releases, etc., to the public and define these tasks clearly in the CAP. Assigned public affairs representatives from the Board and NASA should manage these tasks closely.

- Identify a standing accident investigation entity on at least an annual basis. This standing team could also participate as needed in the training simulations, at least annually.

## Abstract

## Driving Event / Background
Initially, NASA took a strong lead in organizing the Columbia accident investigation only to be required to allow the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) to take the lead causing team leadership and public image concerns.

## Lesson Learned
NASA should recognize from the beginning that NASA will not be the lead public investigative entity of a manned spaceflight mishap.

## Recommendation
- Expand the charters of the NASA Accident Investigation Team (NAIT), the Columbia Task Force (CTF) and the [Columbia] Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) more clearly in the NASA Contingency Action Plan (CAP).

- Assign point(s) of contact for releasing reports (including interim and final), video imagery, public releases, etc., to the public and define these tasks clearly in the CAP. Assigned public affairs representatives from the Board and NASA should manage these tasks closely.

- Identify a standing accident investigation entity on at least an annual basis. This standing team could also participate as needed in the training simulations, at least annually.

title: Accident Investigations/Independent Server/Local Area Network (LAN) for Investigation Support

sections.abstract: Late establishment of an independent database server for use by the Accident Investigation Board prevented maximum utilization of the data storage and searching features by board members and investigators.
sections.driving_event: To make information readily available to investigators and members, the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) used existing JSC computers, networks, and communications infrastructure resident in Regents Park III. However, to remain independent, the CAIB concluded that all CAIB generated work product and data be housed on a server, connected to the JSC network, but exclusively managed and administered by CAIB IT support staff. Consequently, an independent CAIB Database Server was deployed approximately six weeks into the investigation and authorized users were granted access to independently store, view, and share files.
sections.lesson_learned:
1. The independent CAIB Database Server provided a resource for storing documents and databases containing privileged and sensitive data.

2.

3. Investigators stored CAIB documents under shared and personal folders on the Server. This permitted data to be backed up and stored off-site for disaster recovery purposes, and allowed users to share files without relying upon JSC e-mail.

4. As a result of the server not being deployed until six weeks into the investigation, CAIB members and investigators did not utilize the data storage and searching features of the CAIB Database Server to the maximum extent possible.
sections.recommendation:
- Set up an independent server at the outset of an investigation for sensitive and privileged data. This will permit controlled access to sensitive and privileged documents and databases.

- Default map users to an independent server for backup purposes. Do not rely on individual users to backup their files on hard drives (i.e. “my files” or “my documents”) or CDs and diskettes. This will ensure that all material generated by individual investigators is saved to a central server where regular backup tapes are made for disaster recovery purposes.

- **Organization:** Johnson Space Center (JSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1469

## Abstract
Late establishment of an independent database server for use by the Accident Investigation Board prevented maximum utilization of the data storage and searching features by board members and investigators.

## Driving Event / Background
To make information readily available to investigators and members, the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) used existing JSC computers, networks, and communications infrastructure resident in Regents Park III. However, to remain independent, the CAIB concluded that all CAIB generated work product and data be housed on a server, connected to the JSC network, but exclusively managed and administered by CAIB IT support staff. Consequently, an independent CAIB Database Server was deployed approximately six weeks into the investigation and authorized users were granted access to independently store, view, and share files.

## Lesson Learned
1. The independent CAIB Database Server provided a resource for storing documents and databases containing privileged and sensitive data.

2.

3. Investigators stored CAIB documents under shared and personal folders on the Server. This permitted data to be backed up and stored off-site for disaster recovery purposes, and allowed users to share files without relying upon JSC e-mail.

4. As a result of the server not being deployed until six weeks into the investigation, CAIB members and investigators did not utilize the data storage and searching features of the CAIB Database Server to the maximum extent possible.

## Recommendation
- Set up an independent server at the outset of an investigation for sensitive and privileged data. This will permit controlled access to sensitive and privileged documents and databases.

- Default map users to an independent server for backup purposes. Do not rely on individual users to backup their files on hard drives (i.e. “my files” or “my documents”) or CDs and diskettes. This will ensure that all material generated by individual investigators is saved to a central server where regular backup tapes are made for disaster recovery purposes.

title: Accident Investigations/Contingency Action Plan/Personnel Planning

sections.abstract: Because of the need for rapid staff up, NASA should identify in advance basic personnel requirements for support to the NASA Task Force.
sections.driving_event: Personnel requirements for the NASA Task Force were unknown until accident occurred.
sections.lesson_learned: Basic personnel requirements for support to the NASA Task Force should be identified ahead of time at each NASA center.
sections.recommendation:
- Identify and update basic personnel requirements in each Center's emergency action plan at least annually. For this Task Force, the “application/volunteer process” worked well to identify potential candidates after the fact. The Task Force director should have immediate access to this personnel database. The following recommended guidelines can assist the Task Force Director in selecting technical and professional personnel: Process-oriented Self-Initiators requiring little or no direction to accomplish task "Big Picture" individuals who pay attention to detail, but don't get stuck there. Can commit 24/7 time and energy through "start-up phase" (~1 to 2 months) Problem solvers that may not know all the answers, but knows how to get them "Whatever-it-takes attitude" No personnel (civil service or contractor) who were involved in day-to-day shuttle operations or management of the activity in progress when the accident happened.

- Staff up immediately. Part of the stress early on was based on an overwhelming amount of work, and not enough people to do it. People should be pre-identified and known to be on-call. Preplanning can determine the number of people (at different phases in the task), and types of expertise that are required.

- Assign Contingency Response Teams of technical, operational and administrative personnel at all operational Centers. Stagger assigned duties to respond to major and minor incidents.

- Make team building and training part of this permanent team.

sections.abstract: To avoid witness scheduling and pre-hearing preparation legal complications, a specific individual on the Investigation Board staff should propose and coordinate witnesses for public hearings.
sections.driving_event: The Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) conducted approximately ten (10) public hearings. The CAIB, at times, was slow to identify witnesses for Public Hearings causing extensive legal complications in assuring that witness scheduling and pre-hearing preparations were accomplished.
sections.lesson_learned: An accident investigation board should assign a specific individual on the Board staff to propose and coordinate witness for the Public Hearings.
sections.recommendation:
- Request the Board assign the Board's Legal Counsel or other Board staff member to initiate witness identification as early as possible. Witness identification and notification process should include representation by public affairs officer and NASA Task Force legal counsel.

- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1460

## Abstract
To avoid witness scheduling and pre-hearing preparation legal complications, a specific individual on the Investigation Board staff should propose and coordinate witnesses for public hearings.

## Driving Event / Background
The Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) conducted approximately ten (10) public hearings. The CAIB, at times, was slow to identify witnesses for Public Hearings causing extensive legal complications in assuring that witness scheduling and pre-hearing preparations were accomplished.

## Lesson Learned
An accident investigation board should assign a specific individual on the Board staff to propose and coordinate witness for the Public Hearings.

## Recommendation
- Request the Board assign the Board's Legal Counsel or other Board staff member to initiate witness identification as early as possible. Witness identification and notification process should include representation by public affairs officer and NASA Task Force legal counsel.

- Do not present or imply privileged information in Public Hearings.

- Recommend that the Board Chairman establish the ground rule that formal interviewees will not be called as public witnesses at Public Hearings.

title: Accident Investigations/Minutes Taking Support to Board

sections.abstract: The hiring of safety and mission assurance/engineering personnel, not skilled in minutes taking, to support the Investigation Board provided unsatisfactory results. Subsequent hiring of skilled minutes-takers resolved the problem.
sections.driving_event: The Columbia Task Force (CTF) was tasked with hiring minutes-taking support for the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB). The CTF hired safety and mission assurance/engineering personnel from The Aerospace Corporation to do this task. These personnel were not skilled in minutes taking and regressed to a process of audio recording of board deliberations. The Aerospace personnel then provided quasi-transcripts of these tapes as minutes. The products were not delivered in a timely fashion (sometimes weeks after the meeting) for review by the CAIB executive secretary and were, for the most part, of very poor quality. Tracking of meeting minutes was also problematic with the Aerospace personnel. This problem was remedied finally by the hiring of a skilled minutes-taking person who produced a quality set of minutes within hours of the board meeting.
sections.lesson_learned: To support the minutes taking requirements of an accident investigation board in a professional manner, the hiring of non-skilled personnel to do this task is totally unacceptable.
sections.recommendation:
- Hire professional meeting minute takers at the outset of the investigation

- Add this requirement to the Contingency Action Plan (CAP)

# [NASA LLIS #1477] Accident Investigations/Minutes Taking Support to Board
- **Date:** 2003-08-31
- **Organization:** Johnson Space Center (JSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1477

## Abstract
The hiring of safety and mission assurance/engineering personnel, not skilled in minutes taking, to support the Investigation Board provided unsatisfactory results. Subsequent hiring of skilled minutes-takers resolved the problem.

## Driving Event / Background
The Columbia Task Force (CTF) was tasked with hiring minutes-taking support for the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB). The CTF hired safety and mission assurance/engineering personnel from The Aerospace Corporation to do this task. These personnel were not skilled in minutes taking and regressed to a process of audio recording of board deliberations. The Aerospace personnel then provided quasi-transcripts of these tapes as minutes. The products were not delivered in a timely fashion (sometimes weeks after the meeting) for review by the CAIB executive secretary and were, for the most part, of very poor quality. Tracking of meeting minutes was also problematic with the Aerospace personnel. This problem was remedied finally by the hiring of a skilled minutes-taking person who produced a quality set of minutes within hours of the board meeting.

## Lesson Learned
To support the minutes taking requirements of an accident investigation board in a professional manner, the hiring of non-skilled personnel to do this task is totally unacceptable.

## Recommendation
- Hire professional meeting minute takers at the outset of the investigation

- Add this requirement to the Contingency Action Plan (CAP)

title: Accident Investigations/Investigator Tool Kit/Digital Cameras

sections.abstract: A supply of both digital and film cameras should be immediately available by NASA to the Investigation Board.
sections.driving_event: During the Columbia accident investigation, the issue of whether to use digital or film cameras was never settled. Board use of digital cameras was expensive purchase item, especially in the procurement of SmartMedia Cards, Memory Stix, etc. On the other hand, waiting for photo lab services was inefficient.
sections.lesson_learned: For accident investigations, an initial supply of both digital and film cameras should be made available to the Board immediately by the NASA centers photo laboratory or imagery department.
sections.recommendation:
- Set up an agreement with the Center Photo Lab to minimize film-processing delays, and provide and process cameras (including disposables), batteries and film with overnight processing. (At JSC, assign overall responsibility to the JSC Imagery Working Group.)

- Have a limited number of digital cameras available at startup for checkout by Board.

During the Columbia accident investigation, the issue of whether to use digital or film cameras was never settled. Board use of digital cameras was expensive purchase item, especially in the procurement of SmartMedia Cards, Memory Stix, etc. On the other hand, waiting for photo lab services was inefficient.

For accident investigations, an initial supply of both digital and film cameras should be made available to the Board immediately by the NASA centers photo laboratory or imagery department.

title: Accident Investigations/Software Tool Selection

sections.abstract: Difficulties with the single software tool selected to support the Columbia accident investigation point to a need for a functional requirements analysis by a team experienced in the IT requirements of a large-scale mishap investigation prior to tool selection.
sections.driving_event:
The main driver for software tool selection to support the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) was the requirement for a single tool with remote access capability and strong security to protect sensitive mishap investigation data. Without defining a clear set of functional requirements in advance, one tool was chosen to be all things to all people [collaborative environment (i.e., portal for group calendar & file sharing, announcements, links, etc.), action tracking database, library management, data archive). As a result, after significant start up investment was made to get off the ground with the selected tool, subsequent unidentified requirements required custom software engineering, causing delays in functional capability and frustrations for investigation staff members. In addition, the selected tool was set up in an untested environment involving additional layers of network security that interfered with the normal operation of the tool and
complicated/delayed fixing problems that arose.
sections.lesson_learned: A functional requirements analysis should be performed prior to software tool selection, and this analysis needs to be performed by a team of people experienced in the IT requirements of a large-scale mishap investigation. In addition, clear IT security requirements need to be identified in advance of tool selection to ensure appropriate safeguarding of sensitive data.
sections.recommendation:
- Integrate a set of individual tools into a CAP system that is vetted and available prior to the start of the investigation. Widespread, long-term buy-in and use by the investigation and support teams of a single on-line software solution for configuration management, electronic library capability, action tracking database, and document search & retrieval may not be attainable.

- Avoid tools that would not be familiar to investigation staff ahead of time, or tools that would be overly complex requiring steep learning curves. The tools should be easy to use and easy to learn. By vetting the CAP system of tools in advance, problems with IT availability, access control, and security issues can be avoided.

- **Date:** 2003-08-31
- **Organization:** Johnson Space Center (JSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1466

## Abstract
Difficulties with the single software tool selected to support the Columbia accident investigation point to a need for a functional requirements analysis by a team experienced in the IT requirements of a large-scale mishap investigation prior to tool selection.

## Driving Event / Background
The main driver for software tool selection to support the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) was the requirement for a single tool with remote access capability and strong security to protect sensitive mishap investigation data. Without defining a clear set of functional requirements in advance, one tool was chosen to be all things to all people [collaborative environment (i.e., portal for group calendar & file sharing, announcements, links, etc.), action tracking database, library management, data archive). As a result, after significant start up investment was made to get off the ground with the selected tool, subsequent unidentified requirements required custom software engineering, causing delays in functional capability and frustrations for investigation staff members. In addition, the selected tool was set up in an untested environment involving additional layers of network security that interfered with the normal operation of the tool and
complicated/delayed fixing problems that arose.

## Lesson Learned
A functional requirements analysis should be performed prior to software tool selection, and this analysis needs to be performed by a team of people experienced in the IT requirements of a large-scale mishap investigation. In addition, clear IT security requirements need to be identified in advance of tool selection to ensure appropriate safeguarding of sensitive data.

## Recommendation
- Integrate a set of individual tools into a CAP system that is vetted and available prior to the start of the investigation. Widespread, long-term buy-in and use by the investigation and support teams of a single on-line software solution for configuration management, electronic library capability, action tracking database, and document search & retrieval may not be attainable.

- Avoid tools that would not be familiar to investigation staff ahead of time, or tools that would be overly complex requiring steep learning curves. The tools should be easy to use and easy to learn. By vetting the CAP system of tools in advance, problems with IT availability, access control, and security issues can be avoided.

title: Accident Investigations/Off-site Storage of Investigative Data and Evidence

sections.abstract: A small appliance fire at the Investigation Board's facility pointed to the need for a process to duplicate and secure unique electronic data at an off-site facility to provide disaster recovery protection.
sections.driving_event: The Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) generated unique and irreplaceable documents, data, and media that were housed at the Regent Park III facility. On Sunday, 30 March 2003, a small appliance fire occurred at the facility. The local fire department responded to the call and promptly secured the area. This event alerted the staff of the importance of protecting unique and irreplaceable documents, data, and media.
sections.lesson_learned:
1. At the beginning of the investigation, unique electronic data such as interview and public hearing tapes were not duplicated and stored off-site. Mid-way through the investigation, document management staff began duplicating this media and delivering it to a secure off-site storage facility. This process provided disaster recovery protection that had not previously existed.

2.

3. A backup of data stored by the investigators on JSC and personal computers was left to the individuals to perform on diskettes and CDs. These backups, if performed at all, were typically stored on-site in close proximity to user desktops. Consequently, if the fire had caused severe damage to the facility, this data may have been lost forever.
sections.recommendation:
- Develop a process for duplicating and safely storing irreplaceable documents, data, and media generated by the investigation team at the outset of a major investigation. This will ensure that such data are recoverable if a disaster should occur at the facility.

- Map investigators to an independent server to preserve data, rather than rely on individual hard drives which may not be backed up. This will ensure that all material generated by individual investigators is located on a central server where nightly backups are performed and tapes are stored at a secure off-site storage facility for disaster recovery purposes.

- Make data storage policies part of the Contingency Action Plan (CAP)

# [NASA LLIS #1472] Accident Investigations/Off-site Storage of Investigative Data and Evidence
- **Date:** 2003-08-31
- **Organization:** Johnson Space Center (JSC)
- **Mission Directorate:** Human Exploration and Operations
- **Source URL:** https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1472

## Abstract
A small appliance fire at the Investigation Board's facility pointed to the need for a process to duplicate and secure unique electronic data at an off-site facility to provide disaster recovery protection.

## Driving Event / Background
The Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) generated unique and irreplaceable documents, data, and media that were housed at the Regent Park III facility. On Sunday, 30 March 2003, a small appliance fire occurred at the facility. The local fire department responded to the call and promptly secured the area. This event alerted the staff of the importance of protecting unique and irreplaceable documents, data, and media.

## Lesson Learned
1. At the beginning of the investigation, unique electronic data such as interview and public hearing tapes were not duplicated and stored off-site. Mid-way through the investigation, document management staff began duplicating this media and delivering it to a secure off-site storage facility. This process provided disaster recovery protection that had not previously existed.

2.

3. A backup of data stored by the investigators on JSC and personal computers was left to the individuals to perform on diskettes and CDs. These backups, if performed at all, were typically stored on-site in close proximity to user desktops. Consequently, if the fire had caused severe damage to the facility, this data may have been lost forever.

## Recommendation
- Develop a process for duplicating and safely storing irreplaceable documents, data, and media generated by the investigation team at the outset of a major investigation. This will ensure that such data are recoverable if a disaster should occur at the facility.

- Map investigators to an independent server to preserve data, rather than rely on individual hard drives which may not be backed up. This will ensure that all material generated by individual investigators is located on a central server where nightly backups are performed and tapes are stored at a secure off-site storage facility for disaster recovery purposes.

- Make data storage policies part of the Contingency Action Plan (CAP)

title: Accident Investigations/Configuration Management (CM)/Personnel Issues

sections.abstract: Pre-planning to include set of draft processes for data and configuration management developed in advance and ready for implementation might improve accident investigation start-up efficiency.
sections.driving_event: For the Columbia accident investigation, personnel and processes were not in place to assist in startup. Although heroic efforts on the part of key CM personnel minimized the number of individual problems, better planning might have improved startup efficiency.
sections.lesson_learned: Have a set of draft processes ready to implement for data management and configuration management.
sections.recommendation:
- Include CM processes defined for the Task Force as an initial reference in the NASA Contingency Action Plan (CAP). Revising a previous or pre-established process will be easier than starting from scratch and the Board will run more smoothly as well.

- Ensure that adequate CM personnel resources are available at startup.

- Use these guidelines for CM personnel requirements (EPs): (1) Action Trackers (Start-up: 4, Peak: 8, Std Ops: 4) (2) Data Entry and Librarian/Archivist: 5, Library function includes expertise on scanning and archiving. Bring in someone familiar with library science to assist with the document management function. Create a library group. (3) IT Support/Processes (Start-up: 3 Database Administrators: 2 (Prime/Back-up): Individual should have knowledge of existing NASA action tracking AND document management databases (4) Meeting Coordinator/Minute Recorder: 3

title: Accident Investigations/Database/Collaborative Tool PBMA (Process Based Mission Assurance)

sections.abstract: Unfamiliar database tools cause delays and use of multiple systems cause additional delay and tax the IT support staff.
sections.driving_event: Columbia accident investigation personnel were required to learn database tools with which they were unfamiliar, adding inefficiencies in Board and Task Force startup time.
sections.lesson_learned: Database tools that most people are unfamiliar with will cause delays in initiating investigation. Multiple systems, implemented to satisfy specific needs, cause additional startup delay and tax the time of IT support staff.
sections.recommendation:
- Develop an appendix/annex to the Contingency Action Plan (CAP) and annually update the definition of critical tool requirements based on established selection criteria. A criteria-based tool selection process was not used resulting in a tool being procured whose capabilities were not fully understood by the primary Board and TF users.

- Avoid real time, verbal, or informal tool requirements as they will be treated by the developers as requirements that they can freely interpret and make judgments on without consultation with users, ultimately resulting in product deliveries that do not meet expectations.

- Concentrate, when possible, on database systems that local Center IT and CM personnel are familiar with to minimize coordination, expedite implementation, and reduce potential system/transmission interface issues.

- Recognize that all data from the investigation will be archived.

- Do not permit contractors to define and manage the Board and Task Force's IT requirements. This becomes a financial driver for them.

- Separate database administrator function and general task force IT support (SRs, user configuration set-up, etc.).

- Identify a candidate database and data management tools that could be implemented quickly. The data management tool and approach should meet the anticipated availability, security, firewalls, capacity, and on-site/off-site access requirements for supporting a major mishap investigation without significant modification or development.

- Make a data management tool/approach a part of the NASA CAP, and review annually at a minimum.

- Avoid having the same information in too many places, as data will diverge.

- Brief the Board Chairman and Board members upon arrival regarding their electronic tools and advise them not to bring in new systems to be force-fit with systems initially laid in by NASA IT administrator.

title: Accident Investigations/Investigation Organizer (IO)/IO Standard and Ad Hoc Report Capability

sections.abstract: A combination of factors, including lack of time by investigators to search through "Investigation Organizer" links on a personal computer and the tool's lack of a logic tree report capability severely limited its use.
sections.driving_event: Investigation Organizer (IO) - is a Web-based pre-decisional collaborative information management and modeling tool designed to support mishap investigation teams. IO provides a centralized information repository that can be used by a distributed team of investigators to store digital products relevant to an ongoing mishap investigation. IO was used by the Columbia Accident Investigation Board (CAIB) to connect data from various sources to the storyboard that the Board used to guide its investigation. Documents, digital photographs/video, links were uploaded to the IO database to support the engineering/management investigation logic tree. IO however did not have a capability to provide printed output (reports) for the investigators. Investigators characterized IO as a “one way street” with data going in, and no value to their activities coming out.
sections.lesson_learned: Investigation Organizer (IO) was touted supporting the CAIB's engineering/management investigation logic tree. It was believed that the extensive linking of data gathered across the groups would prevent “stove piping” of data and allow investigators to cross-reference information in support of their findings and recommendations. A combination of factors, including lack of time by investigators to search through the IO links on a personal computer and IO's lack of logic tree report capability, severely limited use of the system by other than personnel keying in IO data.
sections.recommendation:
The IO Project at ARC must:

- Develop a set of standard and ad hoc reports for use by investigators. Particular attention should be given to logic trees and lists of supporting data. While it is useful for investigators of major mishaps to spend time behind a personal computer sorting through various logic trees and their associated linked documents, their time to accomplish this is very limited. This leads to the rendering of IO to a data archiving tool and not an investigative tool.
